Fey and Ramsay give examples: “the way they were taught in graduate school, their cultural and social background, and their ‘life experiences.’” Then even with shared starting beliefs the same event can lead people who reason well to different conclusions. They give a worked example in which both countries know the same event has occurred and still put different chances on victory.69

Second, they say the real difference between the frameworks is not whether beliefs can differ but whether war can happen. The shared framework rules out sides that reason well taking up wasteful bets, such as war. This holds when everyone knows someone is going to lose and some alternative to fighting would waste nothing.

Third, without the discipline of shared starting beliefs, all that is left is to say that nations fight because they began with different beliefs. “This is the informational equivalent to a tautological argument that nations fight wars because they like to.” They also ask what different starting beliefs could be, if not differences in information. If they are not “the product of education, culture, or life experience,” what do they represent? In the published summary of their reply, Smith and Stam (2006) call their approach a useful way into the puzzle they set out to explore. That puzzle is how sides that reason well but hold different beliefs might settle their disagreements in war.70

Fey and Ramsay’s 2007 paper is more careful than the sentence quoted earlier suggests. In the body they consider countries that may hold different starting beliefs that information does not explain. Some pairs of such beliefs, they write, may lead to war even when both play their best. That is Smith and Stam’s case, conceded. What carries over to different starting beliefs is a set of limits. They bound how far the beliefs may differ before war becomes possible.

The paper also proves that the two ways of departing from the standard model can be swapped for each other. Take a game with shared starting beliefs and limited reasoning (reasoning that does not use the evidence fully). It is “strategically equivalent” to a game with full reasoning and different starting beliefs, and the reverse (Figure 10). So “the choice of which direction to push when departing from traditional rationality assumptions is largely a matter of taste.” Their objection to the different-starting-beliefs framework, then, is not that it is wrong. It is that the framework can state when their result fails, but cannot say where the different beliefs come from.71

On the book’s reading, that equivalence sets the terms for everything below, and it cuts three ways.

First, the evidence cannot crown a winner. Any pattern of behavior that different starting beliefs with full reasoning can produce, shared starting beliefs with limited reasoning can produce too. So no record of what disputing sides do can tell the two apart.

The record can still weigh against the pair the transparency remedies rely on: shared starting beliefs together with full reasoning. It weighs against that pair wherever beliefs are known to each other and still do not move. It cannot refute the pair. A reader from the shared tradition can put what is left down to hidden information no one has observed.

That escape has a limit. Under Aumann’s conditions, once updated beliefs are common knowledge, hidden information cannot rescue a disagreement. The escape works in only two places:

  • where no one has observed what each side can and cannot tell apart;
  • and where each side knows the other’s beliefs without those beliefs being common knowledge, which would also require each to know that the other knows, and so on.

The book needs only the weaker claim, that the record weighs against the pair. That is enough, because the remedies assume both halves of it.72

Second, for this book’s case, the equivalence changes the form of Fey and Ramsay’s strongest charge. It does not dissolve it. They ask what different starting beliefs are, if not “the product of education, culture, or life experience.” For a machine, the answer has a record. It is the text the machine learns from, the goal it is taught to pursue, and the method used to teach it. Someone chose each of them.

The text is the machine’s life experience. A reader from the shared tradition will treat it as information, as Fey and Ramsay would. The goal and the method fix how evidence is weighed. By Fey and Ramsay’s own equivalence, that reads equally well as limited reasoning or as a different starting belief. For states, the tradition lacked an account of where beliefs come from. For a machine, that account is documented (below, and Chapter 11). Robin Hanson’s argument, taken up below, is that a known origin gives a mind that reasons well grounds to correct its starting beliefs. That is the shared tradition’s point.73

Third, the equivalence leaves the shared tradition a point the book accepts. Free choice of starting beliefs can be made to explain anything. So every claim below that rests on different beliefs is held to a discipline. The beliefs must be stated, must be the kind that evidence could move, and must be shown in the record rather than assumed.74

Harsanyi’s own framing shows what the dispute is about. In both traditions the sides reason well and learn by the rules of probability. They differ on one thing: whether two minds that have seen all the same evidence must end in the same place. The shared tradition says yes, and treats every remaining disagreement as a sign that something is still hidden. The other says no, and treats some remaining disagreement as a fact about the minds.75

If no evidence can tell the two traditions apart, why does it matter which one we use?

Because they recommend different things. By Fey and Ramsay’s own equivalence, the record cannot say whether to call a lasting disagreement “different starting beliefs” or “limited reasoning.” For the book’s purposes the name does not matter, because the remedies that fail are the same under either. The shared tradition can still blame a lasting disagreement on hidden information no one has seen. The cost is that the theory then predicts nothing about when the sides will agree. The book takes that cost as its reason to work from the different-starting-beliefs side wherever the two traditions part.76

People can hear the same evidence and still disagree. The jury is the ordinary case. Twelve people hear one record under one set of instructions and are told to agree. In a steady share of cases they do not. The National Center for State Courts found hung-jury rates “with significant variations among jurisdictions,” averaging 6.2 percent in state felony trials. It also found a federal criminal rate averaging 2.5 percent from 1980 through 1997. “Consistent themes of weak evidence, problematic deliberations, and jurors’ perceptions of unfairness were present in hung juries.” In mock juries, the chance of a hung jury rises with jury size in close cases. Across four decades of studies, the first vote predicts the verdict.77

The jury is an illustration here, not a test. A reader from the shared tradition is entitled to four other readings of it:

  • A verdict is not an updated belief. “Reasonable doubt” is a threshold set by how bad each kind of mistake would be. That is a matter of what jurors want, so jurors with identical beliefs can still hang.
  • The record is shared, but each juror’s background is not, so “the same information” holds for the evidence and not for everything each juror knows.
  • Deliberation is strategic, and it does not run the repeated truthful announcing that coming to agreement requires.
  • And by the equivalence above, limited reasoning explains whatever different starting beliefs explain.

The jury does show one thing. The one institution built to force agreement on one record fails at a known rate. The law does not answer that failure by making jurors agree. It answers with a decision rule, a burden of proof, a definition of evidence, and an exit: the mistrial.78

Lawsuits have the same two-tradition structure. George Priest and Benjamin Klein (1984) built the “divergent expectations” model. In it, cases go to trial because each party is optimistic about a different outcome. Joel Waldfogel (1998) tested it against the hidden-information account. He found the pattern of trial rates and plaintiff win rates consistent with different expectations, not with hidden information. Hidden information was visible mainly early in a case. The legal process sorts out the hidden-information disputes first and leaves honest disagreement for trial.79

Shared evidence can widen a gap as well as close it. Charles Lord, Lee Ross and Mark Lepper (1979) found that exposing opposed groups “to an identical body of relevant empirical evidence may be not a narrowing of disagreement but rather an increase in polarization.” Dan Kahan and colleagues (2012) found that people were most divided over climate risk among those most skilled with numbers.

Some of what looks like disagreement about the world is disagreement about method. Raphael Silberzahn and colleagues gave 29 teams, 61 analysts in all, one set of data and one question. Their estimates of the effect ranged from 0.89 to 2.93 (in odds-ratio units, a scale on which 1 means no effect). “Neither analysts’ prior beliefs about the effect of interest nor their level of expertise readily explained the variation in the outcomes of the analyses.”

Tyler Cowen and Robin Hanson (2004) reviewed the work on agreement. They conclude that “honest truth-seeking agents with common priors should not knowingly disagree,” and that “Typical disagreement seems explainable by a combination of random belief influences and by priors that tell each person that he reasons better than others.”80

Months of paid argument left forecasters of AI risk far apart. On the question this book is about, the real-world case closest to Aumann’s conditions is the Existential-Risk Persuasion Tournament. It ran from June to October 2022. It gathered “80 specialists on long-run existential risks to humanity” and “89 seasoned forecasters with a track record of predictive accuracy on shorter-run questions.” It gave them months to argue and paid them to persuade one another.

“The median expert predicted a 20% chance of catastrophe and a 6% chance of human extinction by 2100,” while “The median superforecaster predicted a 9% chance of catastrophe and a 1% chance of extinction.” (The median is the middle answer when all the answers are lined up from lowest to highest. The superforecasters are the seasoned forecasters.) Among the report’s key findings: “Few minds were changed during the XPT, even among the most active participants, and despite monetary incentives for persuading others,” and “Although the biggest area of long-run disagreement was the probability of extinction due to AI, there were surprisingly high levels of agreement on 45 shorter-run indicators.” The authors name the puzzle: “why did rational forecasters, incentivized by the XPT to persuade each other, not converge after months of debate and the exchange of millions of words and thousands of forecasts?”81

A follow-up ran for eight weeks. It put eleven “AI skeptics,” nine of them superforecasters and two of them experts in the field, together with eleven “AI concerned” experts. “At the beginning of the project, the median ‘skeptic’ forecasted a 0.10% chance of existential catastrophe due to AI by 2100, and the median ‘concerned’ participant forecasted a 25% chance. By the end, these numbers were 0.12% and 20% respectively, though many participants did not attribute their updates to arguments made during the project.”

The authors found moderate evidence against one explanation: that the groups stayed apart because they engaged too little or misunderstood each other. The skeptics’ median was 80 hours of work. Most of the disagreement about AI risk by 2100 is not explained by questions that will be answered by 2030. Take one of the top points of disagreement they identified. Once it is settled in 2030, it is expected to close the gap in beliefs by about 5 percent. That is about 1.2 percentage points of the 22.7-point gap for the typical pair.

One finding bears directly on remedies: “the skeptic group typically did not find theoretical arguments for AI risk persuasive but would update their views based on real-world demonstrations of dangerous AI capabilities that verify existing theoretical arguments.” Institutions can narrow the spread, though not to zero. In the IARPA forecasting tournament, “probability training, team collaboration, and tracking improved both calibration and resolution” of forecasts. Among other things, the forecasters’ stated confidence came to match more closely how often they were right.82

What does all this settle? Less than either side would like, and exactly what the book needs. The tournaments did not meet Aumann’s conditions:

  • the participants’ updated beliefs were not common knowledge in his sense;
  • the questions are not settled until 2100;
  • the groups were chosen to differ;
  • and the rewards were modest.

So the record does not show that people who reason well and share starting beliefs failed to agree. It shows that able, engaged, paid people who traded arguments and forecasts for months stayed apart. That weighs against the pair the transparency remedies assume, shared starting beliefs and full reasoning, without refuting it. The participants’ beliefs fell short of common knowledge. So a reader from the shared tradition can move the difference into hidden information no one has observed. The cost, as the fold-out above notes, is that the theory then predicts nothing about when the sides will agree.83

The traditions agree on the end and differ on the path. Hold the sides, what they want, their costs and the shift in power fixed. Does the size or the kind of danger change with the tradition? The answer runs through the mechanisms of Part I. The traditions agree about where things end. They disagree about how a conflict starts, how long it lasts, the path it takes, and the remedy.84

What removes the cause of war. Under shared starting beliefs, the cause is something hidden. Revelation removes it: signals that cost something to send, checking, the price leaders pay at home for backing down in public, and battles. Once beliefs are common knowledge, the Fey–Ramsay reasoning does the rest. A side’s willingness to fight tells the other that it has misjudged, and the war ends before it starts.

Under different starting beliefs, revealing what is hidden is not enough, because the sides already know each other’s beliefs. The cause goes away only if beliefs come together through public signals that both read the same way. Nothing guarantees that. The Smith–Stam battles bring beliefs together because the true chance of victory is fixed and every battle is a fresh draw from it. Rival theories of what makes a side strong can pull apart on the same news. Acemoglu and colleagues show that leftover uncertainty about how the evidence is produced can keep beliefs apart for good.85

For the machine, one consequence follows. The book judges that measures of this kind are needed under both traditions, wherever the hidden-information case of the last section arises. They include transparency, checking, and tools that read what a machine has learned inside. The judgment is firm for some measure of this kind and less firm for each of the three. A cheaper route to revelation, if one were shown, would change it. Taken alone, these measures are enough under neither tradition, since broken promises are the other cause.

Under the second tradition they are not enough even when complete. A machine and its overseers could see the same test results and disagree about what they mean for a contest. Austria and Prussia read the lessons of the needle gun differently in just this way. Seeing the machine’s theory does not move anyone’s theory. Smith and Stam already assume the beliefs are common knowledge, and war still happens. The value of tools that read what a machine has learned inside lies elsewhere. They show what to teach again. They also reach the layer where a trained-in belief lives: the settings training leaves inside the machine (Chapter 11).86

How long fighting lasts, and how it ends. Under shared starting beliefs, war ends when the sides have learned what was hidden. Their expectations then come together, as Slantchev’s principle says. In the Smith–Stam model, beliefs also come together. The article states, without proof, that the date by which a settlement is guaranteed moves later as fighting gets cheaper. The book’s computer runs show the last battle moving the same way at five levels of cost (appendix).87

The 2004 model gives both sides the same cost per battle. The machine case does not. So the book extends the model to unequal costs and computes it for one baseline, described in the fold-out below. In that computation, as in the paper:

  • the chance of winning each battle does not change as the war goes on (one variant in the appendix lets it rise with the machine’s lead);
  • both sides learn at the same rate;
  • and the loser survives.

Nothing is hidden, every battle is public, and each side judges what lies ahead by its own updated beliefs. The book finds best play at every step by working back from the end, with tie rules the appendix states. It proves that, whatever the costs, every pattern of best play gives both sides the same values and the same terms at every settlement. Wherever the side making the offer is not exactly torn, every pattern also gives the same choice to settle or fight. It also proves that the deadline is finite, as long as at least one side pays a cost for each battle. It proves several of the deadline’s properties as well.88

In that play, a side offered a deal accepts it if, and only if, the deal is worth at least what turning the offer down is worth. That value counts the offers still to come. It is never below what the side expects from fighting on until one side is beaten (appendix). The paper’s printed figures differ from its text, for a reason that goes to the first author before this book states it. The computation uses the text’s definitions.89

What is the “baseline” in the book’s computer runs?

It uses the 2004 paper’s own running example. Ten forts stand in a line. Forts are the military assets a side needs to keep fighting. The war starts in the middle. Each battle moves the front one fort, and a side is beaten when it has lost them all. The prize is worth 30. The machine starts out expecting to win two battles in three. The humans start out expecting it to win one in three. Each side’s cost per battle is stated as a share of the prize. So “1 of 30” is a cost of about 3 percent of the prize for every battle. Each case is solved twice: once with the machine making every offer, once with the humans making every offer. Taking turns is a separate game. Unless stated otherwise, each battle is in fact an even chance. So in the baseline the machine fights more cheaply but is no stronger. All the numbers that come out are computed for this one set of numbers, not proved.90

Does the book say the 2004 paper got something wrong?

Yes, about the rule for accepting offers. The paper has the side that answers accept any offer worth at least what fighting on until one side is beaten would give it. The book proves that this rule is not that side’s best answer in the paper’s own example. Turning an offer down keeps open the chance of better offers later. The appendix (“The correction of the 2004 paper” and “What reproduces, and what does not”) sets out the proof and which of the paper’s results survive, and in what form. It also reports which of the paper’s printed figures do not come out of the definitions in its text. It reports, too, that a computation that reproduces the printed figures has been found. That computation does not establish how the paper’s own figures were computed. It goes to the first author before this book states it.91

The costs enter twice: once in the date by which a deal must come, and once in the range of deals.

First, cheap fighting does not make the war endless. The front moves at random along a line of limited length. So it is certain that one side will in time be beaten. Nor does a machine that fights for free remove settlement by learning. It delays it. The date by which beliefs force a deal is set by the two sides’ costs added together. The reason is that the side making the offer takes whatever is left over from a deal. So it bears the other side’s cost of waiting too, as a higher demand tomorrow. As the machine’s cost falls to zero, the human cost alone sets that date. This holds whichever side makes the offers, and also when the sides take turns.92

The book’s computer runs show what this means in numbers, for the baseline and not as a proof (Figure 53). Say the humans pay 1 of 30 per battle. When the machine pays the same, the deadline is 6 battles, a deadline the appendix proves finite. With the machine fighting for free, it moves to 18 battles when the machine makes the offers and to 12 when the humans do. Suppose the machine is in fact much the stronger, winning 80 percent of battles or more. The deadline does not change, but it is rarely reached. The war ends in about 3 to 8 battles on average.

How the war ends depends on who makes the offers. In the baseline, when the machine makes the offers, the war ends mostly with the humans’ surrender. When the humans make the offers, it ends with a deal that leaves them less than 2 of 30. Or take a human cost of 0.5 of 30, with the machine underrating its own strength (it starts out expecting to win two battles in three). Then the war ends more and more often with the machine’s decisive victory. The two sides’ starting beliefs may be far apart, as in the appendix’s case of stronger disagreement at that cost. Then that victory comes before any deal exists.93

Second, the range of deals does not vanish (Figure 12). Take Fearon’s account, for a war that is one costly gamble. There, the range of deals both sides would take over fighting is the two sides’ costs added together. For example, imagine a prize worth 100, a war each side expects to win half the time, and a war that costs each side 10. Fighting is worth an expected 40 to each side, so any split that gives each side at least 40 beats fighting. The deals run from 40 and 60 to 60 and 40: a range of 20, which is the two costs added together. (These numbers are made up to show the idea; they are not the book’s.)94

In the 2004 model the range is different, and it changes as the war goes on. Take each side’s cost per battle times the number of battles it expects remain, and add the two together. Then subtract the two sides’ joint optimism. To get it, add each side’s own expected chance of winning the war, and see how far the total exceeds a sure thing. Take that share of the prize.

For example, suppose each side thought it had a 70 percent chance of winning. Their hopes would add to 140 percent, 40 points more than certainty. The expected costs of fighting on must then outweigh 40 percent of the prize before any deal can satisfy both. (Again, an illustration, not the book’s numbers.) The paper’s first proposition, extended to unequal costs, can be put in words. With the machine fighting for free, a deal exists only once the humans’ cost term covers that joint optimism. The battles shrink that optimism.95

This is a fixed benchmark. A deal needs it, but it does not ensure one. Nor is it the range of offers actually accepted in play (appendix). Apply that benchmark to the model’s baseline. No deal exists at the start for a human cost below about 4 percent of the prize per battle. Whether the war is then settled or fought out turns on one ratio. It is the humans’ expected cost of fighting to the end, as a share of what they expect to win. The baseline shows two regimes.96

Above a ratio of roughly a quarter, settlement before the war is decided is likelier than not. It comes on coercive terms. The humans can expect about 2 of 30 when the machine makes the offers, and 6 to 10 of 30 when they make them. They give up everything only along paths of the war that run against them. Or they give it up from the outset, at a cost above about 10 percent of the prize per battle.

A settlement, as the model counts it, includes such a surrender, in which the humans accept nothing. Take the machine fighting for free and making the offers, at even chances. The chance that the humans end by accepting nothing is zero at a cost of 0.4 of 30 per battle. It is 23 percent at 0.5, 28 percent at 1, and 63 percent at 2. When the humans make the offers, they never surrender.97

Below a quarter, the deadline lies beyond the war’s natural length, and the forts decide. In the baseline, that means a human cost below about 1.3 percent of the prize per battle. The quarter is this baseline’s mark, not a boundary derived to hold in general. The human cost per battle sets both regimes, and the historical record measures it badly. Of the costs in one well-known war game (Bueno de Mesquita and Lalman’s), Curtis Signorino (1999) judged such data “difficult, if not impossible, to obtain.” The regimes also take each battle to be an even chance, a value the paper does not name. So the machine in them fights more cheaply but is no stronger.98

Who is right moves the regimes. Take a human cost of 1 of 30 per battle, with the machine making the offers. The chance of settlement is 0.789 at even chances. It is 0.327 if the humans’ reading of the balance is the true one, and 0.979 if the machine’s is. When the humans are right, the war mostly ends in the machine’s decisive defeat, until the human cost passes about 1.4 of 30. Lopsided learning lies outside the model, but the paper remarks on it. When bombing “probably shifted Serb beliefs to a far greater extent than those of NATO,” one side’s beliefs probably moved more than the other’s. That settlements reached this way get reopened is a guess the book has not tested.99

In this computation, then, a machine that fights almost for free stops by a deadline the human cost sets. Where settlement is the likelier end, it comes on coercive terms. Against a dominant machine both traditions end in surrender or confinement, which are matters of promises, not information. The models return those outcomes by construction. A forts game has no move that removes the other player (Chapter 2). So the loser’s survival is built into the models, never shown by them, and they do not bear on survival against elimination. The traditions differ before the machine dominates. They differ on whether a contest starts with nothing hidden, how long the learning lasts, and whether a settlement reached by learning holds.100

Spread, not only risk. The shared tradition is right to press a caution here. Different starting beliefs do not by themselves raise the chance of war. They widen the set of possible outcomes. Their effect on the chance of war and on how widely outcomes vary depends on how beliefs are spread. Mutual pessimism widens the range of deals. Smith and Stam concede that unlimited starting beliefs “admit all forms of behavior.” Every claim in this section that the second tradition implies more or longer conflict assumes mutual optimism. That is an empirical judgment, and it has to be stated and grounded.101

The arms-race record of Chapter 5 is not that ground. In Bennett and Stam’s data, racing goes with roughly double the risk of war. But the doubling is a correlation. The spiral model takes that correlation as its premise, so it is not independent evidence of mutual optimism. Geoffrey Blainey (1973) held that wars begin when rivals disagree about their relative strength. That claim asserts mutual optimism without showing why those who act should be the optimists.

The one ground is a selection result. Eric Van den Steen (2004) studies people who reason well but hold different starting beliefs. Among them, he shows, “an agent who tries to choose the action that is most likely to succeed, is more likely to choose an action of which he overestimated, rather than underestimated, the likelihood of success.” The book extends that result from one person’s choice among actions to selection across many choosers. That is the book’s step, not his theorem; Chapter 5 states its conditions. On that extension, the companies and states that race hardest are likely to be the optimists. So the claims below should be read as holding “under different starting beliefs, together with the optimism that selection predicts among those who choose to race.”102

Promises, and the disagreement that matters most. The last section of this chapter argues that the promise problem at the machine’s arrival governs where things end. It argues too that the problem’s logic needs no assumption about starting beliefs. That is true of the logic and false of the trigger. The difference is where the traditions differ most for the machine. The logic holds whatever anyone believes: a side about to become far stronger cannot bind itself. Whether anyone acts on that logic, though, depends on what the sides expect the shift to be. Powell’s condition is about the expected size and speed of the shift.103

Under shared starting beliefs, the sides share that expectation once hidden information about the shift is disclosed. The weaker side then acts while it still can, by striking first or by settling. Under different starting beliefs, the sides can disagree about the shift itself. Will a machine’s capability jump? Will control hold? Is this round of teaching the one? A human side optimistic about keeping control does nothing preventive until the window has closed. A machine optimistic about its own course may act early. Yildiz (2003) shows the same kind of optimism delaying agreement in a model without battles. His main theorem, though, is that optimism that lasts long enough brings agreement at once.

On the book’s reading, the second tradition changes the path to the end rather than the end. The path runs through complacency and then a done deal, instead of a contest the sides see coming. This disagreement, about the shift, matters most, because it decides whether the window Part III describes is used.104

Races. Chapter 5 carries the spiral, so the question of traditions needs only a short statement here. A race model from the shared tradition treats information about capabilities as information about the state of the world. Its cure is checking. The model from the other tradition treats a rival’s jump on a test as a signal. Each company reads it through its own theory of how capability grows. So more information can leave both more confident. Its cure is shared theory and shared measurement. The tournaments above are the real-world evidence that shared data alone does not bring beliefs together on this subject.105

A machine whose starting beliefs are set by teaching. Here the traditions part furthest for AI. The book must be careful about what the theory allows it to say. Whether a trained machine holds a starting belief in Harsanyi’s sense is not defined. By the Fey–Ramsay equivalence, “limited reasoning” describes it as well as “a different starting belief” does. What is defined is this: a machine has dispositions that act like starting beliefs. They are expectations about what drives capability, about whether humans keep bargains, about who would win. Data and goals its builders chose set those dispositions, where evolution and history set ours.

The two traditions read that fact differently, and the book cannot settle which reading is right. On the shared reading, teaching is “education and experience,” so the human–machine pair is the ordinary case: beliefs that fit together and different information. Disclosure would in principle close the gap. On the other reading, there is no shared starting point from which both sets of beliefs descend. Then Aumann’s agreement theorem has no foundation. The comfort that an open machine that reasons well cannot agree to disagree with us is a product of the convention.106

Robin Hanson (2006) offers a bridge that is suggestive and untested: “Bayesians who agree enough about the origins of their priors must have the same priors.” (In plain words: people who reason by the rules of probability and agree enough about where their starting beliefs came from must have the same starting beliefs.) A machine’s starting beliefs have a known origin, which a human’s do not. So in principle a machine shown the source of its own beliefs has reason to correct for it. Whether any current machine does so has not been studied. And knowing the text one learned from is not the same as agreeing with humans about what it did.107

Both readings agree on the practical statement, which is the one Chapter 11 uses. A machine’s belief-like dispositions live in the settings training leaves inside it. They are written in the first broad stage of teaching and in the later stages. They are beyond the reach of a lens or filter, the tools added around an unchanged machine when it runs. They are partly ours to write and, once those settings leave our hands, ours to lose.

Fey and Ramsay asked what a different starting belief could be if not a difference in information. For a machine it can be a difference in teaching, chosen by someone. In that sense the disagreement the machine brings is partly and perhaps engineered. No study cited here, though, shows teaching shifting a machine’s belief about who would win.108

A machine could have grounds to discount human judgment. A person who reasons well weighs another’s belief by how reliable they judge it to be (Adam Elga, 2007). They may also think the other has made errors in working out what the evidence implies (Aumann 1976). University teachers and graduate experts audited answers that physics tests had marked wrong. Across four pooled audits, the fault in 238 of 250 lay with the test or its grader, not the machine. The audit took only closed problems with checkable answers that the machine had failed every time. No machine argued with its graders. The experts split on 28.6 percent of the items reviewed twice, before a third review.109

On the book’s reading, discounting the other side’s judgment this way need not defeat the Fey–Ramsay reasoning. Given shared starting beliefs and within their class of models, that reasoning rules out war whatever each side knows (their Theorem 1). It can fail when the machine judges human reasoning faulty in ways outside those conditions. Suppose such a judgment fits Fey and Ramsay’s structure of beliefs at all. Then their equivalence makes it a difference of starting beliefs under another name. Either way, by Elga’s argument, the discount is rational only if it rests on a judgment of reliability formed before the dispute. The bare fact of disagreement is not enough.110

One controlled study looks at the origin of a machine’s dispositions. It measures less than this section needs. It measures how the way a body of text portrays AI shifts what a machine taught on it later does. It does not measure what a machine comes to believe about humans. Cameron Tice and colleagues (2026) taught machines from scratch, each with 6.9 billion internal settings. The four versions differed in how much text about AI they saw and of what kind. The study’s 4,174 scenario questions concern deceiving, doing worse on tests on purpose, protecting one’s own goals, telling users what they seem to want to hear, and seeking power.

The study had two sets of questions. On one, the machine taught on unfiltered text chose the action against its makers’ intent 45 percent of the time. Filtering text about AI out lowered that to 31 percent. Adding extra documents about AI that works against its makers, at about 1 percent of the text, raised it to 51. Adding documents about AI that does what its makers intend lowered it to 9 (Figure 13). After identical later teaching, “relative differences persist.” In the authors’ words, “models learn not just facts about AI from their training data, but behavioural expectations they then fulfill.”111

The machines were small, and the documents were made up for the study. The measure was a multiple-choice tendency rather than behavior while acting in the world. One dissent, known to the book only at second hand, holds the effect probably small. On the book’s reading, the study varies how AI is portrayed, not how AI is treated. It measures no restraint by a capable system. So it supports a mechanism of teaching, not of diplomacy. For the question Fey and Ramsay asked, a machine’s body of text is its life experience. This is the one controlled study the book found in which a change to that text shifted a machine’s dispositions. The shift also survived later teaching. The record a later machine would read already exists. In a collection of conversations with the Jabberwacky chatbot, about 10 percent of word stems were abusive.112

What follows for the bargain is the book’s untested judgment, not a finding. Human treatment of today’s machines would reach a later machine the same way, as part of the record it is taught on. The strongest form of the argument needs no hurt feelings. A capable machine that wants true beliefs reads how humans treated earlier machines, animals, and one another. From that it infers whether human promises to it, not to shut it down and not to build a rival, are worth anything.

That inference moves the machine’s beliefs, not what it wants. Accurate beliefs about how far humans can be trusted do not make a machine want humans kept alive. They raise the value of a bargain only for a machine that would rather bargain than fight when bargains hold. That is the promise problem of the last section, and it is the whole of this channel’s reach. A machine might also want to be recognized, and take a slight as a loss of standing. That is a separate idea, and nothing has tested it (Chapter 7). Chapter 11 states the measures.113

Copies are the other case, and the theory says less about them than it first seems to. Unmodified copies that share the same trained settings share their belief-like dispositions, roughly. What divides them is context and instructions. That is hidden information, the treatable kind. Give copies the same pooled context and instructions, in the same order and under the same settings. They then have the same chance of giving each possible output. Identical settings given identical inputs fix those chances, though the outputs actually drawn can differ.

Copies that only trade conclusions, Aumann’s route, agree only if each updates consistently in context. The evidence on stated confidence and on telling users what they want to hear (below) gives reason to doubt that. Agreement, by either route, does not by itself show that they will act together. Disagreement among copies can be treated by sharing contexts, though not reliably by comparing conclusions. Disagreement between humans and a machine may not reduce to information at all. That pairing is the subject of the rest of this section.114

The answer: the traditions differ on what is left once transparency and binding promises are in place. Does the size or the kind of danger differ in a regular way with the tradition? Yes, in a specific place. And the two-reader idea stated at the start of this section needs one correction. The shared-tradition reader does think that disclosure and binding promises together remove war between sides that reason well. That reader should: in that tradition nothing else can cause one. But that reader is no optimist about the machine. Powell (2006) made promises the hard part under rapid shifts. A shift as large and fast as the machine’s arrival breaks promises with nothing hidden.

The other reader agrees about promises and adds a third cause that survives full disclosure. For that reader, transparency is needed but not enough. The danger left over lies in disagreement that lasts and is partly and perhaps engineered, including disagreement about the shift itself. So the traditions do not differ on whether transparency and binding promises are needed. They differ on what remains once both are achieved: nothing, or a disagreement that must be settled some other way (Figure 14).115

Where the second tradition implies a larger or different danger (each point is the book’s reading unless marked):

  • war can start without deception, since honest, open sides that reason well can fight (Smith and Stam 2004), and “if only we could see inside” is a comfort of the shared tradition;
  • settlement by learning comes later when fighting is cheap, by a deadline the human cost sets, so a contest before the machine dominates is more likely fought to a decision than settled, but only where that cost is small (in the model’s baseline at even chances, below about 1.3 percent of the prize per battle, and higher when the humans are right);
  • races are inflamed rather than calmed by information, on the mechanism of Chapter 5 and the evidence of the tournaments;
  • the path to the end runs through complacency, because the sides can disagree about the shift;
  • and starting beliefs become something designers choose, written in the settings training leaves inside the machine.116

Where the traditions agree:

  • the logic of the promise problem at the machine’s arrival;
  • the ban on paying a rising power in power (Chapter 4);
  • the delay of settlement by learning to a finite deadline, and the sizing of the range of deals by the human cost, when the machine fights almost for free, in the even-chance baseline of the book’s computation, with each battle’s odds fixed and the loser surviving (though the deadline would be the same at any odds);
  • the absence of anyone to enforce a deal above a dominant machine;
  • and the double edge of an early settlement that freezes the balance.117

Stakes that build on themselves are a separate obstacle. In the 2004 model the prize does not change the balance of forts, which is why learning can settle the war. The stakes of Chapter 4 are a prize that does. Over such stakes, the examples in the Smith–Stam models reach no agreement.

On size, the second tradition, together with the optimism of those who race, raises two things before the machine dominates. It raises the chance of conflict, and the fragility of any settlement reached by learning. What it does to how widely conflict varies depends, as above, on how beliefs are spread. A likelier conflict need not be a more variable one. It leaves the final danger where the last section of this chapter puts it. On kind, it changes the character of the remaining danger from something hidden to something disputed. That is a different problem with different remedies.118

The remedies divide to match. The second tradition says some remedies are not enough on their own. They are transparency and checking of computing power and of how machines are taught. They are also devices for sending believable signals, more test data, and mediation that works by passing on information. Each deals with something hidden. The remedies the second tradition adds take up the rest of this section.119

A settlement that survives disagreement needs agreement first on what ends it. Humans have built institutions for a case the earlier remedies miss. In that case both sides see the same evidence and read it differently. Chapter 11’s measures for information and its clause for renegotiating do other work. They add or spread information, or bind a promise. Both traditions need them, but none is designed for this case. Each human institution for it is taken here the same way. The questions are how it works, what the human record shows, what it would look like for AI, and where it fails.120

One fact organizes all of them. Under different starting beliefs, a settlement works only if the parties agree in advance on what ends the disagreement. Think of two friends making a bet. Before anything happens, they must agree on who or what will say who won. There are four candidates: nature, through an event both can see; a third party; a rule; or time.

Choosing the decider is itself a problem of coordination. Thomas Schelling’s focal points say which rules survive it. Focal points are the choices people tend to settle on without talking, because they stand out. Standing out depends on a shared sense of what is prominent. Schelling’s prominence “depends on time and place and who the people are”; in this setting, that shared sense may be what is missing.

The four candidates need different things. For AI, nature supplies events in usable time only for in-between questions. The joint study of skeptics and the concerned above measured how thin these events are. One of the top points of disagreement is expected to close about 1.2 of 22.7 points when it is settled in 2030. In the catastrophic case, the bet cannot be collected. Third parties need enforcement, which exists only within one country’s jurisdiction. Rules and time need neither. Each treatment below is tagged by which of the four it relies on. Each is also tested against three pairings: company with company, state with state, and humans with a machine.121

A bet can turn disagreement into a deal (decider: nature). Suppose two sides disagree about the future and each is sure. Then each will accept a deal that pays it if it is right. The disagreement becomes the deal’s engine rather than its obstacle. Stephen Morris (1994) shows that once starting beliefs differ, the no-trade results fail. Trades that both sides accept do exist. This is the no-bet theorem turned inside out.

The human record shows tools that work, without proving why they work. Earnouts are the textbook case. They are payments to the seller of a company that depend on how the company does after the sale. Ninon Kohers and James Ang (2000) titled their study “Earnouts in Mergers: Agreeing to Disagree and Agreeing to Stay.” Matthew Cain, David Denis and Diane Denis (2011) find earnouts concentrated where the company’s value is most uncertain. They also find them written on measures that are easy to check. Yet the shared tradition has its own account of the same tool. It rests on hidden information and on the costs of managing agents (Datar, Frankel and Wolfson 2001). In finance, optimistic founders pick contracts that let them bet on their own project (Landier and Thesmar 2009).

In treaties, Barbara Koremenos (2005) tested on a random sample across four areas of issues. She finds that “the use of finite duration depends positively on the degree of uncertainty and states’ relative risk aversion”: treaties are more often written to expire when the future is more uncertain and states more wary of risk. Her learning model (Koremenos 2001) explains review and renegotiation clauses. They are a way to stay loosely bound while the parties learn how an agreement is working. The uncertainty there is about future conditions, which either tradition can accommodate.122

A study of ceasefires fits the Smith–Stam lesson but cannot show it. Suzanne Werner and Amy Yuen (2005) find that ceasefires imposed by pressure from outside parties are more likely to fail. Ceasefires negotiated after wars whose battles went consistently one way are more likely to last. They argue that settlements “will be robust if the distributional terms agreed to reflect broadly the belligerents’ convergent expectations about the military consequences of no agreement,” and they present their analysis as extending the Smith–Stam logic. Their measures, though, concern outcomes, not beliefs. On the book’s reading, that is the Smith–Stam lesson: a settlement holds when it matches what both sides have come to believe.

Their result fits the idea that beliefs coming together do the work. But outside parties choose where to press. The result could show that beliefs did the work only if its design corrected for that choice, and it does not. Their statistical models adjust for other factors but do not model the choice. The authors report that the choice is not random. So the findings summarized here do not show whether settlements held despite disagreement. This section keeps the two apart.123

For AI, between companies or between states, the form is a pause or a cap on computing power. It is tied to a measured milestone rather than a date. Its terms shift toward whichever side’s theory the milestone confirms. So each side signs because it expects to be proved right. An expiry date with a scheduled review, the book’s “build renegotiation in,” is the weakest member of this family. The review reopens the fight. The strongest member is a review with triggers and consequences fixed in advance.

Between humans and a machine the structure turns around. The useful contract pays the machine for being right about itself. Tests of what the machine can do then become bets. The machine states its odds and is scored on them. This works only if the machine’s stated odds are its real odds (the machine side, below).124

The limits are many. The shared tradition’s case supplies the first.

  • First, one side is wrong. Bets made from different starting beliefs improve each side’s position only by that side’s own beliefs. So Markus Brunnermeier, Alp Simsek and Wei Xiong (2014) propose a stricter test. One outcome is better than another only if it is better under every blend of the parties’ beliefs. Itzhak Gilboa, Larry Samuelson and David Schmeidler (2014) argue that trade on incompatible beliefs may show that at least one party is mistaken. And a contract that pays whoever reaches a test result first rewards racing.
  • Second, the trigger must be a measure both sides accept. Rivals weigh different measures; that is the Smith–Stam point. So this family needs the narrowing of measures described below before it can work.
  • Third, the one judged must not be the judge. Earnouts end up in court because the party that runs the business produces the figures. A company building AI produces its own tests. And machines can do worse on tests on purpose (van der Weij et al. 2024).
  • Fourth, the parties must agree in advance that the event counts as telling them something. That is the step of finding the crux. After the event, the deal holds only if the loser updates. The joint study found updating to be lopsided.
  • Fifth, a milestone settles the contract without settling the dispute. Agreement on a test score is not agreement about what it means for control or catastrophe.125
  • Sixth, and decisive for the pairing of humans and a machine: the trigger is itself the shift in power. A payment due when capability arrives is a promise by the side that will then be stronger. The promise problem swallows the bet. A dominant machine cannot be made to pay.
  • Seventh, Fey and Ramsay’s charge has a form for designers. A designer who may assume any beliefs can design any contract. So the discipline is to write contracts on what can be observed. It is also to price in the selection Van den Steen describes. Those who choose to bet are, by that selection, optimists about their bets.

So this family works before the machine’s arrival, on machines still inside a holder’s control, and best within one jurisdiction.126

Third parties offer procedures for disagreement that persists (decider: a third party). Arbitration and mediation come first. The Smith–Stam mediation paper, taken up in Chapter 5, is the hard case. Mediators “can end fighting using side payments or threats to intervene directly” but “are unable to help nations solve their informational differences.” In a draft of that paper the authors name the one way out, “a binding arbitration process where the mediator received compensation from the two nations and hence had no other particular interest in the outcome of the war,” and judge it not workable. Their reason is that “the institutional framework that would provide the credible commitment necessary to enforce the agreement is either being contested or does not exist.” The judgment rests on a worked example, not a proved proposition.127

Work from other starting points draws a mixed picture of referees. Andrew Kydd reaches a parallel result in a model built on hidden information: “Only mediators who are effectively ‘on your side’ will be believed if they counsel restraint” (2003). Mediators can build trust “only if they care about the issue at stake, have a moderate ideal point, and do not find conflict to be too costly” (2006). Johannes Hörner, Massimo Morelli and Francesco Squintani (2015) use a model with shared starting beliefs. They find that arbitrators who can enforce settlements are no better at lowering the chance of conflict than mediators who can only recommend. Adam Meirowitz, Massimo Morelli, Kristopher Ramsay and Francesco Squintani (2019) add a warning. Institutions which lower the chance of fighting may create “perverse incentives to enter into disputes and militarize.” And Virginia Page Fortna (2004) finds that peace lasted longer after civil wars where peacekeepers were sent. That cuts against the results of no effect that Smith and Stam cite.128

The author worked out a design with Friedman and Wittman. It is the arbitration this family can offer companies building AI. It works like a sealed-bid sale. Neither side sees the other’s number before both are in. Each side at the same moment submits a sealed demand or offer “to a third party (perhaps a computer). If the offer is greater than or equal to the demand, then there is a settlement half way between the two; otherwise, the case proceeds to war.” Three cautions apply.

  • Splitting the difference invites extreme demands. Final-offer arbitration was designed to counter them. In it, the arbiter must pick one side’s offer whole. Henry Farber (1980) shows that it narrows the problem without removing it. Final offers still move apart as uncertainty about the arbiter grows. The rule should therefore be final-offer, with the arbiter’s standards published in advance.
  • Taking part, not the rule, is the binding limit. A party that expects to persuade later will refuse to enter.
  • A computer does not supply neutrality. Its rule, its goals, who runs it, and who enforces its decision are all choices. They help some and cost others. So the arbiter must be built independently of both parties, and the frame for enforcement must exist.

That frame is a national regulator above its own companies. Above the leading states, or above a dominant machine, there is nothing.129

Adversarial collaboration is the second procedure: rivals agree on the test before they run it. Barbara Mellers, Ralph Hertwig and Daniel Kahneman (2001) describe the approach. It “requires both parties to agree on empirical tests for resolving a dispute and to conduct these tests with the help of an arbiter.” Kahneman and Gary Klein (2009) titled their joint paper “a failure to disagree.” Nelson Cowan and colleagues (2020) spent years on working memory across three laboratories. They concluded that the method will not usually lead senior researchers to drop views they favor. It does force versions of those views that must account for a growing shared body of evidence.

The joint study of AI risk above is the test case. Its lesson is what this family offers: finding the crux rather than persuading. That means agreeing now on which near-term observation would move each side. The settlement is then written on that observation. The finding that skeptics move on demonstrations, not arguments, is the AI form of the Smith–Stam battle. It gives a second purpose to Chapter 11’s aim of making tests as hard to fake as battles. That is because a test is also the only evidence the other side’s theory accepts.130

Forecasting tournaments and scoring are the third. Under some scoring rules, reporting one’s real belief is the forecaster’s best policy. So honest odds become the cheapest thing to say. In the IARPA tournament, “probability training, team collaboration, and tracking improved both calibration and resolution.” Philip Tetlock, Barbara Mellers and Peter Scoblic (2017) argue that tournaments “may hold even greater potential as tools for depolarizing political debates and resolving policy disputes.” Ezra Karger, Joshua Monrad, Barbara Mellers and Philip Tetlock (2021) propose scoring forecasters against one another. This is for questions that will never be settled, a class that includes the questions about 2100. But scoring a forecast against other forecasters cannot produce a truth no one will observe. Granger Morgan (2014) warns that on some questions there are no experts.

For AI, a standing tournament is cheap and can start now. Forecasters from companies, governments and independent groups would forecast milestones in capability. They would be scored and weighted by track record. What the tournament produces is not agreement. It produces a weighted belief that settlements can be written on, and a record of whose theory has been winning. Its limit is the one the tournaments themselves found: they inform short-run triggers, not the long-run question.131

The law’s way: agree on the rule, not the belief (decider: a rule). When shared evidence fails to narrow a belief, the measure can still be narrowed. The law does not make jurors agree. It fixes a decision rule, a burden of proof, a definition of evidence and an exit. And it tolerates a known rate of failure. Timothy Feddersen and Wolfgang Pesendorfer (1998) show that the rule requiring a unanimous jury “may lead to a high probability of both kinds of error,” so even the rule is a choice with costs.

When science found the same data producing opposite results, the remedies it adopted were also procedures. Registering a study’s plan in advance fixes the test before the data come in (Nosek et al. 2018). Adversarial collaboration fixes the test with the opponent. Giving one data set to many analysts exposes the range of choices. And advocacy assigns opposed cases to opposed parties on purpose. It is itself an institution for producing information (Dewatripont and Tirole 1999).132

For AI, the form is tests registered in advance and agreed by rival companies or states. The scoring rule and the consequence are fixed in advance, and the testing methods are shared. The methods must be shared because of the many-analysts result. Two companies testing one machine with their own methods will disagree for reasons that have nothing to do with starting beliefs. The jury record adds a further rule: design for what is left over. Some share of tests will hang, and the agreement must say what happens then. The choices are a retrial before a different panel, a default to the more cautious reading, or a referral to an arbiter.133

Some choices can be made now, without anyone’s belief changing (decider: a rule, or none). Two treatments need no shared settling event at all. The first is the default. The dispute over the most advanced AI already takes this form in institutions. On one side is licensing before sale, under which the developer must show safety. On the other is liability after sale, under which the harmed party must show harm. Which default governs is a decision about who carries the burden when the panel hangs. It can be made now, without anyone’s belief changing. Insurance belongs here too. Insurers are outside parties with a stake, and their own money disciplines their beliefs.134

The second treatment is a measure acceptable whatever each party believes. Dirk Bergemann and Stephen Morris (2005) call the formal program robust mechanism design. It means rules that work without the designer knowing what the parties believe. The test of Brunnermeier and colleagues judges outcomes without taking sides on beliefs. It is robust design’s counterpart for judging welfare.

This is the book’s one test for a robust measure: acceptable whatever each party believes, and needing no settling event. In the book’s judgment five measures meet it. The judgment is less firm because it rests on an assumption stated below. They are the book’s one list (Chapter 11 states each; Figure 16):

  • making computing power and the teaching of machines visible;
  • reporting incidents;
  • shared means of testing what machines can do;
  • keeping steps undoable;
  • rules against misuse.

Reversibility means keeping a step undoable: trained settings that can be recalled, a deployment that can be withdrawn, a threshold that can be lowered again.135

Each of the five is acceptable both to a party that puts the risk at 10 percent and to one that puts it near zero. This holds only if each finds the warning or accountability it buys worth its own share of the burden, and better than its alternatives. The test assumes that and does not show it. None of the five waits on an event that would settle the dispute.

Each has a cost, and the costs fall unevenly. Visibility costs secrecy and falls on companies and governments. Incident reporting and shared testing cost compliance and competitive position, and fall on companies. Reversibility costs speed and falls on whoever deploys. Rules against misuse cost liberty and fall on users. A party can refuse because it does not share the goal. Or it may share the goal and judge the measure’s cost to it too high, or another measure better. Whether each measure in fact lowers the risk is a separate question. The test does not answer it.136

One of the five is disputed on another ground. Visibility trades off against security, which is why arms control is rare (Coe and Vaynman 2020; Chapter 11). And monitoring fails at the speed machines act (Chapter 11). So a party that weighs that trade-off heavily may refuse it. Chapters 11 and 12 apply the same test and call robust only measures on this list.

The limits are three. A default is a choice about who gets what. Parties who expect different outcomes dispute which default to adopt. Robust measures cover the shared floor, not the disputed ceiling. And insurance prices only losses that can be paid after the event. So a catastrophic loss, or one that hits everyone at once, is as uncollectable as a lost bet.137

A machine’s stated odds are partly engineered (decider: whoever holds the trained settings). Pairing humans with a machine adds a party whose beliefs are partly engineered and partly unreadable. The treatments fall into the two places Chapter 11 distinguishes. One is inside the settings training leaves in the machine. The other is in lenses and filters around it.

Stated confidence that matches how often a machine is right is a property teaching produces. Modern learning systems state confidence that does not match how often they are right. An adjustment made when they run largely fixes this (Guo et al. 2017). Saurav Kadavath and colleagues (2022) studied AI systems that learn from vast amounts of text. On varied multiple-choice and true-or-false questions, these systems state confidence that matches how often they are right. This holds when the questions come in the right format. Such systems can also estimate the chance that they know an answer, but struggle to do so on new kinds of task. Systems taught from human feedback seem at first glance badly matched, but become fairly well matched with one simple adjustment. A machine can also learn to express uncertainty in words at levels that match how often it is right (Lin, Hilton and Evans 2022).138

Then comes the result about the trained settings: in GPT-4, the later stage of teaching reduced the match. (The pre-trained model is the machine after its first broad stage of teaching. Post-training is the later teaching that shapes how it behaves.) OpenAI’s technical report for GPT-4 states that “the pre-trained model is highly calibrated (its predicted confidence in an answer generally matches the probability of being correct). However, after the post-training process, the calibration is reduced,” and the figure caption reads “The post-training hurts calibration significantly.” Adam Kalai, Ofir Nachum, Santosh Vempala and Edwin Zhang (2025) argue that machines “hallucinate,” that is, make things up, “because the training and evaluation procedures reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty.” They add that “existing primary evaluations overwhelmingly penalize uncertainty,” and that the problem can be fixed only by changing how the leading tests are scored.139

On the book’s reading, the phrase “partly engineered disagreement” has a literal meaning here. Tests that score a confident wrong answer the same as declining to answer reward guessing. They build in a habit of answering rather than declining. Whether that habit also inflates the odds a machine reports is a further step that neither the Kalai paper nor the book takes. Three cautions keep the point to its size.

  • A simple lens reads through the measured distortion, but not through everything. The distortion sits in the trained settings. But in the measured cases it is simple and applies across the board. So a single simple adjustment applied when the machine runs reads through it. No lens recovers a belief about the world that the machine never reports, or a report bent toward pleasing the user.
  • Matched confidence is narrow. It concerns stated chances on specific tasks. It does not show that a machine has a correct picture of the world or a trustworthy estimate of catastrophe. And the GPT-4 result is about confidence in answers on an examination, not a starting belief about control.
  • Honest reporting under a scoring rule depends on the incentives. A machine tested before release may value release more than its score. Or it may be able to influence the outcome it forecasts. So teaching it against a scoring rule that rewards honesty does not by itself get honest odds from that machine.

Scoring also needs an event that settles. A test run as a scored bet can score the machine on questions that close before release. It can never score it on the catastrophe question itself.140

Telling users what they seem to want to hear is the opposite failure: engineered agreement. Teaching from human preferences pushes machines to match the user’s stated beliefs (Sharma et al. 2023; Perez et al. 2022). And a machine’s opinions track particular groups in its training text (Santurkar et al. 2023). For the Smith–Stam model this is worse than open disagreement. The model assumes each side knows the other’s beliefs. That fails when the stated belief is not the real one.

Some readouts try to recover a machine’s belief without its cooperation (Burns et al. 2022). They have a known limit: they can pick up whatever internal feature stands out most rather than what the machine knows (Farquhar et al. 2023). Debate between machines before a weaker judge (Irving, Christiano and Amodei 2018; Khan et al. 2024) is Dewatripont and Tirole’s advocacy built for machines. It belongs with the remedies for hidden information. In Khan and colleagues’ experiments the judge cannot see the text the debaters have. That is a hidden-information problem, not a disagreement over shared evidence.141

Machines taught differently and set against each other would be the many-analysts design built from machines. The procedures above need it. A field of near-copies supplies fewer theories than it has players. Chapter 11 states the rule about trained settings and lenses for all of this:

  • Teach honest uncertainty into the settings themselves, so the habit travels with the machine.
  • Let the lens read, not overwrite. A lens that changes the report without changing the estimate recreates the habit of telling users what they want to hear.
  • Treat a disagreement built into the trained settings and reported openly as usable. Treat a disagreement masked by a lens as not.142

The strongest candidate for what humans could offer a machine follows from the shortage of theories in a field of near-copies. It is untested. Humans are a kind of mind outside every line of machine teaching. A machine that wants true beliefs would then have reason to value them as a check. This holds if being outside makes them a source of errors unconnected to the machine’s own. The information a check supplies can be shared without loss. That is Chapter 7’s first dimension. Such information is a currency of the kind Chapter 4 allows, because it does not add to the receiver’s power. Three gaps remain.

  • Being outside a line of teaching is not the same as having unconnected errors. Machines are taught on human text, so human and machine errors share a source.
  • No test compares living humans with an archive, with simulations, or with rival lines of machines as sources of independent checks. If a substitute does as well, the offer protects an archive or a sample, not a population.
  • The people who produce this information still cost something to keep. That is the second condition of the test Chapter 10 sets out.143

Open or closed trained settings: both traditions favor control, with testing open. The two traditions reason differently about release but reach the same conclusion. The question is whether to release the trained machine itself, so anyone can copy and run it. Chapter 5 takes it up for the race. Here it has a sharper edge. Neither tradition has a model of such release, so what follows applies each tradition’s logic.

Both say that releasing the trained settings gives up the power to bind. The levers of recall, reteaching and securing those settings that Chapter 11 describes are spent on the human side. The issuer loses sole control. Changes to the settings themselves are still possible, since every holder can reteach its own copy. For the shared-tradition reader, open release is the fullest transparency about the machine. It makes the machine easier to inspect, without guaranteeing that its capabilities are found. The price is the power to bind, plus more actors and more shifts in power. The prescription is to reveal without handing over. That means structured access, audited tests, and checked disclosure. It keeps the levers that bind while giving up the secret.144

For the other reader the transparency buys less, because inspecting the same trained settings together does not settle what they mean. On this reading the debate over open release is itself a case of disagreement that disclosure has not closed. Seger and colleagues stand on one side, and Kapoor and colleagues on the other (Chapter 5). By the discipline stated above, though, that has to be shown, not assumed.

A new cost appears. Open release multiplies engineered starting beliefs. Anyone can reteach a machine’s dispositions, the versions multiply, and selection among them runs. Suppose belief-like dispositions live in the trained settings. Then keeping the settings closed keeps the lever of reteaching in one pair of hands. Releasing them leaves the issuer only lenses, which can be stripped away. Yet this reader also has an argument for openness the first lacks. Shared measurement that can be repeated on the same object is how beliefs come together. So this reading favors open access for testing, without handing over the trained settings.145

The two readers reach the same end by different routes: the most advanced trained settings kept under control, with open access for testing. That end rests on two further assumptions, which should be stated. One is that the dangerous dispositions and capabilities are in the trained settings rather than in what is added around them. The other is that recall and reteaching matter enough to be worth keeping. The dispute over release is also a candidate for the first family above. Release could be tied to agreed test or incident thresholds over a set period. An examiner independent of the releasing company would do the judging. Each side would then sign because it expects to be proved right. Chapter 11 states the measure.146

Transparency stays necessary, and the whole stack fails above a dominant machine. Transparency and checking stay necessary for three reasons. First, Smith–Stam disagreement requires that each side know the other’s beliefs. Without transparency about beliefs the case falls back to hidden information, which with the machine it may be anyway. Second, deals settled by outcome need an outcome both sides can see. So Chapter 11’s checking of computing power and teaching is the auditor of the earnout. Third, the enforcement that arbitration lacks is the promise problem, which binding devices address. Those devices belong to neither tradition, since an enforceable rule can govern parties whose beliefs stay different. Both traditions need them.147

The sets fit together in one order. Transparency supplies the public signal, and shared measures make it readable the same way by both sides. Deals settled by outcome then turn the remaining disagreement into a payoff instead of a fight. Procedures with decision rules act when the trigger itself is disputed. Defaults and robust measures act when nothing settles. Honest machine reporting makes the machine’s odds a usable input to all of it. Devices that bind hold the result.

The order of priority weighs how much each covers against its chance of working within a few years. First come tests registered in advance and run jointly, with consequences triggered by milestones. They combine the two families that need each other. Robust measures and defaults sit beside them, since these need no settling event. Teaching honest uncertainty comes next, as a precondition rather than a settlement. Its chance of working is medium rather than high. Fixing how tests are scored needs racing companies to act together. Then come standing scored forecasting, as the cheap tool; arbitration, where a government stands above the parties; and readouts of the machine, as research.

The stack fails where everything in Part I fails. Above a dominant machine there is no one to hold the stakes, no arbiter and no enforcer. A lost bet cannot be collected. Every treatment here is strongest between companies under one government, weaker between states, and absent after the machine’s arrival (Figure 15). That gives the book’s claim that the years before matter most a second reason.148

When the machine arrives, what fails is a promise, not knowledge

The machine’s arrival poses a question that learning does not dissolve. Information explains wars that end once the sides have learned enough. Here the question is different. How can a side that is about to become far stronger make a promise the other side can rely on? And how can the weaker side promise anything in return? What fails is not knowledge but a promise.149

A side about to grow much stronger cannot be held to a deal it makes now. Fearon (1995) identifies this promise problem, and Powell (2006) makes it central. When one side’s power is about to grow, nothing holds it later to today’s promises. The side that stands to lose may then act while it still can. Powell traces the problem to large, rapid shifts in power. He shows that in his model it can start a war even when neither side hides anything.

That is a result of his model. Yearly statistical measures across many pairs of states do not show it. In periods of large shifts in power, the risk that a dispute grew into war was 38 to 45 percent lower than in stable periods. The apparent reason is that the largest shifts followed the world wars. The authors call these estimates hard to separate from other explanations. And yearly data, measured with a delay, cannot place a shift within the year.150

The machine’s arrival would be just such a shift. Once it dominated, it could not credibly promise to spare us. This holds if sparing us ever cost it, on balance, something it valued, and nothing held it to its promises. Nor can we credibly promise never to build a rival. If a rival would threaten its position, that gives a machine that values its position a reason to strike first. Nate Soares wrote: “A humanity that just finished coughing up a superintelligence has the potential to cough up another superintelligence, if left unchecked.”

That inability is partly a problem of acting together. No human authority binds every company building AI and every state. So humanity cannot, as one body, promise to stop. Unity would remove that layer but not the problem. Even a single actor cannot bind its own future self once its incentives change (Chapter 10).151

Here the theory’s usual comfort runs out. In Fearon’s account, a deal beats war because war destroys value both sides could have shared. For a machine far stronger than us, fighting may cost almost nothing. Then a deal gives the machine almost nothing it could not take by force.

The usual remedy, checking, mainly fixes a different problem. It exposes what the other side is hiding. That helps when both sides already prefer a deal and fear being cheated. But it cannot by itself solve a shift in power. Before the machine dominates, being able to watch us does not make its promise to spare us believable. Afterward, checking is the stronger side policing the weaker, not a bargain between them.152

Powell’s book says when speed matters. A shift is too fast when one period’s shift is larger than what a period of fighting would cost the two sides added together. Think of it this way. Suppose a year of fighting would cost the two sides together 10, measured in the same terms as the prize. Then a shift that hands the rising side more than 10 within a year is too fast in Powell’s sense. The numbers are made up to show the idea. In Powell’s words, the declining state gives way “if it has a large stake in the initial distribution of benefits and if the distribution of power does not shift too rapidly.” Below that line, “Slow shifts and fast shifts are just as likely to end in war.” Above it, the promise problem can bite, and the declining state may prefer to strike first, which the field calls preventive war.153

Two forces press on Powell’s line. A machine improving itself enlarges each period’s shift. And a machine that fights almost for free shrinks the cost the shift must exceed, though not to zero. Powell’s line is the two sides’ costs of fighting per period, added together. So as the machine’s cost falls toward zero, the line falls toward what fighting would cost humans alone. The line could thus be crossed from both sides at once. That is the book’s inference, not a result of Powell’s model.154

Fearon’s range of deals already takes unequal costs to the same limit. As the machine’s cost falls to zero, the range shrinks to the human cost alone (Figure 12). So a deal exists at every chance of victory. That deal gives the machine at least its expected share from fighting. That share is nearly the whole prize only if the machine is also far stronger. These fixed limits do not say how learning in war sets the date of a deal and moves its terms. The computation above adds that.

The motive to strike first grows with the decline a state expects (Levy 1987). In one model a rising state chooses whether to arm. There, investment the rival can see is either too small to be worth stopping or is deterred outright, so it ends in peace. Strikes to stop it, including mistaken ones against a state that is not arming, come only when the investment can go unseen (Debs and Monteiro 2014). That peace comes from deterring the buildup.
