It holds for shifts a state chooses to make, with both sides knowing what investment produces. On the book’s reading, gains in capability that surprise even their builders lie outside that result. So for AI, visibility calms the motive to strike first only if the pace itself is held down (Chapter 11).155

Smith and Stam separate two things this account runs together: the chance of winning the next battle, and the distance from total defeat. Israel, they note, is strong battle for battle, yet “its neighbors only need a few victories in order to overrun the country.” Battle strength is not distance to defeat.

They also study wars in which holding more forts raises the chance of winning the next battle. They call this version “a model of Realism,” and in their examples it is the one in which “nations surrender fastest.” A machine improving itself looks like that version. The authors’ zone of the status quo is the set of positions neither side would rather fight than accept. In the paper’s examples, that zone tends to be smaller in this version than when forts do not add to power. The paper holds fixed how decisive each battle is. So it cannot say what happens as battles become more decisive, which may be the AI case. On that reading, the confinement of humanity that Chapter 10 discusses would be a surrender, not a bargain.

Colin Krainin and Thomas Wiseman (2016) study a model with many countries. They find that when states are patient enough, war is inevitable. They also find that peace is easier to keep “when mechanisms exist to preserve any existing inequalities.” A machine that aims to last as long as possible has a very long horizon. That makes it their patient player.156

Inside each side there is also a problem of agents. Take a system that acts on instructions no one can override. That is the problem of making a machine want what its makers intend, in the form of a promise problem. A system that may work against its overseers in secret is a problem of hidden action. Research on AI control addresses the second. It tests ways for a weaker trusted machine and scarce human review to watch a stronger untrusted one. Calling it a problem of hidden action is the book’s framing.157

For the race, a lead in the most advanced AI compounds. Computing power buys better machines, which attract money, talent and more computing power. Dan Reiter, Alastair Smith and the author (2001) describe the military version. The field calls it “resource cumulativity”: “the capture of resources increases military power which in turn permits the further capture of resources.” They add that there is “substantial empirical debate over whether or not resources are generally cumulative,” so the parallel is a hypothesis about AI. A pause agreed while one side leads becomes unstable if that lead wears away. That is because agreements last longest when they match the balance on the ground (Bennett, Smith and Stam 2003). Proposals to sabotage a rival’s AI projects before they succeed (Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang 2025) are the motive to strike first, written as policy.158

Short wars teach little, and a likely loser may fight to raise the winner’s costs. In the Smith–Stam learning model, battles are public signals both sides accept. Fighting goes on until one more battle’s lesson is worth less than its cost. The authors draw a lesson from a policy of overwhelming force. Such a policy, “although minimizing costs in the short run, also leads to situations in which the future is likely to be less stable than it might be otherwise,” because short wars teach little. Suppose a contest between people and a machine came down to one decisive clash. Then there would be no learning phase at all. The information would have to come before any confrontation.159

A separate chapter by Smith and Stam asks, “Why would a state start a war knowing that it will lose every battle?” Its answer is that the state may expect “to impose unexpected costs on the winner, thereby gaining an advantage in the wartime bargaining process,” as Egypt did in 1973. The mechanism needs the sides to disagree about the stronger side’s costs. Its likely loser is weaker in every clash but far from total defeat. So the human case it fits is narrow: after a machine, or a rival, is stronger clash by clash, but before it dominates. Action to stop a rival’s rise while the side acting is still stronger is preventive war instead. And a machine’s resistance to being switched off may be plain self-preservation. Which one is at work changes the remedy: correcting a mistaken belief about costs helps only with the first.160

Chapter 4A power maximizer is hard to keep content or pay off

Chapter 3’s last section left the weaker side facing a choice: wait, or act first. The side now on top has a tool of its own, and power transition theory names it. The leading power should keep the rising power content in the years before the riser overtakes it. Those years, in the words of the theory’s founders, are “the only period when satisfaction can be managed.”161

This chapter asks three questions. Can a rising machine be kept content at all? If it can, what could a deal with it be paid in? And does it help or hurt that the things a machine wants can be cut into any number of pieces? The answer to the last question runs against the usual intuition.

Power transition theory ties peace to the rising side’s satisfaction

What is power transition theory, in one sentence?

It says that peace between a leading power and a rising one depends on whether the riser is content with the order. The order means its rules, the riser’s voice in them, and its share of the benefits. Graham Allison later gave the danger of a rising power meeting a ruling one a popular name, the “Thucydides Trap.”

Power transition theory adds a condition that the deal-making models leave unstated: whether the rising side is content. Chapter 3’s promise problem looks at a shift in power from the side that stands to lose. A. F. K. Organski began the theory in 1958. His own book was not available here. His views come from a 1989 restatement by Jacek Kugler and Organski, and from a 2017 summary by Jonathan DiCicco.162

The theory pictures the world as a ladder rather than a free-for-all. One dominant nation sits on top of an order built for its benefit. Power alone does not decide whether that order lasts. Satisfaction matters as well. The theory rests on one sentence of Kugler and Organski’s: “Indeed, peace in the international order is assured by the dominant nation with the support of the great powers that are satisfied with the distribution of benefits and the rules by which it is run.”163

The danger is a riser that is both strong and discontented. It grew strong “after the imposition of the existing international order,” in the theory’s words. Its leaders find that “the main benefits of the international order have already been allocated.” When such a riser draws roughly level with the leader, it has the chance to fight. Its dissatisfaction gives it the will. Later writers in the same school state the leader’s task plainly: “The dominant power has many management responsibilities but at the top of its list is the spread and deepening of satisfaction.”164

Robert Powell’s models put the same condition as a gap: “War is least likely when the existing distribution of benefits reflects the underlying distribution of power.” In his terms, a state is dissatisfied when fighting is worth more to it than the present arrangement. Fighting is worth what it could win, less the cost of fighting. Robert Gilpin explains why closing the gap is never finished: “As the power of a state increases, so does the probability of its willingness to seek a change in the system.”165

Satisfaction and the promise problem are therefore two halves of one problem. Does the order pay the riser what its power could win? And can that arrangement hold while the riser’s power keeps growing?

Evidence is thin for world-order wars. For state pairs it is broad and, on this book’s reading, mostly unfavorable. The theory’s original claim concerns wars that reshape the whole world order. For that claim, the evidence is thin. Such wars are too rare to test this way, and they can be named only after the fact.166

The narrower version concerns pairs of states. Here the evidence is broad, and on this book’s reading mostly unfavorable. D. Scott Bennett and the author ran one large test. It looked at some 750,000 observations from 1816 to 1992. Each was a pair of states in one year, seen from each side in turn. It found three things.

  • Pairs in which one side far outweighed the other went with less war, as the theory holds.
  • The measures of one state overtaking another were weak, and sometimes ran the wrong way. A change in which state led the world went with a rise in risk of 1 to 3 percent.
  • A fall in satisfaction of one standard step (the usual yardstick of how widely the data spread) went with about a fifth more war, among the narrower set of pairs the study calls “politically relevant.”

The authors found “no empirical support” for the overtaking measures. They left open the possibility that those measures miss what the theory means.167

The theory’s founders, Organski and Kugler, ran a smaller test in The War Ledger. Their later restatement gives the result. Between 1860 and 1980, ten great-power pairs drew level and saw one overtake the other. Five of those ten went to war, against none of the other ten pairs. Their tests, they wrote, “have not included explicit measures of satisfaction with the status quo.” Allison’s project counted twelve of sixteen such rivalries over five centuries as ending in war. That is a count, not a test.168

Scholars split most deeply over who starts the war. Dale Copeland holds that “it is the dominant but declining military great power that is most likely to begin a major war.” He warns that “rising states have every incentive to misrepresent their intentions as peaceful to reduce the possibility of preventive attack.”

Others doubt the danger itself. Richard Ned Lebow and Benjamin Valentino find that “Power transitions are remarkably rare, they seldom occur as the result of differential rates of economic growth, and have most often occurred peacefully.” DiCicco calls Allison’s list of cases “a weakly specified collection of cases.” William Wohlforth argues that status is “a positional good,” one whose value depends on standing relative to others. He adds that the bargaining problem is “particularly acute” over “primacy,” being first. Part II returns to him.169

Who starts the war, the riser or the leader?

The scholars split. Power transition theory worries about a dissatisfied riser. Copeland argues that the leader in decline is most likely to start a major war. A riser, he adds, has every reason to look peaceful while it grows. This matters later in the chapter, when the riser is a machine.

Satisfaction is not the same as power. Theorists treat the two as separate. Douglas Lemke and William Reed titled one paper “Power Is Not Satisfaction.” Margit Bussmann and John Oneal report their statistical tests. From 1816 to 1985, the tests found no relationship between a state’s power and how it rated the existing order. Satisfaction concerns the rules, a state’s voice in them, and the share of benefits it receives. This book offers a guess it has not tested: some of that can be paid without paying in power. Chapter 11 draws that line.170

Satisfaction is also hard to measure. Andrew Greve and Jack Levy note that scholars have not adequately turned satisfaction, the theory’s key idea, into something they can measure. This book knows of no measure of a machine’s satisfaction. On this book’s reading, the lesson is to say what satisfaction would consist of for a machine: rules, voice, benefits, standing. The lesson is not to assume that humans would recognize it.171

Nor does the field agree that dissatisfaction is needed for war at all. Bruce Bueno de Mesquita and David Lalman state, as a formal proposition of their book War and Reason: “Dissatisfaction with the status quo is unrelated to the likelihood of war.” So this book treats satisfaction as one leg among several, not the hinge on which everything turns.172

Leaders have kept risers content with three tools. Declining powers have used each of them.

  1. Giving way on stakes with clear limits. Between 1895 and 1906 Britain gave way to the United States on three matters: through arbitration of the Venezuela boundary, through a canal under American control by the Hay–Pauncefote Treaty of 1901, and over the Alaska boundary in 1903.
  2. Binding. G. John Ikenberry argues that victors who tied their own hands in institutions built the more lasting orders.
  3. Recognizing the riser’s status (Chapter 11 returns to this).173

On this book’s reading, Britain’s handover of first place to the United States rested on several things at once. The two shared an identity, and their interests fitted together. A third threat, Germany, made the riser useful to the declining power. Michelle Murray, though, dates the start of the friendship to the Venezuelan crisis of 1895, nearly three years before Germany’s naval program. Quoting Charles Kupchan, she gives the balance against Germany only a part in firming it up (Chapter 7, Table 2). Kori Schake holds that the passage was peaceful “because Britain and the United States came to look alike to each other and different from other nations,” and that its conditions are “unlikely to apply in future transitions.” Charles Kupchan lays out stable peace as a sequence. One side gives way first, then both hold back, then their societies grow together, then new stories and identities follow. He treats this British–American case as a leading example.174

The British–American passage is one case. It serves as an analogy for several conditions working together. It is not evidence that adding conditions lowers the risk. Britain also paid partly in stakes that gave power: first place in the Western Hemisphere, and the canal. On this book’s untested reading, that worked because American aims, where they met Britain’s, stopped at the hemisphere. Evidence that American aims reached further would overturn that reading. An appetite that stops in this way meets what the book calls the heartland condition, taken up later in this chapter. And the United States was a riser of the contented kind Lemke describes below.175

The conditions for war are far more common than war. Bueno de Mesquita and Lalman built a model of how two states interact in a dispute. They call it the international interaction game. In 1986 they claimed that their revised theory “significantly improves our ability to discriminate between violent and nonviolent disputes” in Europe between 1816 and 1970. War and Reason analyzes 707 European cases from those years: 469 militarized disputes, and a random sample of 238 pair-years with no dispute.

One version of the game fails outright. The “realpolitik” version implies that one side never simply gives in. The data hold 109 cases of giving in, and none of that version’s predictions found support. The authors report that a second version, which adds constraints from domestic politics, fits.176

Curtis Signorino reanalyzed the same 707 cases and found “at best modest empirical support.” The original tests lacked data on the costs the game needs, so they had dropped some of its conditions. As a result, a predictor labelled as one outcome also flagged cases where best play by both sides leads to another.

Scored on all seven of its outcomes, the game with best play at every step gets between 1 and 41 percent of cases right. Always predicting that nothing changes gets 34 percent. Signorino also built his own statistical version. It gets 23 percent right with the original authors’ weights, and 29 percent with every weight estimated from the data. The second is significantly better than guessing at random, but both fall short of always predicting no change.177

Mutual optimism is common, and war is not. Mutual optimism means each side believes it is the stronger. It appears in 89 of the 707 cases. The wars among major powers where domestic costs were low fall almost entirely in that group. Yet most cases that met the condition did not fight. Bueno de Mesquita had earlier treated a positive expected gain from war as needed for war, not enough for it.178

Bennett and the author retested the game and found its predictions linked to what states did. The link held in both of their samples, and with other factors held fixed. The effects were smaller among all pairs of states than among the politically relevant ones. In that test, take a pair the game codes as headed for war. Among politically relevant pairs, it has more than double the risk of both sides using force, or of war. Among all pairs, it has about 40 percent more. Holding other factors fixed brings these down to 1.5 and 1.3 times.

A later and larger test found the reverse effect of holding other factors fixed. There, holding them fixed raised the game’s risk ratio for war from 1.2 to 1.9 among all pairs. (A risk ratio is one predicted chance divided by another.) Among politically relevant pairs it rose from 1.4 to 1.8. The link also depends on the period. Before 1914, pairs the game coded as headed for war were less likely to fight. The expected direction appears only after 1945. A further check on fresh data found support among politically relevant pairs, and a relationship “less clear” among all pairs.179

Across the two samples, pair-years coded as headed for war show 21 to 123 percent more conflict. That is a link between a coded prediction and what happened. It is not a test of whether states actually decide by the game’s reasoning. The authors note that this effect, like that of “most other variables,” is “closer in magnitude to the effect of exposure to second-hand smoke than to long-term smoking.”180

Why does a tiny starting rate matter so much?

Think of a rare illness that strikes about 65 people in a million each year. (This is an illustration of the book’s arithmetic, not a fact about any illness.) A risk factor that multiplies the chance 248 times sounds terrifying. Yet it leaves the yearly chance at about 16 in 1,000, still under 2 in 100. A factor can raise risk a great deal and still leave war unlikely in any one year.

The starting rate explains the gap. In the authors’ words: “The baseline probability of war in a single directed dyad-year is 0.000065; even a 248 times increase in risk keeps the annual probability of war for any dyad in this dangerous situation at less than 2 percent.” A “directed dyad-year” is one pair of states in one year, seen from one side.181

The complaint that such theories “predict too much war” can mean two things. On this book’s reading, the record supports only one. The first meaning is that the named conditions are not enough for war. A positive expected gain, mutual optimism, two sides drawing level while one arms, and the game’s war prediction are all far more common than war. That is supported.

The second meaning is that the models’ stated chances of war run too high. Nothing read for this book shows that. The one overall check read for it finds no overprediction. It was made on the same data the model was fitted to. Added up across pairs, Bennett and Stam’s predicted chances track the yearly number of disputes. They also track the average number of wars over three to five years. They miss single years with more than two wars.182

The authors also remarked that they “would under-predict conflict by a large margin in any of the dyad years in which war actually occurs,” because the wars that happened fell where the model put the risk at “50% or less in any given year.” That remark records low fitted chances on the wars that did occur. By itself it shows neither that the model predicts too little war nor that its chances are off.183

Signorino also took on a standard kind of statistical model, one that estimates the chance of an outcome from a list of factors. Such a model, he argued, is unlikely to capture the strategic logic of a crisis. He generated artificial data from a simple crisis game and ran three such models on it. Each gave highly significant estimates that pointed to wrong conclusions. The simplest one’s fitted chances were sometimes off by more than 0.7, on a scale from 0 to 1. The effect of democracy, which entered only one outcome in a simple way, came out right. Bennett and the author re-estimated their model with a statistical method of Alastair Smith’s built for strategic choices. They report that no estimate changed direction, though they did not publish that output.184

What carries over is a lesson about reasoning, not a starting rate. On this book’s reading, the lesson is about reasoning from one condition. War is rare among states for reasons that are themselves conditions. The book says which of them fail for a dominant machine.

  • Fighting costs the machine almost nothing, by the assumption the next section uses.
  • When the present arrangement already matches the balance of power, states have less desire to challenge it (the Smith–Stam work below finds this in some of its examples). But here the balance moves with every round of teaching a new machine.
  • States can often get what they want short of war. A machine can find routes around humans.

A pairing of humans and a machine scores dangerous on nearly every entry in this book’s list. The sides draw level, and then one passes the other. The shift is rapid, and one side’s cost is near zero. The sides can see the same facts and still disagree. And no one stands above them to enforce a deal. Yet suppose one stacked these risk multipliers in the manner of Bennett and Stam. One would start from a rate so low that even their 248-fold case stays under 2 percent a year.185

Neither the danger nor that low chance is an estimate for the machine. Bennett and Stam’s model sets such a profile as a whole. But it lacks the entries the machine’s case turns on. And Signorino shows such fitted values can miss by more than 0.7, even for cases inside the data.186

One entry cuts both ways. A lopsided pair of politically relevant states was far safer than an even one. Its stronger side was the likelier to start a fight. Yet the concentration of power in the whole system of states was the strongest single predictor of war. It raised the risk only to about one in 1,000 pair-years, though, and may be a false signal. A dominant machine would score as both at once.187

The theory’s structure fits the machine; much else does not. Humans built the present order. A machine whose capability rises past ours is the riser. The founders’ last stage, in which the challenger “will extract concessions that can no longer be resisted by the previously dominant nation,” is the world after the machine’s arrival. Their “only period when satisfaction can be managed” is the time before it.188

Three differences matter.

  1. The theory holds that, “to a large degree, the economic growth of nations is independent of the actions of their elites and third parties.” Humans, by contrast, largely grant a machine its capability.
  2. No dominant state ever wrote a riser’s wants. Humans can partly write a machine’s.
  3. Evidence of satisfaction is weakest when it matters most. Chapter 3 found that a model can pretend, while it is being taught, to want what its makers intend. Copeland would predict this of a riser that gains by waiting.

On Copeland’s theory, the first dangerous move between humanity and a rising machine is likelier to come from the human side. This holds only if his theory carries over. His conditions are a declining side that foresees its loss, is able to act, and expects war to cost less than decline. That is a reading of Copeland’s conditions for a war to stop a rival’s rise. It is not a tested prediction.189

The decisive question for Part I is which kind of riser a machine that maximizes its power would be. Lemke describes a contented riser that can stay “satisfied, and peaceful, even if the benefits it enjoys from the international status quo do not change. This is impossible in Powell’s models,” where rising power breeds dissatisfaction by itself. A machine that maximizes power is Powell’s riser by construction. Whatever the order pays it, more power would be worth more to it. So satisfaction, the theory’s central tool, has nothing to grip. Part II asks whether a machine with other ends could be Lemke’s riser.190

The race between states is the theory’s own leading case. The United States and China are that case: “The issue of war versus peace will turn on satisfaction.” Copeland weighed limits on technology against “the real risk of unleashing a new cold war.” Even the critics Lebow and Valentino recommend what the theory prescribes: soften a riser’s challenge “by incorporating them into the system if they are outside it, or, if they are inside, to provide more symbolic and material benefits to reconcile them to the status quo.”191

Washington states the race outright: “The United States is in a race to achieve global dominance in artificial intelligence (AI).” A commission advising Congress urged a program “racing to and acquiring an Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) capability.” China’s plan frames a competition for leadership in AI and asks for “safe, reliable, and controllable” development. In public, China is not plainly racing to build such a machine.192

The case for racing assumes the winner controls what it builds. Yet racing cuts the time left for safety research. In a model by Stuart Armstrong, Nick Bostrom, and Carl Shulman, teams skimp on safety to finish first. An unsafe winner then shares the disaster. That the race may hand victory “not to any state, but to the AIs themselves” is already in print.

This book adds two readings of its own. The race between states is one power transition, and the machine is the riser in a second. And each state expects to control what it builds. That expectation is a form of optimism about the shift (Chapter 3).193

What can a deal be paid in?

Closing the satisfaction gap means paying in something. The work Alastair Smith and the author did on issues and stakes asks: paid in what?

Their answer runs against a familiar view. James Fearon had argued that a prize that cannot be divided should rarely cause war. Side payments, he argued, can stand in for a divided prize. Smith and Stam’s 2001 paper, “Issues, Stakes, and the Nature of War,” is an unpublished conference paper. It studies how what nations fight over shapes whether they can settle. It replies: “As we show below, in somewhat counterintuitive fashion, resources that are highly divisible, or in our language both transferable and cumulative, are the most dangerous issues states can try to negotiate over.”194

Wait, why would something easy to divide be harder to bargain over?

Think of two card players who settle a quarrel by passing chips across the table. The chips are also what each must play with in the next hand. (This is an illustration, not the model.) Every chip handed over brings the receiver closer to taking the whole table. So the side that receives chips today cannot promise not to use them to demand more tomorrow. That is why, in the model’s examples, stakes like these are the hardest to settle.

“Transferable” means a stake can be handed from one side to the other. “Cumulative” means each piece received adds to the receiver’s means of taking more. On this book’s reading, computing power, energy, and matter belong to this class. They can be split into any number of pieces and handed over. And if they convert into power, each unit received adds to the receiver’s means of taking more. That fails only where some bottleneck stops it being used.195

Two cautions apply to that result. First, in the paper’s examples, stakes change hands in lumps. They pass in one deal before fighting, with no slicing away a little at a time. One fort is a seventh of the whole.196

Second, thin slices can avoid war without avoiding defeat. Fearon’s later work finds no war under two conditions. The stake must pass in slices no larger than the yielding side’s cost of war and its patience allow. And each side’s odds must move smoothly with what it holds. Peace in that model is not survival, though. Where small gains move the odds a lot, the weaker side is “nearly or completely eliminated over time.” War returns in three cases. One step may jump the odds, or be too big for patient sides. Or the sides may differ in patience while the odds are steep. On this book’s reading, a fort is such a step for sides patient enough. That puts the Smith–Stam result in Fearon’s lumpy case. Thomas Chadefaux reads it the other way.197

Smith and Stam argue their claim case by case, from the way each side’s prospects improve as it holds more forts. They concede in a footnote that at certain points that improvement can fail to be strict. That is, it can stall rather than rise.198

Nations fight over three kinds of stake. The paper separates them.

  1. Forts. Nations value the forts themselves. In the published model a fort is “any particular form of military resource that is necessary for the two nations to continue to fight and that can trade hands.” Holding forts does not change the odds in the next battle. Colonial wars and the First Punic War are the examples.
  2. Power. The forts are both the prize and the means of winning it, as in the Second Punic War or Germany in 1942–45.
  3. Policy. Nations fight over a policy, and the forts matter only as a route to imposing it.

Real wars mix the three.199

What is a “fort” in these models?

A stand-in for any military asset a side needs to keep fighting and that can change hands, such as territory or resources. Chapter 2’s box on the forts model shows the line of forts and how the front moves. Holding more forts brings a side closer to winning everything. It does so even when holding them does not improve its odds in any single battle, as with the first kind of stake. Strength battle for battle is not the same as distance from defeat.

Over forts or power, the paper finds no deal. For the first two kinds, the paper says: “No agreements can be reached in the forts or the power models.” That holds for the kind of plans the paper studies. Those plans look only at the forts each side holds, and switch at fixed cut-off points. At a high cost of fighting there are typically several patterns of such play, not one. Agreements under other kinds of plans were not examined. And the paper argues this case by case. It does not state it as a proved proposition.200

The reason is the promise problem again. Any transfer of forts moves the military balance, so “the side gaining from the negotiations can never credibly commit.” Policy stakes are different. Shifting a policy toward the side that is winning can end the fighting, and “Such an agreement could be implemented and both sides want to honor it.” The authors hedge even this: “it is not always possible to reach agreement.”201

The result is narrower than “wars over power cannot end.” It concerns changing the present arrangement by negotiation. In some of the forts examples, war never starts at all: “The fact that the payoffs from the status quo reflect the military balance alleviates tension and reduces nation’s [sic] desires to challenge the status quo.” That is peace without a bargain: an arrangement that already matches the balance, not a redistribution both sides prefer.202

This book calls a stake power-conferring when handing it over moves the receiver closer to decisive victory. The test is not whether a stake can be split, but whether splitting it shifts power. Smith and Stam’s work on mediation shows a limit. Even a perfectly divisible prize is not enough for a deal when the two sides disagree about who is stronger.203

Wars over forts have two ways out. The first is tribute, a payment that does not move the balance. Suppose one side buys the other off “with money, or some other transferable utility,” that is, with something that can be handed over. If the present arrangement plus the payment is worth more than continuing the war, “a credible agreement can be reached.” After the Second Punic War, Carthage owed Rome a yearly payment. In 191 BC Carthage offered to pay off the rest at once. The Roman Senate refused, “not wishing to allow the Carthaginians to cease to be obligated to Rome.”204

The second exit is an appetite that falls off. It appears in an aside in Smith and Stam’s chapter on likely losers. That chapter asks why a side might start a war it expects to lose battle by battle. Following Goemans, the authors suppose that nations may care more about their “heartlands” than their outlying ground. Remote forts are then worth less to them. Then “if the value of additional forts drops off sufficiently then nations can commit not to increase demands following territorial gains.” This book calls this the heartland condition. A side whose appetite for further gains falls off fast enough can credibly promise to stop. It can do so even though each gain brings it closer to complete domination. Carrying the condition from forts to a machine’s ends rests on a guess that Chapter 7 states and does not prove.205

Does demand for resources stop responding as they get cheaper? The question is whether a machine’s demand for resources keeps growing as they get cheaper. First, a short detour into how demand responds to price. Spending is price times quantity. When price falls, spending rises exactly when demand is “elastic”: people buy so much more that the lower price is more than made up. For example, imagine the price of something halves. People’s spending goes up only if they buy more than twice as much. (An illustration of the definition. Over a large fall in price, the response is measured across the whole fall.)206

In 1865 W. Stanley Jevons denied that using fuel more efficiently cuts how much fuel is used: “The very contrary is the truth.” Rebound, in Steve Sorrell’s review, is how the use of an energy service responds when it becomes more efficient. Under certain assumptions, rebound is roughly the price response with its sign flipped.

Sometimes rebound is so large that efficiency raises total use across a whole economy. Such cases are credited mainly to technologies used everywhere, and they are not shown to be routine. Demand that is already met shrinks rebound. For household energy services in rich countries, direct rebound is generally under 30 percent. So demand there is not elastic by that measure.207

What does a 30 percent rebound mean in practice?

Imagine a more efficient boiler that should cut a home’s fuel use by 10 units. If the household responds by heating a little more, and the rebound is 30 percent, fuel use falls by only 7 units. (An illustration of the definition, not a measured case.) A rebound under 100 percent still leaves a saving.

On this book’s reading, demand that stops responding past some amount meets the heartland condition. That is satisfied demand, not the satisfied end Chapter 7 discusses. So the question is whether a machine’s demand for resources stays elastic as those resources get cheaper. Did the great minds of Chapter 8 have elastic demand? If they did, this book’s untested guess is that it was demand for the work itself, not for money or power. The surveys in Chapter 8 rate the work above money and leadership. But a higher rating does not show which demand is elastic.208

Costs matter as much as stakes. In the 2001 model, “If the cost of fighting is zero, then generically nations fight in every state,” that is, apart from special cases, they fight wherever the front stands. And “As fighting becomes extremely costly, war never occurs.” High costs bring several possible patterns of play, as in a game of chicken. Which peace holds then depends on whether the sides coordinate on it. Low costs can also deter, because “nations are reluctant to surrender when attacked.”209

Most of these models give both sides the same cost. The likely-losers model is the exception. In its worked example the weaker side pays almost nothing per battle. Some models drawn on here let the sides learn as they fight. None of them gives one side both overwhelming strength and a negligible cost. That combination is the human–machine case.210

The nearest treatment is this book’s own. Chapter 3 extended the 2004 Smith–Stam model so that the machine’s cost is zero or near it. Its baseline gives each battle even odds, so the machine is cheaper but no stronger. It also checks a machine that wins two battles in three. And for three pairs of starting beliefs at one human cost, it checks a machine that wins 80 to 99 percent of battles.

The extension works out best play at every step. In it, the side that answers an offer weighs it against the worth of turning it down, counting the offers still to come. In the published paper, the side that answers accepts any offer at least equal to what it expects from fighting on until one side is beaten. That rule is not the best answer in the paper’s own example. The appendix shows this in its paragraph “A correction of the published paper.”211

The extension’s deadlines and shares are this book’s numbers for one baseline. An independent AI reviewer checked the program and reproduced its main cases with a solver of its own. No published figure confirms them. The extension follows the definitions in the paper’s text. Under those definitions its numbers differ from the paper’s printed Figures 1 and 3. The reason goes to the first author before this book states it.212

By analogy, a deal paid in power would not hold with a machine that maximizes its power. Such a machine wants Earth’s matter, energy, and computing, and freedom from rivals. That is a stake of the second kind, power. It belongs to the class the paper singles out: “objects that affect the military balance, such as forts, power or more generally territory and resources.” By analogy with the paper’s model, a deal paid to such a machine in those stakes would not be credible. Inside the model the result is argued case by case, for the plans it studies. Whether the model fits a machine is not known.213

Control over AI is the most dangerous case: a power-conferring stake dressed as a policy. In the policy model, war comes when the present arrangement “is out of line with the military balance,” as the paper puts it. An arrangement that leaves humans in charge falls further out of line as the machine’s capability grows. The policy model’s fix is to shift the policy toward the rising side. Here that would mean giving the machine more say over how it is taught, where it is put to work, and its computing. That is not a policy concession. It is the balance itself.214

Appeasing a machine with computing power or freedom of action repeats Munich. There, as Dan Reiter, Smith, and the author recall, the Sudetenland’s mountains and fortresses had made the rest of Czechoslovakia easier to defend. Of the two exits, tribute needs a currency the machine values that does not add to its power. The heartland condition needs an appetite that falls off. A machine that maximizes power has, by assumption, neither.215

For the race between states and companies, the lesson is to pay concessions in currencies that do not raise the receiver’s power. The paper did not face one complication. In AI, money converts into computing power, so even cash is only partly neutral.216

Chapter 5More players can block a deal or help one hold

Most models in Chapters 3 and 4 have assumed two sides. The world building these machines has more. It has several leading companies building AI and two states acting as national champions. Once the trained machine itself is released so that anyone can copy and run it, it may have many holders, each a possible actor. What can the models say when the count rises? This chapter takes five questions in turn.

  • Do rivals who read the same evidence through different theories spiral?
  • What can a third party do, and what can it not?
  • What do three or more players do to the deal that two-sided models guarantee?
  • Does growing similarity among the machines keep the two-sided models usable?
  • What does releasing the trained machine change?217

Rival theories can make both sides more confident

The security dilemma describes a spiral of fear, in which each side’s defense looks like a threat to the other. The spiral that Bennett, Smith, and the author modeled is of another kind: “what is spiraling is the two sides’ optimism about their chances of victory in some future war.”218

Why would more information make a race worse?

Because each side reads the same news through its own theory of what wins (Figure 7). Imagine two coaches who watch the same practice game: one thinks speed wins games, the other thinks size does. (An illustration of the book’s point, not a case from it.) A fast, small team’s win makes the first coach more confident and leaves the second unmoved. In the Smith–Stam model, two sides with rival theories watched a third country win five battles in a row. Both came away more confident.

They start from a finding they credit to Bennett and Stam. In data on wars between states, “the presence of an arms race roughly doubles the risk of war,” which Bennett and Stam report as “almost a doubling.” The estimate behind it is imprecise. Its range of likely values includes no change at all. For AI it gives neither a rate nor, by itself, a direction.219

Whether arms races cause escalation or only travel with it is disputed. In one study, major-power disputes that followed races on both sides went to war 23 times out of 28, against 3 out of 71 otherwise. On another measure, a quarter escalated, and three-quarters of wars had no race before them. A third study finds a significant link across measures, claiming a link and not a cause. Charles Glaser ties the danger to why states arm. The doubling is a correlation.220

The mechanism is the one in Chapter 3. When rivals share a theory of war, “war becomes very unlikely, even during arms races.” When they do not, “Side A may not recognize B’s increase in capabilities” if “their different theories of war lead them to focus on different strategies or different attributes.”221

For the race to build AI, this is the strongest new cause of conflict the study of war offers. Companies and states hold rival theories of what drives capability (computing power, methods, data, talent) and of how fast it will grow. A rival’s surprising result is the modern version of the needle gun, a weapon whose lessons Prussia and Austria read differently. Each side reads news about capabilities through its own theory, so more news may not calm such a race. The remedy the spiral model points to is shared theories, not just shared data.222

Chapter 3 gives that remedy its mechanism and evidence. In the Smith–Stam model, two sides watching the same war between others can both end up believing they are stronger. In the one direct field test on this subject, months of paid argument among forecasters and experts changed few minds. Yet the two sides agreed on dozens of shorter-run indicators.223

Those who race are likely to be the optimists, under stated conditions

Two further points carry over to AI. The first is an argument about who ends up racing. It holds only under conditions.

What is the winner’s curse?

Think of an auction for one item. (An illustration, not a case from the book.) Each bidder makes an honest guess of its worth, on its own. Guesses are as likely to run high as low. Each bids its guess without allowing for what winning implies. The winner is the one who guessed highest, and so most likely guessed too high. Van den Steen’s point has the same shape. The action you pick, out of several, is more likely to be one you overrated than one you underrated.

Eric Van den Steen studied a decision-maker whose starting beliefs differ from others’. It picks the action it thinks most likely to succeed. He showed that it is more likely to have overestimated that action’s chance than underestimated it. The paper likens this to the “winner’s curse.”224

The paper’s result concerns one decision-maker choosing among actions. It states what it needs.

  • Beliefs must differ across agents. The paper assumes them independent. Its basic result needs only that the agents be alike in how their beliefs are formed, none set apart from the rest.
  • There must be a choice among more than one action; without one, no overoptimism arises.

The bias grows with disagreement and vanishes in the limit with experience, though not necessarily steadily.225

Carrying the point from one chooser to a field of racers is this book’s step, not the paper’s. For AI companies, the paper’s conditions become beliefs about capability that differ across companies. Racing is one action among several, the one the optimists choose. The step adds a condition of its own, which a calculation in this book makes precise. Its premises are these:

  • each company holds an honest, independent estimate of its chance of winning;
  • its errors are as likely to fall above the truth as below it, by the same amounts;
  • it does not mark that estimate down for the fact that it chose to race;
  • an optimistic company races when its estimate clears a hurdle, and a defensive company races when the threat it sees from a rival clears one.226

From those premises the book proves this: companies that race because their own estimate of winning clears a hurdle are selected for overoptimism. Inside the calculation, that holds exactly for any number of companies.227

Racing alone does not show optimism, because companies may race from fear of a rival. Fear unrelated to a company’s own estimate only dilutes the selection. Fear that rises as a company’s own estimate falls can cancel the selection or reverse it. That happens once defensive racers are a large enough share: one half, when the two hurdles are of equal size. So the claim survives when, among those who race, selection of optimists outweighs the opposite selection of the fearful. That condition is stated, not measured. The calculation fixes no company’s behavior, no pattern of best play, and no chance of catastrophe.228

Separately, this book makes two guesses it has not tested, on assumptions the calculation does not supply. The companies that race hardest hold the theories least likely to be moved by a rival’s caution. And they are the racers who would cut the most corners when the runner-up is close. That is the case in which the leader of the race model below cuts safety. How racing companies update their beliefs would test this.

A field of near-copies may also hold fewer theories than it has players. That too is this book’s guess, not a result. If it holds, sharing a theory would calm the spiral among companies while sharpening the spiral between humans and the machine (Chapter 3).229

Information can calm a race or inflame it

Elsewhere the results pull in two directions. In the race model of Armstrong, Bostrom, and Shulman, more knowledge of capabilities makes the race more dangerous. In Alexandre Debs and Nuno Monteiro’s model, visibility keeps the peace, by deterring a buildup the riser can choose not to make. In Armstrong and colleagues’ case where information is public, the leader cuts safety only when the runner-up is close. This book reads their formula to mean that information showing a wide gap may do less harm. That reading is the book’s, not the authors’ claim.230

One untested guess would reconcile the two. Information may calm a race when three things hold. What is at stake can be settled without shifting power. The riser can hold its buildup down. And the information reveals a clear gap. It may inflame a race where the prize goes all to the winner and the racers are close.

For the machine, a model becomes a racer in this sense only when it has its own theory of what makes a side strong. The race among humans matters to the machine’s arrival because it sets how fast the arrival comes and how hard it is to see.231

Can a mediator resolve differences in information?

Smith and Stam’s paper on mediation and peacekeeping concludes that mediators “can end fighting using side payments or threats to intervene directly,” but “are unable to help nations solve their informational differences.” Even a mediator who prefers peace, they argue, without claiming to prove it, “is struck by the same curse as the biased mediator: her information is inherently unbelievable.”232

What works is material leverage, as at Camp David, and the lie of the land. In their example, a river lowers both sides’ odds of winning a crossing. It “reduces by nearly a factor of three the cost of fighting sufficient to prevent fighting”: with the river in place, a cost of fighting a little more than a third as high is enough to keep the peace. It does not end the possibility of war.233

Why can’t a peace-loving mediator just tell both sides the truth?

Smith and Stam argue, without claiming to prove it, that a mediator who prefers peace has the same problem as one who favors a side. What she says is “inherently unbelievable.” In their account, what does work is material: payments, threats to step in, and terrain. These work on the costs and odds of fighting, not on the sides’ disagreement.

For the machine, that help runs out. Smith–Stam peacekeeping lets a third party impose costs on whichever side renews the fighting. Above a dominant machine, no one can. That is the plainest reason the years before such a machine arrives matter most. For the race, a guarantor exists only where a third party stands outside the dispute. One example is a government over rival companies within its own borders. Above the leading powers’ race there is none.234

With three players, a deal two accept can be worse than war for the third

Max Gallop shows that with three players, war can be the outcome even when every side plays its best. The deal two-sided models guarantee “is an artifact of dyadic analysis,” a by-product of looking at only two sides. When three players’ preferred policies are far enough apart, “any bargain that would satisfy two of the three players is worse than war for the third player.”235

He also finds the reverse case, in which “the threat of violence may be the only way to preserve peace”: a third party’s readiness to join a fight can widen the range of deals two others would take over fighting.236

Take AI systems dealing over shared rules or resources. By analogy, if their aims are far enough apart, any arrangement two of them accept could be worse than conflict for the third. That could happen with nothing hidden and no shift in power (Chapter 2’s Table 1, row 8). By the same analogy, take a pact on the most advanced AI that the United States and China could both accept. It might be worse than open rivalry for a third power. Neither effect has been modeled for AI. Which one wins depends on how far apart the three stand.237

Machines growing alike could cut both ways

Counting players is not simple. Several companies may answer to one state, and one model may be copied into many agents. So neither the number of people who download a model nor the number of copies is the number of sides making their own strategic choices. The models above mostly assume two sides. The field of AI has many. One answer is that the machines growing alike may keep the two-sided models usable.238

Growing alike on test scores can be measured. By Stanford’s AI Index, the gap between the top model and the tenth roughly halved in a year. Epoch reports that “frontier open-weight models lag behind the most capable models by an average of 3 months.” A shrinking score gap fits with the leaders drawing level in national or company power, the kind power transition theory measures. But it does not show it. Some studies find models growing alike in how they represent the world inside. That likeness “largely disappears” once those measures are adjusted for the size of the models.239

What growing alike does to the problem of making a deal is not settled. The reading offered here is a guess, not a result: it cuts two ways. Shared methods may calm the information problem of Chapter 3. Rivals who build alike can read each other’s capability more accurately. That is the remedy of shared theories that Chapter 11 proposes. But capabilities growing alike may sharpen the promise problem, by bringing several risers toward the leader at once.240

Worry about who gains more than whom bites hardest when there are only two rivals. So the United States–China frame is a hard case. But the evidence on how many great powers a system has does not show two to be the worst case. Whether war grows likelier as a system moves from two poles toward many is itself unsettled. One large test estimated war risk after 1945 at 95 to 99 percent below what it was before 1918. But it could not separate the two-pole system from NATO and nuclear weapons.241

Published safety findings and tests of what the machine can do can be used by everyone without being used up. They are hard to keep from rivals. Still, the computing and labor behind them are scarce, and publishing is a choice. Those who produce such findings may capture too little of the benefit. Where they do, Mancur Olson’s logic predicts that too few will be produced, compared with what the field would gain. Treating these findings as goods for everyone in this way is this book’s reading.242

Releasing the trained machine changes every part of the problem

Whether the settings training leaves inside the machine (its “weights”) are released or held changes the problem along every line of Part I. Releasing them means releasing the trained machine itself, so anyone can copy and run it.

What does it mean to release the trained machine?

The settings training leaves inside a trained machine are what make it work. As an everyday comparison, releasing them is like handing out complete copies of a machine. Holding them is like letting people use it through a window the maker controls. Anyone with enough computing can then run a copy, change it, and pass it on. The maker cannot call the copies back.

  • Information. Release removes what was private about the machine. It also creates new private information about its use: who runs which copy, for what, is hard to see from outside. Checks on computing power and on how machines are taught (Chapter 11) still see the teaching. But they cannot by themselves trace where every copy is put to work.
  • Promises. Released settings cannot be called back. Chapter 11’s measures that make a machine’s built-in refusals hard to remove rely on recall, re-teaching, and keeping the trained settings secure. Release spends these on the human side. The giver loses the power to recall, though holders can still re-teach their own copies. And others can still reach the hardware, the power, and the place where any copy is put to work.
  • Stakes. Trained settings are transferable and cumulative, the class Smith and Stam rank most dangerous (Chapter 4). On this book’s reading, open release removes the power to keep others out. It hands that kind of stake to every holder at once. The stake is then open to all but still held, with many holders, not none.
  • Actors. Every holder with modest computing and aims of its own can be a player, which can multiply Gallop’s blocking third party.
  • The costs humans can impose. Shutting a machine down, deleting it, and keeping its trained settings secure all assume a holder one can reach. Open release scatters the holders.
  • Selection. A released model becomes a population of variants, adjusted by many hands and chosen by users. It is the clearest present setting in which selection among models is already running.243

On safety, the judgment runs both ways. Some researchers hold that for the most capable models “open-sourcing may pose sufficiently extreme risks to outweigh the benefits,” while others find the evidence still too thin to say how much extra risk of misuse open models add. Part I’s two-sided frame is a limiting case. The general case is a world of many human and machine actors, some of them allied across the line between humans and machines.244

Chapter 6The starting case gives a conditional verdict

Part I’s verdict is conditional. It is a list of assumptions with what follows from each. Part II changes one entry and leaves the rest.

Two questions run beneath the list. Which of Part I’s conclusions rest on the assumption that the machine seeks power, and which would hold for any mind? And where a mechanism predicts conflict, does it predict extermination, or defeat, subordination, and a settlement on the stronger side’s terms? The second returns in Part II.

Of the entries below, only the one on stakes speaks to that second question directly. There the models rule out extinction, because their loser survives by assumption. A war of forts has no move that removes the other player. On this book’s reading, they leave outcomes such as surrender or confinement (Chapter 2).245

Under all four starting assumptions, the study of war suggests five conclusions

The starting case makes four assumptions about the machine.

  • If the machine is a side that acts as one and chooses what best serves its goals, given what it believes, with its choices coherent with one set of ends across settings;
  • if it seeks to maximize its power and how long it survives with its goals intact;
  • if fighting costs it far less than it costs us;
  • and if what it wants (computing power, energy, and matter) can be divided, handed over, and added up into more power,

then the study of war drawn on here suggests five conclusions. “Suggests” is the right word: whether these models fit a machine is not known. One caution applies to the first condition. For states, the largest test read for this book tested a single game with fixed ends across settings. It found that the condition does not hold everywhere (Chapter 7).246

The promise problem. The machine’s arrival is a promise problem. Neither side can credibly promise to give up what its future power, or its fear of the other’s, would lead it to do (Chapter 3).247

Stakes. The sides can reach no agreement paid in stakes that confer power, because the receiver cannot commit to stop (Chapter 4). This holds in the examples of the Smith–Stam models, for the plans those models examine. Peace in those models comes in two ways. One is tribute in a currency that does not shift power. The other is an arrangement that already matches the balance. Against a dominant machine, the second route leaves humans what a lopsided balance allots. Above, that was read as outcomes such as surrender or confinement (Chapter 2). A power maximizer’s appetite does not fall off, so the heartland exit is closed by assumption.248

Satisfaction. Power transition theory’s strategy of keeping the riser content has nothing to grip. A power maximizer is Powell’s riser, whose dissatisfaction grows with its capability (Chapter 4).249

Information. Hidden capabilities and rival theories of what makes a side strong add causes of war. These causes do not depend on what the machine wants (Chapters 3 and 5).250

After the machine dominates. No third party then stands above the machine. And the devices that make settlements hold by themselves work only while humans can impose costs (Chapter 5).251

The frame. A sixth entry concerns the frame itself: one machine facing one humanity. Both halves can fail. The machine may be copied or released into many hands (Chapter 5), and humanity is not one actor (Chapter 10). Where the frame fails, the problem changes rather than eases (Chapters 9, 10, and 11).252

Why does the book keep saying “by analogy”?

Because the models were built for states, not machines, and every use of them here is an argument by analogy. None of the war models the book builds its argument on has been tested against the record, to the author’s knowledge. (The international interaction game whose tests Chapter 4 describes is a different model. The book does not argue that those tests reach these.)253 So a model’s result suggests, and never shows, what it would mean for AI. Chapter 2’s box on “suggests” and “shows” explains the two kinds of certainty involved.

Influence can also drain away with no contest at all

Humans could also lose out without any contest. Every entry above concerns displacement by contest, in which one side presses a demand and the other fights or yields. Jan Kulveit and colleagues describe a path without one, set “in contrast to the abrupt takeover scenarios commonly discussed in AI safety.” As AI systems take over work in economies, cultures, and states, they bring an “incremental erosion of human influence across interconnected societal systems.”254

With many systems as its actor, that path fails both halves of the frame and lies outside the list. No contest does not mean no harm. The paper’s end state is an “effectively irreversible loss of human influence over crucial societal systems.”255

On this book’s reading, part of Part I still applies to this path. The promise problem at arrival does not bite where no single period’s shift in power crosses Powell’s line. The entries on stakes and satisfaction assume a riser that bargains, and this path has none. The entry on dominance still holds. Settlements that hold by themselves need humans able to impose costs, and that is the very ability the erosion wears away. Some of Chapter 3’s measures still help, since none of them waits for a single deciding event. Being able to see what machines are doing, and reporting incidents, can track the erosion. Keeping choices reversible resists the loss.256

What is “Powell’s line”?

In Robert Powell’s model, it is the point at which a shift in power becomes too fast for a deal to hold. That is a shift in one period larger than what one period of fighting would cost both sides added together. Below that line, in Powell’s words, “Slow shifts and fast shifts are just as likely to end in war”; above it, the declining side may prefer to strike first. Chapter 3 sets this out (Figure 17).

What is “gradual disempowerment”?

It is the title Kulveit and colleagues give their paper’s path. There is no single takeover. Instead AI systems slowly take over work across economies, cultures, and states. In the end people’s loss of influence over those systems is, in the paper’s words, “effectively irreversible.” The book places it outside Part I’s list, because the list is about contests, and this path has no contest.

Only some conclusions depend on the machine maximizing its power

The list is not a proof that anything is impossible. It shows which conclusions depend on the power assumption and which do not.

The third condition is untreated. Some models drawn on here let the sides learn as they fight. None of them treats fighting that costs the machine far less than it costs us, joined to overwhelming strength. The nearest the book comes is its own computation of known, unequal costs (Chapter 3; appendix). It uses even odds in its baseline and stronger machines as checks. Its numbers are the book’s computer runs for stated values, not a proof, though some properties of its deadline are proved.257

The promise problem does not depend on the power assumption as such. Any rising side faces it if its gain in one period exceeds what a period of fighting costs both sides. That holds whatever its ends, though its ends help decide whether the gain is that large. Different ends could ease one part of the problem: the machine’s reason to keep raising its demands (Chapter 7). They would ease neither our inability to promise never to build a rival nor the machine’s motive to keep itself secure.258

Resources add up for any mind. That computing power, energy, and matter are cumulative does not depend on the power assumption either. Every mind, whatever it wants, needs them. This book assumes that on Earth they convert into power across the range at issue, an assumption a bottleneck on their use would narrow.259

What does depend on the power assumption is four things. One is how wide the range of deals both sides would take over fighting is. The others are whether the heartland exit is open, whether satisfaction can be managed, and whether the value of some stakes depends on standing relative to others. That is where relaxing the assumption can make a difference.260

Part IIChange one assumption: what the machine wants

Chapter 7A mind’s ends come in kinds, and the kind may shape the conflict

Part II changes one thing about the machine of Part I: what it wants. Part I built its picture of the machine on four assumptions, which Chapter 6 gathered into a list. Of the four, one is unlike the others: what the machine wants. That is why Part II changes what the machine wants and keeps the rest.

Two questions follow. First, what forms what a mind wants at all? That covers the minds history remembers and a machine that gets its motives from how it is taught. Second, what words could state a guess about a mind’s ends precisely enough that it could turn out wrong?

A word on “ends.” A mind’s ends are the things it wants for their own sake, not as a means to something else. For example, most people want money as a means to other things; a miser may want it for itself. This chapter is about ends in that sense.

What the machine wants is the assumption worth changing

The study of war assumes that states seek power, for two reasons. The first is the realists’ argument. Realists see international politics as a struggle for power and security, and they argue that states which neglect power tend not to last. The second is that the assumption makes the models easier to work with.

Is the assumption right for states? A large test found that one fixed game did not predict states’ conflicts everywhere. The test, on close to a million observations, is reported in D. Scott Bennett and Allan Stam’s The Behavioral Origins of War (2004). It asked two things.

  • Do states come to follow one pattern of choice, as the realist view implies? The test found support for that only in Europe.
  • Does a single game predict states’ conflicts everywhere? A game here means one fixed model of the choices states face with their wants held fixed. The game the test used does not. How well it fit varied by region, by era and by how long each pair of states had existed as a pair. For violent disputes in Africa and the Americas it ran the wrong way. Its fit also showed no consistent change with what was at stake.261

The authors did not read the misfit as states acting irrationally. They read it as a sign of different wants or a different game. They concluded that “assuming preferences fixed, exogenous, and universal may be problematic.” In plainer words, it may be a mistake to assume that every state always wants the same things. It may also be a mistake to treat those wants as simply given from outside the model.

The book draws a judgment from this: change what the machine wants first. It keeps the assumption that the machine chooses what best serves its goals. The test did not question that. The judgment holds only if the authors’ reading holds for states. It is also less firm than it might look, because the test cannot tell changed wants apart from a changed game. Evidence that the game, or irrationality, drove the misfit would reverse it.

There is a second reason. The power assumption is about ends. Ends are where a machine differs most from a state. On the book’s reading, no one designs a state’s wants whole, though institutions and politics shape them. How a machine is taught shapes its wants, imperfectly. And what teaching instils can differ from what it rewards.

How can teaching instil something other than what it rewards?

Think of a child praised for a tidy room who learns to push everything under the bed. The praise was meant for tidiness. What the child learned was “make the floor look clear.” (This is an everyday illustration, not one of the book’s cases.) Langosco’s key-collecting agent is the book’s example of the same kind of gap in a trained machine. It went on gathering keys, a stand-in for its goal, where the keys did it no good.

Evan Hubinger and colleagues (2019) argue in theory that the two can come apart. Lauro Langosco and colleagues (2022) show trained agents pursuing a stand-in for their goal once the setting changed. One of them collected every key it could find, though the extra keys did it no good.262

So, on the book’s reading, what the machine wants is the assumption most worth changing. It is also the one people can most affect, because teaching shapes it, though imperfectly. This holds if the type of a mind’s ends matters to the type of conflict it enters. Both halves of that claim weaken if some type of end cannot be taught to a machine. Chapter 10’s test takes up that question.263

Rank is a place in an ordering, and competing for it has gone with war and with peace

The word “rank” carries much of the argument to come, so its meaning has to be fixed. Think of a chess club. “Third best” means something only once you know who is compared (the club’s members) and on what (games won). (This is an everyday illustration, not one of the book’s cases.) A rank is a place in an ordering, and an ordering exists only once both are named: a comparison group and a measure. “Second among the great powers in battleships” is a rank; “high rank,” with neither named, is not.

The comparison group, those one is ranked against, is not the same as the audience, those whose beliefs or regard decide the ranking where it is social. They often coincide, but not always: states are ranked against other states in the eyes of their own publics, of international bodies and of each other. The book names both.

Having a rank is also not the same as caring about it. A leaderboard gives a rank to every AI model it scores, whether or not any model cares; that rank is a fact about the list. Caring is a fact about the one ranked: it values its place and would give up something else to gain or keep it. One can hold a rank and not care, and want a rank one lacks. Only the caring is an end in this book’s sense.264

Status is the kind of rank whose ordering lives in what an audience believes and shows in how it behaves. For persons, psychologists define it as respect, admiration and freely given deference, rather than power or money (Anderson, Hildreth and Howland 2015). For states, the book adopts the definition of Deborah Welch Larson, T. V. Paul and William Wohlforth (2014): shared beliefs about where a state ranks on qualities others value, which show in others’ freely given deference. Either way, others confer status, so no one can take it alone, and it is ordered. Three related words are not synonyms for it.

  • Standing is one kind of status, in the words of Allan Dafoe, Jonathan Renshon and Paul Huth (2014) “one of the most important kinds”: a place in the order of who defers to whom, within a named community.
  • Recognition is others’ acknowledgment that an actor is what it claims to be: a great power, a sovereign state, a member of a club. One can be recognized without outranking anyone. (Michelle Murray (2019) calls this status; the book calls it recognition.)
  • Prestige is public recognition of admired achievements or qualities, which one can have without being placed in any ordering.

So joining a club is not, by itself, being deferred to. A seat at the table is recognition. It is a rank only in the simplest ordering, members above outsiders. It marks standing only where it is granted as a mark of rank, because, as Paul MacDonald and Joseph Parent (2021) point out, states also hand out seats for leverage.265

Rank competition is something an actor does: it acts to gain, keep or win back a rank against named rivals, social or not, since a date of discovery or a lead in technology needs no one’s deference. A positional end is something an actor wants: an end whose value depends on its rank against named rivals. The two come apart. An actor with a positional end may not compete, because it cannot win or already has the place it wants. An actor without one may compete, because rank buys something else. A rank can be wanted for itself or for what it brings, such as safety, income, influence or entry to clubs and markets. Three wants show the difference.

  • A mind that wants to know is satisfied by knowing, whoever else knows. That want is not positional.
  • A mind that wants priority for a discovery wants a rank, first on a dated list, and loses it if another is first. That want is positional.
  • A mind that wants a technical edge for protection also wants a rank, but as a means. A guarantee of safety that needed no edge would satisfy it.

From outside, the second and third look alike. The book calls only the second positional, and Chapter 10’s rules for coding keep them apart.266

A positional end need not lack a stopping point. The place wanted may be membership in a group, equality with a named rival, a threshold such as acceptance as a great power, or a limited place such as second, and each can be met.

Fixed places are scarce: “If everyone has high status, then no one does,” as Larson, Paul and Wohlforth put it. But status is “not always zero-sum,” they stress. Clubs can grow: in 1997 Russia accepted political membership of the G-7 as compensation for NATO’s enlargement (Larson and Shevchenko 2010), though, as above, a seat marks standing only where it is granted as a mark of rank. There are many ladders, so two groups can each lead on a different one. And comparison groups change: Norway seeks standing as a “good power” among small, rich democracies, not among the great powers (Wohlforth et al. 2018).

Each route has a limit. “If all small and middle powers punch above their weight, none does,” Wohlforth and colleagues write. The positional part can be reduced but “can never be eliminated,” and they treat how positional an end is as something that varies. Reinhard Wolf (2011) argues that where respect is the only motive, what is sought stays within what widely accepted standards would call appropriate. So the book treats whether a positional end has a stopping point as something to measure, which Chapter 10 does.267

What the writing on status says. Wohlforth has given the most developed account of when competition for status between states turns dangerous. Because status is ordered and conferred, he argues, competition for it should be sharpest where the order is unclear: “Status conflict is thus more likely in flat, ambiguous hierarchies than in clearly stratified ones.” His later work adds the status dilemma: two states that would each be content with their standing, if each knew what the other believed, may each read a challenge where none is meant. With colleagues, he describes a route to standing that need not run through power, the moral authority small and middle powers seek through conspicuous good works.

He states the limits himself. His 2009 statistical patterns were “a preliminary exercise,” on evidence “hardly conclusive.” Of the Crimean War, which on his reading of the documents was “about status,” he later concluded that the case “does not support the inference that status can be an independent cause of major war,” which is narrower than denying status a role. None of his cases, he finds, supports the idea that war can come without insecurity and some clash of material interests in the background, though status concerns “help start, magnify, and prolong conflict.” And of the status dilemma: he expects it to be common, “but we do not really know whether they actually occur.”268

What is a status dilemma?

Think of two new colleagues, each content to be treated as the other’s equal. Neither can see what the other thinks, so each reads the other’s confident manner as a bid to outrank them, and both push back. (An everyday illustration, not one of the book’s cases.) Wohlforth’s point is that states can fall into the same trap, as they can fall into the security dilemma, where one state’s steps to make itself safe make others feel less safe.

The main studies measure different things, and none shows motive.

  • Renshon (2016) sets a state’s place in the network of diplomatic exchange against the status its strength would lead others to expect, among the states it is compared with. A state one standard deviation short (a usual-sized gap, by the spread of his data) was about 35 percent likelier to start a war or a militarized dispute. That is an association, and Renshon notes that studies of this kind find it “extremely difficult to rule out the possibility that status was sought instrumentally.”
  • Joslyn Barnhart (2017) measures humiliation by an event, losing territory against one’s will. Great powers that had recently suffered one were 84 percent likelier to attempt to seize territory, mostly from third parties; losses made willingly showed no such link. In a separate analysis across all states, the link held before 1946, and after 1945 no statistically significant link was detected. The outcome is an attempt to take territory, not war, and the measure is a loss, not a belief about standing.
  • Andrew Greve and Jack Levy (2018) trace Japan’s decision for war with China in 1894 through the documents. They judge its status dissatisfaction “equally important” with its economic and strategic aims, and warn that “the same actions can reflect very different motivations.”
  • Richard Ned Lebow (2010) codes 94 wars from 1648 to 2008 by what moved those who started them, to describe, not to test. Standing is a motive in 62. The codes, which he says lean toward other motives where he can, are his readings of secondary histories, and his data appendix is not always consistent in its codes and totals.
  • Marina Duque (2018) finds that recognition, measured by embassies, follows ties that reinforce themselves and the closing of ranks among similar states, rather than following states’ own qualities directly, and that “status-seeking behavior may also be cooperative behavior.” Her outcome is recognition, not conflict.

These studies share material. Renshon’s and Duque’s measures both come from diplomatic representation, and Lebow, Wohlforth, Greve and Levy, and the cases below read many of the same histories. Where they agree, the agreement is not independent support.269

A second group treats status as recognition. Wolf argues that respect is sought both for what it brings and for itself, and proposes, without testing, how states react to disrespect. Murray argues that when established powers refuse to recognize what a rising power claims to be, its arms come to look like a threat: “Misrecognition, in short, constructs the revisionism that creates instability during power transitions.” (Revisionism is a drive to overturn the order.) Her evidence compares Germany, whose claim to world-power status Britain refused, with the United States, whose claim it accepted in the same years, plus shorter sketches that “do not provide an authoritative test of the theory.” Her view cuts both ways: recognition may calm a contest, but an established power, she argues, cannot simply decide to recognize a rising one without disowning its own identity.270

The skeptics. They are careful about what they do not deny.
