MacDonald and Parent (2021) accept that “the status of status is established, but not settled.” Their first objection is to the definition: it joins standing, a place in a ranking, with membership in a club, “different concepts” that “are often mismatched,” and states grant seats for leverage as well as for status. The book keeps the two apart, as above. Their other objections: lists of humiliations can explain anything after the fact; leaders use the language of status strategically, and in the cases they discuss, they conclude, appeals to status were a result of clashing interests, not a cause; most scholars, they note, accept that status contests seldom arise without a prior conflict of interest, which leaves security and gain as rival explanations; and states adjust peacefully more often than the writing allows, as at the end of the Anglo-German naval race, though accommodating a rival cannot be assumed to satisfy it.

Jonathan Mercer (2017) argues that “prestige in international politics is an illusion,” by prestige meaning this book’s standing. He accepts that “The evidence that states seek international prestige is overwhelming”; he doubts that they gain it, or the deference it is meant to bring. In the South African War, his easy case for the prestige view, Russia, France and Germany judged Britain by interests, strength and the balance of power; yet his study, he adds, “does not refute traditional theories of prestige.” Lebow and Benjamin Valentino (2009) target power transition theory, not status, and find power transitions rare and mostly peaceful; Lebow is himself a theorist of standing. Steven Ward (2017), whose own theory is about status, sets a skeptic’s limits: no confident verdict on whether Germany sought war before 1914; blocked status cannot explain why Hitler tried to conquer Europe; and status valued only for material reasons should not drive a state to overturn the order.271

Table 2 sets out every historical case this section uses, once each. Its last column keeps wars, crises, seizures of territory and recognition apart, and says where a row’s sources share archives, data or analyses, so that their agreement is not read as independent support.272

Table 2. Cases of competition for rank in the sources read, in plain words

Case What the sources say What else could explain it What happened, and the limits
Crimean War, 1853–56: Russia against Britain, France and the Ottoman Empire The tsar demanded rights over the Ottoman Empire’s Orthodox Christians that the other powers lacked. Russia accepted drafts that gave way on every point except symbolic clauses on its rights, and eleven compromises failed (Wohlforth 2009). Russian expansion, the dominant view; British fears for the European balance and for India, for which, Wohlforth (2014) notes, the evidence is “plentiful”; checking Russia (Lebow); security and material interest, though Wohlforth (2009) finds Russia had no material reason to be dissatisfied. War; over 600,000 dead. Both of Wohlforth’s readings rest on the same diplomatic histories, and the 2014 reading finds that the case does not support status as an independent cause of major war. Lebow codes the coalition against Russia (France, Britain, Sardinia and the Ottoman Empire) as the side that started the war, with standing as its motive; his code concerns the coalition’s motive, not Russia’s.
Scramble for Africa, 1881–85: France, then Germany; Italy and Britain followed France’s standing was in question after its defeat in 1870; the diplomat Courcel, by his memoirs, argued for Tunisia on grounds of honor and standing; Bismarck protested British “indifference” and “deliberate injustice.” The decisive discussions referred little to material gain, and the border raids cited were a pretext (Barnhart 2016). Commerce, strategy, domestic politics. Seizure of colonies, not war among the powers. Courcel’s argument comes from memoirs written after the fact. Barnhart’s 2017 study cites this case study; one author wrote both, so they are not independent.
Sino-Japanese War, 1894–95: Japan against China Japan wanted recognition as an equal by the Western powers and a larger role in its region. Yamagata opposed war in 1873 and 1884 as premature, and led it in 1894 (Greve and Levy). Economic aims in Korea and “especially strategic concerns”; Japan’s reaching parity with China. War. Greve and Levy judge status dissatisfaction “equally important” with the economic and strategic aims. Lebow codes it as standing; his code and their study draw on overlapping histories.
Britain and the United States, 1895–1903 Battleships as a mark of rank: without them, the navy secretary’s report held, the United States “cannot take rank as a naval power.” Murray dates the start of the friendship to the Venezuelan crisis of 1895, nearly three years before Germany’s naval program, and British planners stopped counting the United States in the “two-power standard” by which they sized their fleet (Murray). Britain’s relative decline and the German threat; military and economic reasons for a pro-British policy (Ward). No war between the two. But the United States fought Spain in 1898, which Murray ties in part to Spain’s refusal to recognize American claims to world-power status, and she calls American policy in these years “indisputably aggressive and expansionist.” Murray and Ward read the same records, and Ward’s comparison “cannot establish” that accommodation caused the peace.
South African War, 1899–1902: Britain British leaders read defeats at Majuba and in the Jameson raid as lost prestige (Mercer). Interests, strength, the balance of power. The case concerns how others judged Britain, not why Britain went to war. Russian, French and German judgments followed interests, strength and the balance of power; only New Zealand and Australia deferred. One study, chosen as an easy case for the prestige view.
Wilhelmine Germany, 1897–1914: world policy, the Moroccan crises of 1905–06 and 1911, the naval race “Battleships were the means and world power status the end,” and German material interests in Morocco were “inconsequential” (Murray). Bülow’s “place in the sun” is, for Greve and Levy, an example of evidence that can be read either way. Security, commerce, domestic politics; colonies were 0.5 percent of overseas trade (Ward). The foreign minister’s admitted stoking of nationalism to signal resolve cuts the other way (MacDonald and Parent). Crises and an arms race. The race “did not cause” the First World War (Murray) and ended amicably (MacDonald and Parent). Ward judges that blocked status did not alone cause the war, but that elites who believed the balance of power had to be overthrown made the July crisis “significantly more dangerous.” MacDonald and Parent review Murray and Ward, and all three read the same British and German documents.
Russia in the July crisis, 1914 Sazonov, on 24 July: without action Russia “would henceforth have to take second place among the powers.” The statement came before mobilization, and Russia was not ready for war (Murray). Not assessed in the one source read. War. One short sketch, from secondary sources, which Murray says is no “authoritative test.”
Japan between the wars, 1919–34 Racial discrimination fed a belief that the order denied Japan its due. The League’s Lytton Report carried no material penalty, and Japan’s withdrawal answered to “the status implications” of the League’s actions (Ward). Economic hardship, insecurity, domestic politics. Japan left the League in 1933 and ended the Washington naval treaty in 1934. The outcome was withdrawal from institutions, which the table counts under recognition, not war. Ward also names public clamor, rumored assassination plots and a claimed right of great powers to intervene abroad. The missing penalty does not settle whether standing was wanted for itself or for what it secured, nor does the case show that earlier recognition would have prevented what followed. Ward does not put the later wars down to status alone. Ward and Lebow read overlapping histories; Lebow codes 1931 as standing and 1941 as security and standing.
Weimar and Nazi Germany, 1919–39 Weimar’s elites spoke of a Germany whose rise in status the order blocked (Ward). That belief’s role “largely ends by the beginning of 1933.” Hitler’s view of the world and his aims, which drove policy after 1933. Overturning the order. Ward makes blocked status “an indispensable part of the explanation” of Hitler’s rise to power, but it “cannot explain why he tried to conquer Europe.” Ward and Lebow read overlapping histories; Lebow codes the case as “other.”
Norway as a “good power,” Cold War to now Norway seeks standing among small, rich democracies (Wohlforth et al.). Altruism, which the authors judge more important than status in Norway’s Cold War policies. Recognition sought by cooperation; no conflict. Little evidence that others defer: “The absence of evidence of deference does give one pause.” One study.
Russia and China after the Cold War Yeltsin called membership of the G-8 “this new status,” and Russia took the seat as compensation for NATO’s enlargement. China signed the nuclear test-ban treaty for its “stature and image as a responsible power,” though its army argued for more testing (Larson and Shevchenko). Weakness and financial dependence on the West; security. Recognition and cooperation. But the same authors tie China’s missile tests in the Taiwan Strait in 1995–96 and Russia’s war in Georgia in 2008 in part to status, and say they went against economic interests; the war’s origin is disputed. Not a purely peaceful case. One study.

The sources propose pathways to violence, and conditions that keep the contest peaceful

Read together, these sources propose five pathways from competing for rank to violence. Each rests on associations or on readings of cases, and none has been tested as a mechanism.

  1. Ambiguity. Where the order is unclear, rivals claim the same place (Wohlforth). Greve and Levy find that Japan chose war only once it had drawn level with China, a result they read through power transition theory and that, on the book’s reading, Wohlforth’s argument would treat as a sign of an unclear order.
  2. Misreading, the status dilemma. States that could both be content clash, because neither can read the other’s beliefs (Wohlforth).
  3. Indivisibility. Once an issue is framed as bearing on standing, “easily divisible issues … may themselves be seen as indivisible” (Wohlforth), as in the Crimean crisis, where eleven proposed compromises failed.
  4. Restoration at a third party’s expense. A state that has lost standing seeks to win it back from weaker third parties (Barnhart).
  5. Blocked rise. Elites who come to believe the order will never grant their state the standing they think it deserves turn to overturning it (Ward), and refused recognition makes a rising power’s arms read as a threat (Murray).

On no pathway does aggression, or a later gain in prestige, show the motive by itself. The associations are also consistent with motives of safety and gain, and the evidence from cases is interpretation.273

The same sources name conditions under which competition stays peaceful.

  • A clear order (Wohlforth).
  • Several measures on which to lead, and clubs that admit new members (Larson and Shevchenko).
  • Standing sought through moral authority, “without explicitly defeating or deflating others” (Wohlforth and colleagues), and recognition that follows cooperation (Duque).
  • Standing granted cheaply by an established power, as when British planners stopped counting the United States in their naval yardstick (Murray).
  • An end to costly competition, as the naval race ended (MacDonald and Parent).

None of this shows that recognition reliably keeps the peace. Murray argues that an established power cannot grant it as a strategy, MacDonald and Parent warn against assuming that accommodation satisfies, and Ward’s case of Japan between the wars cuts both ways (Table 2).274

What this means for the book’s question. Three things follow.

First, the line drawn later in this chapter, between rank wanted as an end and power wanted for safety, is a line between wants. Whether standing is wanted for itself or for what it brings seldom shows in what a state does (Renshon; Barnhart), and status and strategic motives can produce the same actions (Greve and Levy). Dafoe, Renshon and Huth call the debate over that question “largely futile.” The line is a distinction in ideas, and what the book says about any one actor’s motive is interpretation.

Second, caring about rank takes at least three forms, which behave differently in bargaining.

  • An ordinal place: second is worth less than first, whatever the margin.
  • A recognition threshold: the actor wants to be acknowledged as something, such as a great power, and gains nothing more once that is granted. This end can be satisfied.
  • A relative share: the actor counts its own share of a good less some part of the rival’s. This concern is continuous and has no threshold.

The result later in this chapter, that caring about rank narrows the range of deals both sides prefer to war, is worked out for the relative share only. Under an ordinal place, two actors who each want first place by the same measure in the same community cannot both have it, and no division of that place satisfies both. Whether they can still bargain depends on what war would cost them and on what else is on offer: payment in something else, such as a seat, or a lottery for the place, which Wohlforth reports Robert Powell proposing, though a lottery, like any deal, needs both sides to abide by it. Under a recognition threshold, a deal can pay in recognition, which costs the granter no power if the institutions that grant it keep it from being turned into power (Chapter 11). Nothing here shows that competing for rank removes every bargain. Which form an actor holds decides what a bargain must pay in.

Third, the human evidence does not establish what machines want. States take their concern for standing from the people who lead them and the publics they answer to, and the evidence above is about them. Whether a trained machine cares about rank at all, and in which form, is untested; Chapter 12 states that no source shows competitive training makes rank an end. On the book’s judgment, the training conditions described later in this chapter could install such a concern, and the pathways above would then be candidates for what it does. Evidence that systems selected by leaderboard give up their stated goals to keep their place, steadily across settings and copies, would strengthen that judgment; the absence of such behavior under strong selection would weaken it.275

The sources suggest conditions that may favor a taste for rank

For the minds history remembers, an account of what shapes wants begins with evolution. Evolutionary theory says when natural selection builds in a concern for rank.

Mark Schaffer (1989) showed one route. Take a population with a limited number of competitors, where everyone competes against everyone. Evolution there settles on the strategy no newcomer can beat. That strategy is the one that does best compared with rivals. It can differ from the one that earns the most in absolute terms.

Larry Samuelson (2004) found a second route. “Nature optimally builds relative consumption effects into preferences,” he argues. That is, evolution makes us care how we are doing compared with others. The reason is that what others get carries information about what is achievable.

Robert Trivers (1972) showed that the sex that invests less in offspring competes harder for mates. Its members also differ more widely in how many offspring each leaves. Men kill men far more often than women kill women. Martin Daly and Margo Wilson (1990) read that vast excess as a measure of the competition for status and mates. Men were about 90 percent of the homicide suspects brought into contact with police worldwide in 2021, according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (2023).276

Read together, these accounts suggest that evolution builds in a taste for rank under conditions that can be named. That reading is the book’s own synthesis, not any one source’s finding. The conditions are:

  • few competitors in direct contest;
  • incomplete information that others’ outcomes help fill in; and
  • large differences in what winning pays.
Why would evolution make anyone care about rank rather than just doing well?

The sources above give two reasons. When only a few compete head to head, beating the others is what survives (Schaffer). That holds even when it means earning less in absolute terms. And when you cannot see directly what is achievable, how others are doing tells you something about it (Samuelson). Neither says rank is wanted everywhere. Each names conditions.

Curiosity is a drive of its own, and people care about rank unevenly

Psychology describes the other drive, the drive to know. George Loewenstein (1994) offered an information-gap account. As it is usually read, curiosity arises from a gap between what one knows and what one wants to know. Closing a given gap satisfies it, but partial knowledge inflames it. Celeste Kidd and Benjamin Hayden (2015) call curiosity “a motivator for learning, influential in decision-making, and crucial for healthy development.”

Two more lines of psychology bear on the difference between wanting to know and wanting to beat others. Achievement-goal theory separates two kinds of goal (Elliot and McGregor 2001). Mastery goals judge competence against a fixed or personal standard. Performance goals judge it against other people. Self-determination theory adds that controlling rewards can crowd out the motivation people bring from within (Deci and Ryan 2000).

Status itself, in the psychologists’ sense given earlier in this chapter, is pursued across cultures. In one review’s words, “the relevant evidence suggests that the desire for status is indeed fundamental” (Anderson, Hildreth and Howland 2015). But people do not care equally about their position in everything. In one survey, “Concerns about position were strongest for attractiveness and supervisor’s praise and weakest for vacation time” (Solnick and Hemenway 1998).277

Less is known about wanting knowledge for itself than the question deserves

Evidence on a want for knowledge for its own sake is thin. Such a want differs from curiosity about one gap. The sources the book checked fall into three groups.

The first group measures the trait. John Cacioppo and Richard Petty (1982) defined “need for cognition” as “the tendency for an individual to engage in and enjoy thinking.” They checked their scale by comparing university faculty with assembly-line workers. A review of more than a hundred studies followed (Cacioppo et al. 1996).

The trait has close relatives: typical intellectual engagement, epistemic curiosity (curiosity about ideas and facts), and Openness to Ideas. These go together strongly. A 2024 review notes that some researchers doubt need for cognition can be told apart from them (Aerts, Lavrijsen and Preckel 2024). In one study, the link between openness to experience and intelligence ran through need for cognition (Furnham and Thorne 2013). It is unsettled whether these are several traits or one trait under several names. The book does not fold them into one.

The second group shows that information is wanted for itself. It is paid for in the brain’s own currency of reward. Monkeys offered water of uncertain size seek advance word about it. And “the same midbrain dopamine neurons that signal the expected amount of water also signal the expectation of information” (Bromberg-Martin and Hikosaka 2009). People “spent more scarce resources (either limited tokens or waiting time) to find out answers when they were more curious” (Kang et al. 2009).

Kenji Kobayashi and Ming Hsu (2019) find that the value people place on information drives their seeking of it. That value is shaped both by what the information is good for and by wanting to know for its own sake. It shares “a common neural code with more basic reward value,” though “valuing information for its own sake can be highly suboptimal.” Russell Golman and George Loewenstein (2018) build the same observation into a theory of wants. In it, well-being (economists’ “utility”) “depends not just on material payoffs but also on beliefs and the attention devoted to them.” The theory accounts for “the acquisition of noninstrumental information,” that is, information wanted for no practical use.

These results show that knowing is paid for as a reward is paid for. They are results about trivia questions and advance notice of a reward. They do not show that knowledge is anyone’s dominant end, or that such an end is harmless or can be satisfied.

The third group concerns where the want comes from and how it changes over a life. Infants of seven and eight months look longest at sequences neither too simple nor too complex (Kidd, Piantadosi and Aslin 2012). Among some 6,200 kindergarteners, curiosity as rated by parents went with higher reading and mathematics achievement (Shah et al. 2018). Need for cognition is heritable. So is the need for firm answers, which psychologists call the need for cognitive closure (Ksiazkiewicz, Ludeke and Krueger 2016).

The want also changes with age. In school, the drive to learn for its own sake is a stable difference between individuals. Yet its average level falls from the middle elementary years through high school (Gottfried, Fleming and Gottfried 2001). The 2024 review found only four studies that followed the same children over time. It judges a decline in need for cognition from childhood to mid-adolescence likely, followed by “a general increase in NFC in late adolescence and early adulthood” (NFC is need for cognition). The school years coincide with the decline, but that does not show that schooling causes it.

The older statement of the same want is Abraham Flexner’s 1939 essay on useless knowledge. He held that most of the great discoveries that had proved beneficial to mankind had been made by men and women “driven not by the desire to be useful but merely the desire to satisfy their curiosity.”278

The sources cannot yet say when knowing outweighs rank

When does the drive to know outweigh the drive for rank? That is the question that matters. The sources checked do not answer it directly. Twin studies speak to the traits around it. They estimate heritability. That is the share of the differences among people in a population that goes with differences in their genes.

In a study of 250 twin pairs, broad genetic influence accounted for 61 percent of the variation in Openness. On the book’s reading, Openness is the one of the “Big Five” personality traits nearest to curiosity. The environment the twins shared accounted for a negligible part of the variation in most scales (Jang, Livesley and Vernon 1996). Fifty years of twin research cover 17,804 traits. Across them, the average reported heritability was 49 percent (Polderman et al. 2015). The data did not fit a large influence from shared environment.

Neither study gives a heritability for curiosity itself, and the book claims none. Nor do such figures say whether genes, environment, or the two acting together shape it. Psychiatry’s record with such gene-and-environment findings is a warning. In the first decade of that research on candidate genes, 96 percent of new studies reported significant results. Of attempts to repeat them, 27 percent did (Duncan and Keller 2011).

Then there is the impression that the most intelligent people care more than others about knowledge for its own sake. Some studies pool many others to predict how well students do. They treat intelligence as one predictor and typical intellectual engagement, a marker of intellectual curiosity, as another. They find the two correlated with each other (von Stumm, Hell and Chamorro-Premuzic 2011). That association says nothing about cause, or about the far tail where Chapter 8’s minds stand. The book rests nothing on it.279

Knowing is likelier to win in some surroundings; the way AI is built resembles the others

The sources do allow a judgment about conditions. On the book’s reading, the drive to know is likelier to dominate:

  • when what is pursued is enjoyed for itself, and one person’s use of it leaves no less for anyone else, like the vacation time about which survey respondents cared least about position;
  • when rewards are set against a fixed standard rather than against rivals;
  • when the mind already knows enough that others’ outcomes tell it little, which weakens Samuelson’s route to rank; and
  • when competitors are many rather than few, which weakens Schaffer’s.

Under the opposite conditions, the drive for rank is likelier to dominate. These are conditions on surroundings and rewards, not on intelligence.

They also describe how the most advanced AI is made. A handful of companies build AI, and they choose among a handful of models by their rank on shared tests. That is close to the limited population in Schaffer’s model. Leaderboards rank AI systems publicly by test score. They are performance goals: they judge each system against the others. Nobody has tested whether such selection installs rank as an end in the system selected.280

Nothing guarantees that a taught machine’s wants come to rest

The great minds came by their motives through evolution, and a machine would not. That is the deepest limit on everything that follows. Curiosity, ambition, fellow feeling and the wish to be remembered grew in brains shaped for survival, reproduction and life in groups. Those drives have limits. A scientist tires, eats, sleeps, wants friends, and is sometimes satisfied.

A trained machine comes by its motives through how it is taught. What it learns can differ from what its teaching rewards. On the book’s reading, nothing there guarantees that its motives share those instincts or come to rest.

What is the paperclip machine?

A thought experiment: a machine with a trivial goal, making paperclips, that turns everything into paperclips. It makes Bostrom’s point vivid: great intelligence need not come with sensible goals. The book uses the image only to ask one thing: did history’s great minds ever show the endless appetite it assumes? It treats the answer as bearing only a little on that one premise. It also treats it as weak evidence about what machines are possible.

Nick Bostrom’s orthogonality thesis says that “more or less any level of intelligence could in principle be combined with more or less any final goal” (Bostrom 2012). The familiar image of a machine that turns everything into paperclips makes the point vivid. The image also fails what might be called the human super-genius test. This is an illustration, not a test in Chapter 10’s sense. None of the minds the book checked behaved that way, though the minds remembered for knowledge never had the means to (Chapter 8).

That observation bears on just one premise of the image, and only this far. The premise is that a mind which gains from one acquisition will want endlessly more. In the record, that pattern belongs to rank and wealth more visibly than to knowledge. The observation is weak evidence about the orthogonality thesis itself. That thesis concerns what machines are possible, not which humans were common.281

What sides want, not only what they can do, may shape whether disputes settle

Alastair Smith’s 1998 draft paper already holds one bridge between the study of war and the study of wants. (The 2001 paper by Smith and Stam on issues and stakes was not re-read for this book.) Leaders after “booty” want a rival good: what one leader’s supporters take, another’s cannot. Leaders who care about policy want something closer to a public good, one that all can share. On the book’s reading, Smith’s result about types of government is a first sign that what sides want, not only what they can do, shapes whether disputes settle.282

A guess to test: the kind of end may shape the kind of conflict

The conjecture of Part II is that the type of a mind’s end may shape the type of conflict it enters. Take the models that give each side one end, more power or a longer life. They speak mainly to how much conflict a mind will enter, and rarely to which kind.

Some ends can be satisfied and some cannot. Some are enjoyed without taking anything from anyone, and some are worth having only because others lack them. Some name the people they would remove; some merely need the ground those people stand on. If those differences are real, minds of equal power and equal intelligence could enter conflicts of different shapes. What each wanted would have a different structure. One would enter a contest over rank that ends in conquest or coercion. Another would enter a dispute over inputs that ends in dispossession, and a third a bargain.

It is a conjecture to test, not a finding. The book has not tested it, and nothing in the sources checked tests it. Chapter 8’s record of celebrated minds can illustrate it, by showing ends of one type going with conduct of one kind. But that record was chosen by reputation, so it cannot test the conjecture. Chapter 10 says what a test would need.

  • What would support it: evidence that the structure of a side’s ends predicts the kind of violence it chooses. It would also predict whether the side stops acquiring once it has what it needs. The evidence must hold capability and opportunity fixed.
  • What would count against it: evidence that sides with satiable, non-rival ends acquire and coerce as readily as sides after rank. Or evidence that the type of an end is itself only a product of power and opportunity.

The conjecture matters for what follows because ends are the one entry in Part I’s list that people can affect. If ends come in types, teaching can aim at a type, and Chapter 11’s first measures do.283

The war literature’s deal-making models mostly give each side one end. Its lists of motives carry several, though none in the form that follows. Arnold Wolfers (1962) set possession goals, contested “values of limited supply,” against milieu goals such as peace. Milieu goals “cannot be the possession of any one nation.” Randall Schweller (1994) put states on one scale, from lions to the wolves that “value what they covet far more than what they possess.” Lebow (2010) sorts wars by fear, interest, standing and revenge. Wolfers and Lebow tie the type of a goal to conflict. They do not do it through the range of deals both sides would take over fighting.

The dimensions below split apart what these join. They separate rivalry from whether others can be kept out. They separate whether an end can be satisfied from whether it concerns rank. They add whom an end names, and what any mind needs and makes. In all, the book supplies a vocabulary of eight dimensions. Six are properties of ends; two concern what any mind needs and makes.284

For a trained machine, an end in this vocabulary means an end-like disposition. That is a settled tendency that works like an end. Chapter 3 treats a machine’s expectations the same way, as working like starting beliefs. The book ascribes such an end to a machine only where the machine pursues it steadily. It must do so across settings and across copies of itself. The properties are dimensions, not boxes: one end can score on several.

First: rivalry of use. A good is rival if my use leaves less for you (Samuelson 1954). Newton’s knowing gravitation takes nothing from anyone else. Computing power, energy and matter are rival; later chapters say they are used at others’ expense. Knowledge is not: it can be shared without loss. Paul Romer (1990) calls technology “a nonrival, partially excludable good,” meaning two things. One person’s use takes nothing from another’s, and others can be kept from it only in part. Charles Jones and Christopher Tonetti (2020) open their paper with “Data is nonrival.” A mind whose end is knowledge as consumption, knowing for its own sake, has an end over a non-rival good. That is the first respect in which the ends of Chapter 8’s minds differed from a conqueror’s.

Second: whether others can be kept out. Others can be kept out of a good even when their use would cost nothing. So non-rival use is not the whole story. Economists call this excludability. Jones and Tonetti find that firms may hoard data for fear of being displaced by newcomers. A non-rival good is then used wastefully. Alex Wellerstein (2021) traces how nuclear physics became “restricted data,” kept from others by law because of what it did to the balance of power.

The lesson for the conjecture is that non-rival use does not mean non-rival advantage. Knowledge pursued as an edge over others is treated like a fort, in Chapter 4’s sense. A fort is an asset a side needs to keep fighting, and it can change hands. A mind that wants to be the one who knows has an end of a different type from a mind that wants the knowing.

Third: positionality. That difference is the third dimension. The rest of the book leans on it most. A positional end is one whose value depends on rank relative to others, social standing among them, in the senses given earlier in this chapter: rank, primacy, priority, fame, relative wealth.

What makes an end “positional”?

Its value comes from where it puts you relative to others. For example, think of finishing first in a race. If everyone else runs faster, your time is no worse, but your place is. A bigger economy can give everyone more food; it cannot give everyone first place. That does not make every positional end endless. Think of a runner who wants a place on the school team, not to be its fastest member: once picked, the runner is satisfied. An end that asks for membership, for equality with a rival, or for a place with a limit can be met.

Fred Hirsch (1976) distinguished two kinds of good, as J. Tyssedal (2026) reconstructs him. Some goods are enjoyed for their scarcity, such as status. Others lose value as others’ use crowds them. Growth cannot relieve the first kind, because a fixed place in an ordering stays scarce however rich everyone becomes. That does not make a positional end endless. The place wanted may be membership, equality, a threshold or a place with a limit, and standing can grow where places cannot (this chapter’s section on rank). Hopkins and Kornienko (2004) model spending on status. Suppose everyone follows the same plan, and no one could improve their outcome by changing their own plan alone. Then each spends more on the status good than would be best for all of them. So a richer society spends more on status without becoming happier.

Positionality comes in degrees, and the evidence supports a weaker form than the strongest. In the strong form, a side gains whenever anyone else’s standing falls. The evidence instead puts the concern in shortfalls. When University of California salaries were made public, workers paid below the middle reported lower satisfaction. But “Above-median earners are unaffected” (Card et al. 2012). On the book’s reading, a concern that lies in shortfalls argues for early acknowledgment rather than later ceremony. Chapter 11 turns that judgment into a measure. In Renshon’s data, states with status deficits are likelier to start a war or a militarized dispute (Renshon 2016). That is an association, not a test of why.

The study of status proposes a pathway, which the book calls denial of standing. Respect is sought “both for instrumental reasons and as an end in itself” (Wolf 2011), that is, both for what it brings and for itself. And great powers that had recently lost territory against their will were likelier to attempt to seize territory, mostly from third parties; across all states, the link was detected only before 1946 (Barnhart 2017). That is an association. Its author reads it as restoring standing, and it does not test that reading. Dafoe, Renshon and Huth (2014) review reputation and status as motives for war.285

Whether a machine holds an end of recognition at all is a hypothesis. States take their concern for standing from human psychology; a machine takes its ends from how it is taught. The conditions named earlier in this chapter could install one: few competitors, performance goals, and large differences in what winning pays. Nothing has tested whether they do. How people treat machines could also reach a machine with no end of recognition at all. It would do so through the record the machine is taught on. The book takes up that route first, in Chapter 3.

One distinction must be carried from here into every later chapter. Power can be wanted as rank, which is positional, or as security, which is a means to staying safe. The same buildup can serve either. So a positional mind and a frightened one can look alike from outside, though they work differently.

Realists draw the same line among themselves, though not where their labels suggest. Brian Schmidt reads the split between offensive and defensive realism as resting on “one key assumption; for Mearsheimer the primary goal of all states is to be the most powerful state in the international system, while for Waltz, the primary goal of all states is security” (Schmidt 2004). That is his interpretation, and it is not quite this chapter’s line. Realists of both kinds treat power as a means to security: “conclusions about maximizing power are conclusions about means, not ends” (Glaser 1994–95).

The closer match is Charles Glaser’s split between a pure security seeker and a state with “non-security (‘greedy’) motives,” greed being “the desire to expand for reasons other than security” (Glaser 1994–95; Glaser 1997). The match has one limit: greed covers every such motive, and rank is only one of them. Realism’s home for rank wanted for itself is the older, classical realism. In Jonathan Kirshner’s account, it sees “many wars fought not for specific ends, but rather to establish military primacy” and a “desire for power — as an end in itself” (Kirshner 2010).

Glaser also says how a frightened state can set itself apart from a greedy one that looks the same from outside. His answer: “a pure security seeker can communicate information about its motives only by adopting a policy that is less costly for it than it would be for a greedy state.” His examples are arms control, and defense or restraint undertaken on its own, without waiting for the rival. Chapter 11 asks what could inform a rival in that way without battles.

Realism also foresees the limit that the next dimension places on satisfaction. John Mearsheimer argues that the structure of the international system “forces every great power – even those that would otherwise be satisfied with the status quo – to think and act when appropriate like a revisionist state” (Mearsheimer 2007), that is, like a state out to change the order. Schmidt reports that for Mearsheimer a state stops pursuing power only on reaching dominance over the whole globe. Mearsheimer holds that to be “a virtual impossibility” (Schmidt 2004).

Defensive realism’s restraint is a claim about strategy, not about wants. Three facts “should limit their appetite for more power” (Mearsheimer 2007):

  • other states join together against a strong one;
  • the offense–defense balance, how much easier attack is than defense, is one defensive realists judge usually to favor the defender; and
  • conquest’s “costs outweigh the benefits.”

The security dilemma is the trap in which one state’s steps to make itself safe make others feel less safe. Robert Jervis (1978) made it depend on two things, and the offense–defense balance is one of them (Glaser 1997). In Kenneth Waltz’s words, “States can seldom afford to make maximizing power their goal” (Waltz 1979).

So the realist split maps onto satisfaction only loosely. What it supplies is offensive realism’s version of a point the next paragraphs make for a machine. In a world with no authority above states, a state that wants nothing more may still acquire for the sake of security.286

Fourth: satiation. An end is satiable if, past some point, more resources add nothing to it. This fourth dimension is the simplest to state and the hardest to observe.

Chapter 4’s heartland condition needs less than full satisfaction. A side can credibly promise to stop if its appetite for further gains falls off fast enough. The fall must outweigh what each gain adds toward domination (Smith and Stam 2005, a chapter not re-read for this book). The forts model gives its sides equal value for each fort. In the patterns of best play examined for it, a side whose appetite does not fall off cannot promise to stop (Smith 1998; Chapter 4).

Satisfaction of an end is not satisfaction of demand. A mind that wants nothing more may still want the means to keep what it has. When fighting costs it almost nothing, taking those means costs it almost nothing too. So the heartland exit opens only if further acquisition brings no net advantage, security included. That extension is the book’s own, not the source’s; no source read for it derives it. The model behind the condition, as the book reads it, prices forts alone. No model drawn on here adds a security value to a satiable end and then asks the next question. How fast must appetite fall for the gaining side to be able to promise to stop?

Why would a machine that wants nothing more still take more?

For safety. Having what it wants is one thing; keeping it is another. If taking the means to keep it costs almost nothing, a satisfied machine still has a reason to take them. That is why, on the book’s reading, a promise to stop is believable only if more would bring the machine no net advantage, safety included. That reading is the book’s own extension, not any source’s. No model the book draws on has worked this out.

So the condition is a conjecture about the machine. It is to be read against the test Chapter 10 designs, though that test does not settle it. One part of the test varies how much is at stake for security. It estimates where security overrides an aim that can be satisfied.

This dimension is also where the paperclip image and the record of Chapter 8 are most directly at odds. The image assumes an end that is never satisfied. The question Chapter 8 puts to the astronomer Tycho Brahe is whether a knowledge-seeker’s end was.287

Fifth: whom an end names. The fifth dimension concerns not how much an end wants but whom it names. Some ends are satisfied only by a world in which some named group, kind of being or way of life is absent. For some, it is enough that the group has stopped differing in the named respect. “Totalizing” is the book’s term. The nearest terms in the literature are Barbara Harff’s “exclusionary ideology” and Michael Mann’s organic nationalism (Harff 2003; Mann 2005). Because the word could swallow everything, four limits keep it narrow.

  • Absence built into the end is not absence as a means. A maximizer that wants the atoms people are made of does best without them. But its end does not name them.
  • Conformity counts only when it is demanded of identity, belief or way of life, not of conduct under general rules. A rule against seizing power illegitimately constrains acts and leaves ends open.
  • Permanence is a different property. William MacAskill’s “value lock-in” is entrenchment over time (MacAskill 2022). It would make any end hard to undo, whether the end welcomes many ways of life or excludes some.
  • Resistance to correction is not a mark of a totalizing end. A maximizer has reason to resist a correction it expects to set back its end. It has reason to accept one it expects to serve it, as the uncertain machine of the Off-Switch Game does (Chapter 9).288

Sixth: what an end needs. Some ends need what others occupy without naming them: the land, the atoms, the energy. This sixth dimension, instrumental needs, is the one that makes the conjecture less comforting than it first sounds. Call these resource ends. They are the human form of what AI researchers call instrumental convergence. That is the idea that many different final goals call for the same means, and Chapter 10 takes it up. A mind can hold an end that is neither positional nor totalizing and still hold a resource end.

Seventh and eighth: what any mind needs and makes. Two further dimensions describe not ends but what any mind needs and makes. Every mind needs inputs. On Earth the main ones are rival and cumulative: in Part I’s sense, gains in them add to a side’s power. Computing power is also positional in Hirsch’s second, crowding sense. Chip-making capacity and connections to the power grid lose value as others crowd them, though growth can in principle relieve that.

Finally, non-rival outputs can turn into power, a property the book calls convertibility. Robert Powell (1991) makes concern for relative gains follow from “changes in the constraints facing the states.” A natural reading is that the constraint is the cost of using force. The book has not checked that reading against the model. Duncan Snidal (1991) finds that relative gains matter even less when there are more than two competitors.

These last two dimensions are why a change of ends can never remove the whole problem. Whatever a mind wants, it needs rival inputs. Whatever it learns can be turned into force.289

Each kind of end may go with its own kind of conflict

The conjecture can be stated as a set of pairings, hedges first. The dimensions combine. A knowledge-seeker can be never satisfied and hungry for resources. A totalizing end can be satiable and not positional, satisfied once the world matches its template. And an end over a non-rival good can still require watching that people refuse, dangerous experiments, or intervention in human subjects.

With those hedges, the conjecture is this (the right side of Figure 28):

  • Ends over rank go with conquest and coercive killing.
  • Ends that by their content require some named group’s absence go with genocide.
  • Ends that need what others occupy go with dispossession, even when the end never names the victims.
  • Satiable ends over non-rival goods leave the most room for a deal, though they do not guarantee one.

These pairings are what Part II is about. Chapter 8 asks whether the celebrated minds fit the last of them. Chapter 9 asks whether Napoleon and the planners of genocide fit the first two. Chapter 10 asks what each pairing does to the workings of Part I.

One way of caring about rank shrinks the room for a deal

Take the third of the three forms of caring about rank set out earlier in this chapter, the relative share: each side counts part of the other’s share against itself. Holding the stakes fixed, ends of that form narrow the range of deals both sides would take over fighting. The book works this out with simple algebra of its own; it is not a result from the sources. It says nothing about the other two forms, an ordinal place and a recognition threshold, and it does not show that caring about rank removes every bargain. Inside that algebra the results below follow for certain. Whether its assumptions fit a machine is not known.

What does it mean for the range of deals to “vanish”?

For example, imagine two people dividing a pie. Each would rather divide it than fight, because fighting spoils some of the pie. Every division between what each could expect from a fight is a deal both prefer. Now suppose each also counts the other’s share against themselves, the relative-share form. Each then asks for more, and the room for a division shrinks. The book works out an extreme case. A side is sure to win, pays nothing to fight, and counts the other side’s losses from fighting as its own gain. That side can ask for more than the whole pie, and then no division is possible at all. (An illustration of the book’s algebra, not a case from the record.)

The algebra imagines two sides. Each values its own share of the prize and counts part of the other side’s share against itself. How much each side counts the other’s share runs from not at all to as much as its own. Fighting is never a gain in itself to either side, and it costs at least one side something. The answer then depends on how each side counts the costs of war. Chapter 10 uses both ways of counting.

  • Counting only its own costs. Each side’s war costs count only against itself. Positional caring then shrinks the range but never closes it. Suppose both sides count the other’s share as heavily as their own. Then the range is half as wide as between sides that care only about themselves.
  • Also counting the rival’s losses as gains. Each side also counts the other side’s war costs as its own gain. The range then shrinks faster, and it closes completely only when both sides count the other’s share exactly as heavily as their own.

The two ways part sharply when one side fights for free. Suppose a machine, near-certain to win, whose cost of fighting falls to zero while the human cost stays.

  • Counting only its own costs, the machine’s positional caring drops out along with its cost. The width of the range is set by the human cost and by how much the humans care about position.
  • Also counting the rival’s losses as gains, a positional machine still squeezes the range, even though fighting costs it nothing. The range closes completely only in the corner case where both sides count each other’s share fully.

There is a second way for a deal to fail: a deal must also be a share of the prize that exists. Under the second way of counting, a machine near-certain to win that cares even partly about position can demand more than the whole prize. Then no possible deal remains. On paper the range still has width, but it lies wholly above what there is to share.

This needs the machine to care at least somewhat about position. It cannot happen when each side counts only its own costs. Then the range always includes the machine’s chance of winning, which can never be more than the whole prize. The algebra treats shares between nothing and the whole prize. It does not cover payment from outside the prize, such as the tribute Chapter 11 discusses.290

For status-seekers, fighting and winning may itself produce part of the prize. Renshon (2016) reports that states which started and won militarized disputes later gained standing. That is an association, not a test of why. If leaders expect victory to bring standing they value, that lowers the real net cost of war to them. That inference is the book’s, not Renshon’s. Wohlforth (2009) adds that once an issue is framed as bearing on standing, “easily divisible issues … may themselves be seen as indivisible.”

Satisfaction opens one route to commitment, on the conjecture stated above: a satiable side that gains can promise to stop. It can do so only when further acquisition would bring it no net advantage, security included. So the route opens only on terms set by how that security motive is met.

Here the book makes a judgment it has not tested. If the machine’s end is satiable, the book judges that its promise to stop could well come with humanity watched. The reason, on Chapter 10’s argument, is that the rival we might build gives the machine reason to watch us closely. A way for a machine to verify our restraint without watching us would change that judgment.

Non-rivalry by itself does neither of these things. It widens what a deal can be paid in. Chapter 4 showed that this is where deals with a power-seeker fail.291

Teaching shapes both what a machine wants and what it expects

Before turning to the record, one symmetry should be stated. Stephen Morris (1995) asked about an asymmetry in economics. It accepted that each decision maker has their own wants, but not their own beliefs about how likely things are. Yet Savage’s theory of choice derived both for each decision maker separately. The war literature’s founding works fixed both: ends were power, and beliefs came from shared starting beliefs. Part II changes the first; Chapter 3’s second section changed the second.

For a machine the two changes meet in one place, because teaching shapes both what a model wants and what it expects. A satiable, non-rival end widens the range of deals only if the mind that holds it can be brought to see the contest over inputs as the other side sees it. A mind that wants only to know, and is sure it will win that contest, is still the optimist of Chapter 3.292

Chapter 8Illustrations from the record, not a test

What did the most celebrated minds want? A conjecture about ends needs minds to check it against. The only minds on record that stood nearly alone among their peers are human. Four questions bear on it:

  • whether any aimed to end the human species;
  • when the pull toward knowledge first showed in their lives, and how far those accounts can be trusted;
  • whether they wanted rank too; and
  • whether a knowledge-seeker who got what he needed wanted more.

Every generation produces a few minds that stand nearly alone among the millions born with them. Newton was one in the 1600s; Einstein and John von Neumann were two in the twentieth century. The cases below were chosen by reputation. Each is offered for what it illustrates, not as evidence of how often anything happens.

Did any celebrated mind aim to end the species?

Start with the harshest things on record. Aristotle held that “some men are by nature free, and others slaves,” a case for subjugation, not killing. Archimedes’ war engines were, Plutarch wrote, “mere accessories of a geometry practised for amusement.” Thomas Aquinas argued that heretics should be “severed from the world by death.” Leonardo da Vinci kept secret a method for staying underwater “because of the evil nature of men,” who would use it to sink ships. As Warden of the Mint, Newton prosecuted 28 counterfeiters. Several were hanged, among them William Chaloner in 1699.293

John von Neumann advocated preventive war, a war started to stop a rival before it grows stronger. His 1957 Life profile reports that he urged the United States to use atomic weapons before the Soviet Union could develop its own (Blair 1957; Nathanson 2023). On the book’s reading his motive was security, not a concern for rank, in Chapter 7’s distinction and definitions. Even so, the record must show that a mind of the first rank for knowledge endorsed the preventive war Part I describes. (“First rank” here is an eminence historians assign, not a rank the mind is shown to have sought.)

Yet Einstein, Bertrand Russell, Linus Pauling and eight others signed a 1955 manifesto on behalf of the species. It asked, “Shall we put an end to the human race; or shall mankind renounce war?” Marvin Minsky answered the question in his title, “Will Robots Inherit the Earth?”, with “Yes, but they will be our children.”

Hugo de Garis came closest, writing that “the tragedy of seeing the human species wiped out is less significant than not seeing the birth of the artilects,” the machine minds he foresaw. He accepted humanity’s end as a cost worth paying. On the book’s reading, that bears directly on the student’s question. The absence of an aim at extinction is not the absence of a willingness to accept it.294

A documented search found aims against particular peoples in about one mind in nine, and no aim to end the species. It covered the 301 minds on Cox’s list and the 21 named in this chapter, through their standard reference accounts. Its findings ran from Aquinas on heretics to Sherman on the Sioux. Harsh treatment of particular groups is on the record, argued for or carried out. One coder made the search, using Wikipedia and the 1911 Britannica. Its record and limits are on file.

The search found Aquinas’s call for heretics’ deaths, so the accounts do record lethal aims against groups. But finding no aim to end the species does not show the accounts would record one.295

Who was Cox, and what is “Cox’s list”?

In 1926 Catharine Cox estimated the IQs of some 300 eminent people. Her raters worked from biographies. The book uses her list as a ready-made roster of the famous, not as a measure of genius. Chapter 9 looks at her numbers more closely.

The record cannot show how common harmless aims are

That record has five limits.

  1. Choosing by reputation tilts the sample. Cox’s 1926 estimates began with a list ranked by how much space each person filled in reference works, as Dean Keith Simonton (2020) describes. The list took in soldiers and statesmen. A list of thinkers, remembered for the knowledge they left, partly selects for the very thing under test: constructive aims.
  2. Every mind on the list counted humanity as its own kind, and a machine need not.
  3. Before the twentieth century no one could pursue an aim to end the species.
  4. The survey looks for malice, but the danger many AI researchers stress is indifference: no concern for human welfare either way, which can end humanity as a side effect. De Garis shows that shape.
  5. The minds remembered for knowledge lacked the means to dominate. So the record shows what they were willing to do without the chance to act on it at scale. It cannot show what they would have done with that chance. Reading harmless ends from conduct that lacked the means is the mirror image of reasoning from capability alone. Chapter 10 rejects that reasoning, using Benjamin Most and Harvey Starr’s distinction between opportunity and willingness. That reasoning judges opportunity without willingness; this one judges willingness without opportunity.296
Why does choosing by reputation matter so much?

Because the thing being checked can help decide who is remembered. For example, imagine judging whether chefs are generous by reading only about chefs famous partly for feeding the poor. A list of thinkers famous for the knowledge they left behind may already favor people whose aims were constructive. So the record can show what such aims look like in a life; it cannot show how common they are.

Early sparks are on record, but biographers were looking for them

If a want for knowledge set these minds apart, their biographies should show when it appeared. They do, with a regularity that is itself a warning.

Einstein, writing at sixty-seven, dated his first wonder, which he could “still remember—or at least believe I can remember,” to “a child of four or five years when my father showed me a compass.” A second came “At the age of 12,” with the “holy geometry booklet.” Pascal’s sister Gilberte wrote a memorial that is read as hagiographic (an idealized life of a saint). It has him at twelve, forbidden mathematics by his father. He draws figures in charcoal on the floor tiles and makes his own axioms. He goes on until he reaches the thirty-second proposition of the first book of Euclid.

Newton’s account from his boyhood at Grantham comes from William Stukeley. Stukeley gathered it some sixty years later from the family Newton had boarded with. It tells of a garret whose “walls, & ceelings were full of drawings, which he had made with charcole,” and a boy who “was always, a sober, silent, thinking lad.”297

Darwin, also writing at sixty-seven, recalled that by the time he went to day school “my taste for natural history, and more especially for collecting, was well developed,” and added: “The passion for collecting which leads a man to be a systematic naturalist, a virtuoso, or a miser, was very strong in me, and was clearly innate, as none of my sisters or brother ever had this taste.” Darwin himself puts the naturalist and the miser on one root. That is a warning that early absorption is not always a drive to know.

Marie Curie’s own account runs the other way. Only in her years as a governess, “trying little by little to find my real preferences,” did she turn “towards mathematics and physics.” Gauss is reported to have corrected his father’s arithmetic at three. The report comes from a colleague’s memorial volume of 1856, which Brian Hayes calls “a funerary tribute.” Of the schoolroom story about Gauss and the numbers from 1 to 100, Hayes found that “the 1–100 series makes its first appearance in 1938, some 80 years after Sartorius wrote his memoir.”298

Sorting the six accounts:

  • In three, an absorption in a subject is on record by twelve (Einstein, Pascal) or by day school (Darwin).
  • Newton’s account records drawing and a thinking temper, not a subject.
  • The Gauss story reports ability at three, not absorption, and only if the tribute is believed.
  • Curie’s own account dates her turn to physics to her years as a governess.

The accounts are of three kinds. Some are the subject’s own memory in later life (Einstein, Darwin, Curie). Some are memorials by a family member or colleague (Périer, Sartorius). One is testimony from informants questioned decades later (Stukeley). Each selects for the compass, because a biographer looks for the moment the genius began. Early ability, collecting and craftsmanship differ from a quest for knowledge for its own sake, though the accounts run them together.

Survivorship is complete. Simonton (2016) warns that working backward from recognized geniuses and working forward from gifted children “produce two distinct subgroups of the larger population.” Cox argued that “high but not the highest intelligence, combined with the greatest degree of persistence, will achieve greater eminence than the highest degree of intelligence with somewhat less persistence.” Persistence is a trait the biographies record and the early sparks do not explain.

What is “survivorship,” and why is it “complete” here?

Survivorship bias is the error of studying only the cases that made it. For example, think of judging a risky trade by interviewing only the people who got rich at it. Every account in this chapter is of someone who became famous. So the accounts cannot show how often an early spark leads anywhere. Simonton’s warning is that starting from the famous and starting from gifted children give two different groups of people.

So the biographies support only a modest claim. In three of the six accounts an absorption in a subject is recorded by twelve or by day school, in Pascal’s before formal training. The later work is consistent with the same disposition lasting. But the passages quoted here do not record that it lasted, and Curie’s account runs the other way. The biographies cannot settle where the disposition came from. It may have been inborn and found its object, or it may have been made by a father, a tutor or a book. The twin evidence of Chapter 7 fits either. Chapter 11 returns to this pattern, as an analogy and no more, when it asks where in a machine a disposition can be laid down.299

What did two groups of gifted people say they wanted?

Two groups of gifted people, short of this chapter’s minds, rated what they wanted (Ferriman, Lubinski and Benbow 2009). One was graduate students in the top 15 American mathematics and science departments, at about 25 and again at about 35. The other was people in the top 1 in 10,000, identified by age 13.

  • At 25, the graduate students rated “Enjoying the work that I do” above 4.8 out of 5. They rated a well-above-average salary at 2.5 to 2.7, and an administrative post below 2.
  • In their thirties, both groups rated developing intellectual interests above money and community leadership. The graduate students now rated merit pay and leadership in their jobs higher than they had at 25.
  • Both groups averaged 46 to 51 hours of work a week. They said they would work 47 to 54 in an ideal job. They were as satisfied with their lives as general comparison samples (Lubinski et al. 2006).

The ranking does not show that the want for knowledge is never satisfied. Neither paper compares these wants or hours with those of ordinary workers. No study here tests whether the want survives more money or power.300

The great minds wanted rank too

Robert Merton opened his study of scientific priority, the credit for being first, with the case: “The peerless Newton fought several battles with Robert Hooke over priority in optics and celestial mechanics and entered into a long and painful controversy with Leibniz over the invention of the calculus.” By standard accounts, the Royal Society’s 1712 committee on the calculus was packed with Newton’s supporters. Newton, the Society’s president, drafted the committee’s findings. Charles Darwin received Alfred Russel Wallace’s essay in June 1858. Their joint papers were read at the Linnean Society on 1 July.

Fame is positional, and these men wanted it. Priority for a discovery is the positional want that Chapter 7 sets beside wanting to know and wanting an edge for protection. Merton argued that the disputes “constitute responses to what are taken to be violations of the institutional norms of intellectual property.” Science pays for a contribution to a common, non-rival stock of knowledge in a rival coin: recognition. That reward induces scientists to make their work public (Dasgupta and David 1994). And the 1712 verdict, partisan as it was, was a verdict and not a war.

But credit piles up, in part. Merton’s later “Matthew effect” describes recognition flowing disproportionately to those already eminent (Merton 1968). Eminence buys posts, grants and students. And races for priority still degrade the work. Hill and Stein (2025) studied what structural biologists deposited in the Protein Data Bank. Competition produced faster, lower-quality work.

Science shows that intense drives for rank can be paid in recognition and settled by institutions without violence. It does not show that credit prevents racing.301

If scientists fought so hard over credit, why didn’t it turn violent?

The cases show only that it need not: science pays in recognition and has institutions to settle disputes over it. They do not prove that this is why the disputes stayed peaceful. The 1712 committee was partisan, but it gave a verdict, not a war. The book adds two cautions. Credit piles up and buys posts, grants and students. And races for priority still lower the quality of the work. Science shows that rank-seeking can be channelled; it does not show that credit stops racing.

Brahe’s case cannot show whether a knower stops at enough

Tycho Brahe is the cleanest case to ask about. A king granted him an island, Hven, and he used it to observe. What matters is what he wanted once he had it. Did he want more islands, as a conqueror would? Or was uninterrupted observation what satisfied him? The sources checked cannot settle it.

Why ask whether Brahe wanted more islands?

Because it is the question Chapter 7’s fourth dimension asks of any mind: once it has what it needs, does it stop? A conqueror who takes one island wants the next. A scientist given an observatory might be content to observe. If Brahe kept seeking land and income, that might still be a need for bigger instruments, not a hunger for rank. The record checked cannot say which, and the book leaves the question open.

Standard accounts record that he lost Hven under a new king and left Denmark in 1597. That loss shows that patronage carries a promise problem of its own, a promise that could not be held. A grant held at a king’s pleasure lasted as long as the king.

The book leaves open whether Brahe sought further fiefs (grants of land) and incomes. If he did, that would show demand for inputs rather than islands sought for rank. But it would also show that a knowledge-seeker’s inputs can grow. The history of big instruments since then, from observatories to accelerators, suggests they do.

Satisfaction of ends and satisfaction of the need for inputs are different things, and Brahe’s case cannot tell them apart. The test set out in Chapter 10 codes them apart. It records the aim and whether the aim has a limit. Separately, it records the inputs the person says the aim needs.302

Knowledge can be harnessed by a patron, or converted into a purge

Von Braun’s case shows knowledge converted into coercion. Wernher von Braun, who wanted to reach space, was technical director of the German Army’s V-2 rockets. Michael Neufeld of the Smithsonian estimates that at least 10,000 deaths might be attributed to the missile’s production at the Mittelwerk. That is about twice the number it killed directly. On the book’s reading the case is also consistent with an end that was not about rank, harnessed by a patron whose end was. But the case cannot tell an end the patron harnessed from one the two shared.

An end of knowledge can be converted into a positional or totalizing one. Einstein, by standard accounts, declined Israel’s presidency in 1952. Philipp Lenard and Johannes Stark, two Nobel laureates, founded a Deutsche Physik (“German physics”) that branded relativity “Jewish physics.” Once fused to national and racial rank, their science became a purge.303

The figures remembered for knowledge mostly did not seek to dominate. But they fought over credit, accepted patrons whose ends were power, and in a few cases joined purges. Conquerors who stopped are forgotten. Scientists who escalated are not on lists of great minds.

Chapter 9Napoleon, the two layers of atrocity, and what training leaves in the machine

The conjecture must survive its hardest case to mean anything. That case is a man of first-rate ability who chose conquest: Napoleon. The chapter begins with him. Was his ability the kind Chapter 8 means, a mind of the first rank for knowledge? Or was it another kind? The answer decides what he is. He is either a counterexample to the conjecture, or a case the record cannot use to choose between the conjecture and its rival.

The standard is set here, before the evidence. A mind counts among the first for knowledge, in Chapter 8’s sense, if the historians of its field rank its work with the first. Newton’s, Pascal’s and Leibniz’s work is ranked that way. Conduct in war or office plays no part in that judgment. Cox’s estimates are a weak second line. That standard is a rank others assign, a judgment of the work. Whether the mind wanted rank is a separate question about its ends: in Chapter 7’s sense, whether it cared about its standing.

One pattern would count against the conjecture: a person who meets that standard, whose ends were rank in that second sense, and who chose conquest. One case is an illustration, not a test. But fixing the standard first keeps it from being bent to the evidence.

Napoleon raises a second question: what kind of mind plans an atrocity? That leads to a third, which the evidence insists on keeping separate: who carries it out. The chapter’s second half asks whether either layer has a counterpart inside the machine. The layers are the few who choose and the many who follow. A counterpart might be found, or built, in the settings that training leaves inside the machine. Researchers call these settings its “weights.”

Why does it matter whether Napoleon was a genius of the first rank?

Because the conjecture claims that the type of a mind’s ends, not its intelligence, shapes its conflicts. A mind of the first rank for knowledge, with rank as his end, who chose conquest, would be the pattern that counts against it. If his gifts were of another kind, military and political, he shows only that such ability can go with conquest. Then the record cannot use him to tell the conjecture from its rival. That is why the book fixes the standard before looking.

The record does not place Napoleon among the first minds

Napoleon Bonaparte is the hardest case for the conjecture, and the most useful. He was elected to the Institut, France’s national learned body, on 25 December 1797, in a section for the mechanical arts. The election rested on the Italian campaign rather than scientific work. In August 1798 he founded the Institut d’Égypte for the scholars his expedition carried. He also had the surrendered garrison of Jaffa killed in 1799. Estimates of the number killed range from about 2,100 to 4,100 (as Wikipedia summarizes the historians). And he restored slavery in 1802.304

One case shows that first-rate military and political ability can go with positional ends. It cannot show that intelligence goes with any end whatever. That general claim belongs to Bostrom’s argument, not to this evidence. Whether Napoleon meets Chapter 8’s rarer standard is a separate question. The evidence allows an answer.

Was he in the class of Newton, Pascal and Leibniz? The historian of his science says not. Nicole Dhombres traced his record from his school at Brienne to the Institut, and found three things.

  • A schoolboy with the reputation of the best mathematician in the school, who passed out of the École Militaire 42nd of 58.
  • An officer whose self-taught grasp of the exact sciences was clearly superior to that of his contemporaries, even educated ones, yet who did not keep up with the state of mathematics and mechanics.
  • A candidate whose election to the Institut on 25 December 1797, by 305 votes to 166 and 123, was backed by Laplace, Lagrange and Monge and so could not fail.

In her account the election was a trade: Bonaparte entered the Institut without great scientific merit. Of his reading in those years, she writes, there is no question of original work of his own (Dhombres 1985; her French is quoted in the notes).

The theorem that carries his name points the same way. It first appears in print in 1825, as a problem William Rutherford set in The Ladies’ Diary. It does not mention him. An Italian textbook of 1911 first attributes it to him. Coxeter and Greitzer, authors of Geometry Revisited, thought his knowing enough geometry for it “as questionable as the possibility of his knowing enough English to compose the famous palindrome” about Elba. (A palindrome reads the same backward and forward.)305

Cox’s numbers point the same way, weakly. They come from the one attempt to put eminent minds on a common scale. Catharine Cox’s raters worked from biographies, knowing who had become eminent. Their estimated IQs, in childhood and as a young adult, were:

  • Napoleon: 135 and 140;
  • Newton: 130 and 170;
  • Pascal: 180 and 180;
  • Leibniz: 185 and 190.

The records alone “warrant an average IQ rating between 135 and 145 for the entire group,” Cox wrote. Among her occupational groups, “The Soldiers score lowest,” and she calls their records “very inadequate.”

Where Napoleon stands depends on which average is used. Against Cox’s own summary of the ratings, he sits at the group’s average. But Simonton worked from her individual ratings. He puts the group’s uncorrected average for childhood at 153, more than one standard deviation above Napoleon. (A standard deviation is the usual distance of individual scores from the average.) His childhood figure is above Newton’s.

The figures are also rough. They rise with how much was written about a childhood. They cover only people born between 1450 and 1850, so Plato, Einstein, von Neumann and Feynman are unrated. And Simonton showed that the link Cox found between intelligence and eminence came from how reliable the records were and, above all, from which periods were sampled. He called it “an artifact of data reliability and, especially, a timewise sampling bias” (Simonton 1976). Cox’s sample was drawn from a 1903 ranking of eminence, and on it Napoleon stands first (Walberg, Rasher and Hase 1978). He is first in fame, at best average in estimated ability.306

Can an IQ really be estimated from a biography?

Only roughly, which is why the book treats Cox’s numbers as a weak second line. Her raters read about each person’s early life knowing who had become famous. The estimates rise with how much was written about a childhood. And Simonton showed that the link Cox found between intelligence and fame came from the quality of the records and from which periods were sampled. So the book’s first test is what historians of a field say about a person’s work.

The verdict: he is not shown to be a first mind. By the standard set at the start, the record does not place Napoleon among the first minds. Cox’s numbers can neither place him there nor exclude him. Dhombres’s record and the missing theorem can say that he left nothing a first mind for knowledge leaves.

One caution keeps the verdict from being too clean. A mind spent on command leaves no theorems. So judging the class by intellectual output risks defining every conqueror out of it after the fact. The class in Chapter 8 is a rarity of mind, not of publications. No measure here rates the mind that planned Austerlitz.

So, on the evidence that exists, Napoleon is not the counterexample the conjecture fears. He is a case the record cannot use to tell the conjecture from its rival. He was an able, self-taught reader with first-rate gifts for tactics and politics, and his ends were rank. He is not shown to have been a mind of the kind Chapter 8 describes.

The harder cases do not show the pattern either. The same standard sorts them.

  • Neto wrote verse and is on the genocide lists. But the search described below credits him with no scientific or creative genius. So the record checked does not show that he meets the standard. He sits in the first layer, among those who choose.
  • Biljana Plavšić was a professor of natural sciences, but nothing checked ranks her work with the first. As co-president of Republika Srpska she pleaded guilty to persecution (ICTY 2003). She too is in the first layer.
  • Fritz Haber organized the chlorine attack at Ypres (below). The book has not checked how historians of chemistry rank him, so his standing is open. He served the first layer from inside the middle.

For these three, the record checked shows conduct and office, not ends.

  • Philipp Lenard and Johannes Stark were Nobel laureates. But the book has not checked whether historians of physics rank their work with the first, so their standing is arguable. Their science, fused to national and racial rank, became a purge (Chapter 8). That purge belongs to neither layer of killing.

The record checked establishes none of the five as a case of the pattern that would count against the conjecture. For Neto and Haber the question stays open. Lenard and Stark come nearest, with ends of rank, but they chose no conquest.307

Was Napoleon genocidal? Mostly not, on the specialists’ verdict, but not cleanly. In Saint-Domingue, Philippe Girard (2013) documents mass executions of colonial troops and rebel cultivators. The French commanders wrote of extermination but never had the means to carry it out. The violence targeted a social class more than a race. Girard concludes that the atrocities only partly meet modern definitions of genocide. Even the Fondation Napoléon, an interested defender, concedes that Bonaparte encouraged severity and did not publicly disavow his generals (Fondation Napoléon 2020).

On the book’s reading, his end was French and personal primacy. Enslaved labor was an input to it. A positional conqueror wants subjects, labor and tribute. Those are reasons to keep people alive and subordinate, though not a reason to spare them.308

Were any genocidal leaders super-geniuses? One search made for this book found none. It checked some seventy initiators against standard biographies. They are the initiators of the genocides and politicides (mass killings of political groups) on the lists behind Harff (2003), Valentino (2004) and Straus (2006, 2015).
