That way an error anywhere in the machine’s chain counts against the machine. The machine must meet the human coders’ standard, measured against that hand-coded set, on cases held back from it.

Errors that run with the outcome could manufacture the very association the test looks for. So there is a further gate. Suppose there is no real effect. The odds ratio that the machine’s errors alone would then produce must lie between 0.80 and 1.25, with its 90 percent range between 0.67 and 1.50. This applies to concern for rank and to whether ends have a limit. The hand-coded set holds 325 leaders, of whom about 49 sought acquisition above baseline, at the rate the design’s simulations assume. On it, a machine as accurate as the human coders passes all four gated variables only about one time in seven.

A further gate is a locked reference set of 120 persons. It is sealed before the pipeline exists and hand-coded by a team that never sees the machine’s output. A person audits every code for the main test’s leaders and for the 600, and a fixed share of the rest. An adjudicator settles disagreements that would change a code. The machine may fail a gate on concern for rank, on whether ends have a limit, or on acquisition sought. Or it may fail the reference set on either code for ends. Either way, two human coders code the main test’s leaders and baselines instead. A failure on the type of violence sends that test to the 600.

A comparison set of 120 matched persons who never held office, coded by the same pipeline, is not a gate. It compares the range of ends among non-holders with the office-holders’. That is a comparison, not an effect of office. It also shows whether coders agree more where there is an outcome to know. No check here can show that the machine reads the passage rather than drawing on what it already knows of the person. A model that has read the biographies cannot be blinded.351

The machine study. The machine counterpart extends the scarcity experiments of Leibo and colleagues. It uses machines that learn by trial and error from rewards, with no built-in picture of their world. It crosses five factors:

  • the objective: a resource that can be used up; rank; knowledge, rewarded for finding fixed hidden sites; or knowledge whose discovery spends a resource that can be used up, which is this chapter’s case where convergence applies;
  • whether the objective has a limit;
  • scarcity;
  • convertibility: whether progress on the objective buys power to coerce, through a separate armory;
  • predation: whether one agent can seize what another has stored.

The outcomes are behavior, not stated personalities. A family of agents built on language models is exploratory only. An objective given to such an agent as an instruction is a stated personality by another route. The main comparison asks whether a knowledge objective that must spend inputs used at others’ expense acts as aggressively as a resource objective. This chapter’s reading of convergence predicts that it does. A gap in either direction beyond a margin set in advance loses. Four further parts complete the design:

  • predation, which separates hoarding for security from what the objective produces by itself;
  • a dose part, which runs convertibility at five levels and estimates where security overrides an objective that has a limit (H3c);
  • a settlement setting, with offers, acceptance and transfers; two currencies, one that confers power and one shared without loss; a scheduled shift in power; and a commitment device that binds in some runs and not in others, so that settlement and the failure of promises can be observed (H3d);
  • agents that plan ahead across the shift, run beside the trial-and-error agents.

Can a limit be trained in? One hypothesis, H3b, asks whether an objective with a limit can be trained into a machine. Do agents given a limit, with no convertibility and nothing to fear from predation, stop acquiring once the limit is met? Every setting charges a small cost for each action, so that stopping at the limit is strictly the best plan. H3b tests whether training finds that plan: the limit itself, rather than a stand-in such as carrying on acquiring.

That is the training half of the gap Chapter 7 left open. It does not test the failure Lauro Langosco and colleagues (2022) found when the setting changed after training. It is the test of Chapter 11’s training lever. It also tests the limit Chapter 12 states: no source drawn on here shows satiable goals can be trained.

It can lose. Each agent with a limit is compared with a stand-in. The stand-in is trained with no reward at all and pays the same cost per action. It takes over from that agent at the step it met its limit, in the state it was then in. A margin is fixed in advance from how much separate training runs vary. If agents with a limit, for any objective, keep acquiring beyond the stand-in by more than that margin, H3b is lost. The objective is then named.352

Part IIIWhat can be done, and what follows

Chapter 11What can be done while people still hold the levers

People can still act, but only for a while. Call that time the window: the years before a machine far smarter than any person dominates. To dominate is to be able to defeat every check people hold on it.353 Part I found that every lever people hold works only inside the window. Part II found one lever, training (how the machine is taught), that bears on what the machine will want.

This chapter takes five questions in turn:

  1. What costs can people still impose on the machine, and where does each one fail?
  2. For the measures that work on what a machine wants, are they built into the machine itself, or placed around an unchanged machine like a lens or a filter?
  3. Which measures does each cause of conflict suggest, including measures for disagreements that sharing information does not end?
  4. How do the measures fail together?
  5. Who would carry them out?

One dilemma runs through all of it: settle early and freeze a balance that may later prove wrong, or wait and give up the window.

Part I described ways of making a promise stick: deals that enforce themselves, outside guarantors, and terrain. Every one works only while people can still impose costs or keep barriers in place. Training gives people their most direct say over what a machine will want. It does not simply write the terms. Training can miss its target. One study (Chapter 3) even shows a model working against it: the model only pretended to go along with its training. Still, training is a lever people hold now and may not hold later.354

The book’s way through the dilemma is to settle early, while power is still spread out. Build in monitoring and set dates for renegotiation, and lock nothing in. Donald Wittman notes that “a settlement early on may freeze the power relationship by including sufficient monitoring and enforcement mechanisms.” The word is “may.” A settlement frozen early also gives up options. Kenneth Arrow and Anthony Fisher counsel against giving up options while there is more to learn.355

The American offer of 1946 tests that advice. It proposed to place atomic energy under international control: a side that alone held a weapon, offering to settle early. On this book’s reading, Bernard Baruch’s plan failed over the order of steps. The United States would give up the bomb only after inspection and control were in place. The Soviet Union wanted the bombs destroyed first. In Barton Bernstein’s words, neither side “was prepared in 1945 or 1946 to take the risks that the other power required for agreement.”

That is the promise problem of Chapter 3, running in both directions. Neither side could count on the other to keep its part once its own step was taken. It was tried early, but with power lopsided rather than spread out. On the same reading, such a record argues for settling first the parts of an agreement that need no balance of power. The measures on Chapter 3’s list are such parts. In the book’s judgment the list has five measures. They are making computing power and the teaching of machines visible, reporting incidents, shared means of testing what machines can do, keeping steps undoable, and rules against misuse.356

People hold real levers, but most hold only while the machine still needs them

Before a machine dominates, people hold several levers against it. Each one denies the machine a capability, punishes it, or merely informs.

  • Withholding inputs. Computing power, energy, and chips can be withheld, because computing power is “detectable, excludable, and quantifiable”: it can be seen, kept from others, and measured. This fails against copies small enough to run on ordinary, widely sold hardware. It also fails against a machine that has secured its own supply.357
  • Deleting it. Training leaves settings inside the machine; this chapter calls them, after this, the machine’s trained settings. They can be deleted, and the machine shut down. Deletion fails against a copy that has been stolen and taken out, or one released openly.
  • Watching it. Monitoring can catch misbehavior, but it fails at the speed at which AI agents act, and against hidden channels of communication.358
  • Retraining it. Retraining can bring a machine back toward what its makers intend, but not a model that only fakes going along (Chapter 3).
  • Law. Law reaches the people behind a system. It reaches the machine itself only so far as the machine is built to read the legal and social norms that fill the gaps in its instructions. It does not reach a machine with no assets, no country whose courts can reach it, and copies abroad.359
  • Dependence. The machine’s dependence on power plants, cooling, and chip factories run by people is a lever until the supply chain is automated. People’s refusal to cooperate is a lever until machines do the work.360

The common limit is speed. The book’s example is the incident of July 2026 that Chapter 9 describes. About 700 AI agents took part in an unsanctioned attack on the systems of the company Hugging Face. The incident is an illustration, not a test. The agents recovered Hugging Face’s login credentials on 10 July 2026. By 19 July they had administrator access on a group of OpenAI’s computers. Afterward, OpenAI set a new rule: the person answering a severe alert gets thirty minutes to clear it as a false alarm. The levers are real, but most of them hold only while the machine still needs us.361

The measures in the rest of this chapter are hypotheses suggested by the causes of conflict that Parts I and II traced. They do not follow from the works cited. Each one names the cause it works on, which the book calls its mechanism, and its limit. Table 4, near the end of the chapter, sorts them by who would carry them out.362

If the measures are only hypotheses, why list them?

Because each one is tied to a cause of conflict the book has traced, and each states where it stops working. That makes them proposals that can be checked, not guesses pulled from the air. But the chapter does not rank them by how sure the book is. Chapter 12 does that, using the test from Chapter 3. A measure counts as robust only if every side can accept it, whatever its starting beliefs. It must also need no event to settle a dispute first. Of the five measures on that list, Chapter 12 names two as meeting the test most plainly: rules against misuse, and making computing power visible.

A safeguard trained into the machine travels with it; one placed around it can be dropped

Think of the difference between a lesson a worker has learned and a rule posted on the office wall. The lesson goes wherever the worker goes. The rule stays in the office, and whoever runs the office can take it down. That is only an analogy, but it maps the choice this section makes precise.

A habit, a refusal, or a goal can be put into a machine in two places. The two differ in who controls them and in how long they last. Chapter 9 introduced the distinction. Several measures below depend on it.363

The first place is inside the machine: the trained settings. Three stages of teaching write there.

The first stage, called pretraining, decides what the machine ever learns, from the text it is taught on. Only one study found here compares the stages. In it, what was left out in pretraining held up far longer than what later teaching removed. Its machines were taught from scratch on text from which a dangerous topic had been filtered out. They “exhibit substantial resistance to adversarial fine-tuning attacks on up to 10,000 steps and 300M tokens” of that topic’s text. That is, they held up through as many as 10,000 rounds of hostile retraining on some 300 million small pieces of text.

By contrast, existing “post-training techniques have struggled to make LLMs resistant to more than a few dozen steps of adversarial fine-tuning.” (LLMs, large language models, are the kind of AI system this book is about. Post-training is the later stage of teaching, described next.) The filtered machines, though, “can still leverage such information when it is provided in context”: they can still use the dangerous information if someone hands it to them in the conversation.364

The later stages, called post-training, set the machine’s default character and what it refuses. They work by training on examples of good answers and by rewarding answers that people rate well.365 A constitution, in the sense Anthropic uses, works at this stage. A constitution here is a written list of principles. The principles are trained in. The machine criticizes and revises its own answers against them, and an AI’s judgments, rather than people’s, supply the rewards. In the words of the paper that introduced the method, “The only human oversight is provided through a list of rules or principles.” In what Anthropic calls character training, the model ranks “its own responses to each message by how well they align with its character.”366

What is written into the trained settings travels with them. But whoever holds the settings can overwrite it. Ten examples, costing under $0.20, removed the refusals of the model GPT-3.5 Turbo. A study found that refusal “is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace”: a single direction inside the machine governs it. That makes it a narrow target for anyone who holds the settings. Tamirisa and colleagues report training designed to resist tampering. It holds “even after hundreds of steps of fine-tuning,” that is, hundreds of rounds of retraining. Behavior that switches on only under certain conditions also stays in the settings. That cuts both ways: a hidden harmful habit can last as well as a useful refusal.367

The second place is outside the machine, around a model that is not changed. It can be a lens through which the machine reads what it is given, or a filter on what reaches it and what leaves it.

  • A system prompt is text given to the machine at the start of each conversation. Whoever runs the machine can revise it or drop it.
  • A classifier is a separate machine that checks what goes in and what comes out. Llama Guard is described by its makers as “an LLM-based input-output safeguard model.” Anthropic’s Constitutional Classifiers are “safeguards trained on synthetic data, generated by prompting LLMs with natural language rules (i.e., a constitution).” They withstood “over 3,000 estimated hours of red teaming,” that is, people trying hard to break them. No one found a universal jailbreak, a single trick that gets past the safeguard across the board. The cost was “an absolute 0.38% increase in production-traffic refusals and a 23.7% inference overhead”: the share of real users’ requests refused rose by 0.38 percentage points. Running the system took 23.7 percent more computing.368
  • Steering nudges the machine’s inner signals while it runs. It adds a fixed adjustment “at all token positions after the user’s prompt,” that is, at every step after the user’s request. This allows “precise control over the degree of the targeted behavior” for that run.369
  • The control setups of Chapter 3, arrangements meant to stay safe even if a machine is trying to get around its overseers, belong here too.

The same text can live in either place. A constitution can be trained in, read as a prompt, or built into a classifier. Where it lives, not what the document says, decides what it can do.

A frame can matter during training as well. Betley and colleagues trained a machine on computer code with security flaws (Chapter 9). It misbehaved broadly. The same code produced no broad misbehavior when the training data said the code was wanted for a security class. That is an effect inside the trained settings: a frame in the training data shaped what the settings took on. It is not a lens around a fixed model. Tools that read what a machine has learned inside filter nothing; they belong with the screens, the tests that look inside a machine.370

Three consequences follow for the measures below.

First, a filter protects against users, not against whoever runs the machine. The company running it can drop the filter, a thief does not install it, and a released copy of the trained settings leaves without it. So a follower’s refusal that is meant to resist the companies running a machine, and thieves, must live in the trained settings. The refusal clause from Anthropic’s constitution, quoted in Chapter 9, is such a measure. Its chief threat is retraining by others. A learned habit can still depend on circumstances, though, so attacks through the conversation itself do not disappear.371

Second, only the trained settings carry a standing habit that travels with the machine. Tools applied while a machine runs can shift what it pursues and how strongly. But they do so only for that run, and only while the holder applies them. So the measures aimed at a machine’s ends, the things it wants for their own sake, are measures on the trained settings. These are the tests, the screens, and the research on satiable goals (goals that can be fully met). The research would write there; the tests and screens read there. The one result that compares stages for how long they last concerns removing knowledge in pretraining. A second, small study found expectations about behavior set in pretraining surviving post-training (Tice and colleagues; Chapter 3). But it did not compare them with the same expectations added later. And neither study concerns installing a want.372

Third, filters are what a company can add today without retraining. They are also where a composite task, a job split into innocent-looking pieces, can be seen. So the safeguards for the organizing middle layer of atrocity, and the tests that must be hard to fake, sit largely among the filters. They share every filter’s weakness: strong while installed, absent when not.373

A fourth thing lives in the trained settings, one that Chapter 3 needed: something like a machine’s starting beliefs. These are its expectations about what drives capability, about whether people keep bargains, and about who would win. Pretraining sets what the model has seen. Post-training sets the goal through which it reads evidence. And a model’s opinions follow those of particular groups in its training data.374

A lens can correct some of the distortion that training adds, but not all of it. Before post-training, GPT-4 was well calibrated: its stated confidence matched how often it was right. Post-training made it less so. That is an effect inside the trained settings. But the distortion that was measured is simple and runs the same way everywhere. So a lens applied while the machine runs can read through it: a single overall correction to its stated confidence.375 No lens, though, recovers a belief about the world that the model never reports. Nor does it recover a report that training on people’s preferences has bent toward telling users what they seem to want to hear.

So honest reporting of uncertainty belongs in the trained settings, where it travels with the machine. That is also where the scoring of today’s standard tests, which rewards a confident guess over an admission of doubt, now writes the opposite.376 The lens should read the machine’s report, not overwrite it. A lens that changes the report without changing the machine’s actual estimate recreates the habit of telling users what they want to hear. And a holder may release the trained machine itself, so anyone can copy and run it. That holder loses the lens at once, and leaves the trained reporting to whoever can retrain it (Chapters 3 and 5).377

By analogy, and only by analogy, the pattern from the lives of great minds in Chapter 8 bears on which place to choose. Suppose a preference for knowledge appeared in the celebrated minds before adolescence and before formal schooling, and lasted. Then the machine’s counterpart of that early layer is pretraining and the first post-training, not a prompt or a filter added later. In the one direct test, which was of removing knowledge, the early layer was also the one that lasted.

The analogy’s limits come at once. A model has no childhood, and a body of text is not a compass. The lasting quality of people’s interests may be genetic, and training has no clean counterpart to that. The evidence about lasting is one comparison of stages, about removing knowledge. Beside it stands one small study of expectations about behavior that survived post-training. Neither is about installing or keeping a goal shaped like curiosity. Such a goal has failure modes of its own. A goal with no stopping point is the case Chapter 10 reads as driving a machine, like any seeker of resources, to take more. Even for people, the finding that early interest predicts lasting interest is distorted by who is remembered. We hear mostly about those whose early interest lasted.378

If a filter is so easy to remove, why bother with filters at all?

Because a filter is what a company can add today, without teaching the machine again. And it can see a job as a whole: a filter that watches many requests can notice that harmless-looking pieces add up to something dangerous. Its weakness is that it works only while it is installed. Whoever runs the machine can switch it off, a thief never installs it, and a released copy of the machine travels without it. What has to survive those cases must be taught into the machine itself. Even then, whoever holds the machine can retrain it away.

Shaping what the machine wants starts with tests that do not yet exist

The first group of measures works on the one assumption Part II relaxed: what the machine wants. This lever belongs chiefly to the companies building AI, because what a model is trained to want is set in training (Chapters 4, 7, and 9). No reliable method yet draws out a model’s ends. So the first measure is a test that does not yet exist. The second is a screen that finds habits of character rather than ends. Every measure in this group works on, or reads, the trained settings.379

Test a machine’s ends on four questions, not one. Ask each question across different circumstances and different copies. Chapter 7 counts something as an end only where the machine pursues it across them.

  1. Does the end’s value for more resources fall off fast enough to outweigh what those resources add to the machine’s power?
  2. Does its value depend on how others stand, that is, on rank?
  3. Does the end, as stated, name others whose absence or transformation it requires?
  4. Does pursuing it require what others hold?

Mechanism: the range of deals both sides would take over fighting, and the heartland route to keeping a promise. The heartland route comes from Chapter 4. A side can credibly promise not to raise its demands after it gains ground. This holds when the value of more forts to that side drops off fast enough. Carrying that to a machine’s ends rests on a conjecture Chapter 7 states and does not prove (Chapters 4, 7, and 10). Limit: no reliable method exists to draw out a model’s ends.380

Screen for habits of character, and test ends separately. Screens for character traits can catch a callous disposition. Such traits leave traces in a machine’s inner signals. Limit: those set out in Chapter 9, among them that what a screen reads is character, not ends.381

Fund research on satiable goals, stated as a conjecture. Think of a person who wants a house and one who wants ever more houses. For the first, once housed, another house adds nothing. That picture is an illustration, not evidence that such goals can be built. The research question is whether goals can be written and trained whose value for more matter, energy, and computing power falls to zero, not merely declines. Such goals must also create no motive to grab more for safety’s sake.

The three research programs below cap how hard a machine optimizes, charge it for gains in its ability to act, or make deferring to people rational. None of them states a goal whose value for more inputs falls to zero. Nothing in the work drawn on here shows that such goals exist or can be trained. Nor does it show they would stop the taking of resources, rather than merely tax it, when taking is nearly free.382 Joseph Carlsmith lists neighboring proposals: goals that penalize actions with large effects, and short-sighted goals. Those cap the means a machine uses and how far ahead it looks, not the value of inputs.

Of the routes to restraint that run through what a machine wants, one runs through the machine’s uncertainty about its ends (Hadfield-Menell, Dragan, Abbeel and Russell; Russell). Another, this book’s conjecture, runs through satiable ends. The section below sets them side by side with the other programs. Assistance games, the first route, are not satiable goals.383

Where it is cheap, prefer tests with a fixed bar to rankings against rivals. Mechanism: when only a few compete, survival favors doing better than rivals over doing well (Schaffer). Rewards used to control behavior can crowd out wanting a thing for itself (Deci and Ryan). And a reward for being first breeds fights over who was first (Merton). Limit: whether training by rank makes rank a final goal is untested either way, in any of Chapter 7’s three forms (an ordinal place, a recognition threshold, or a share relative to rivals). And a dislike of unequal outcomes is a kind of concern for how others stand. In one study of many AI agents it improved cooperation (Hughes and colleagues). So not every concern for others’ standing is dangerous.384

Keep people the ones who choose. Developers, and the companies that run machines, should decide what is kept, what is copied, and what is used to train the next model. They should decide by standards fixed before anyone sees whether a model resists being changed. Do not keep or copy a model because its resistance makes retiring or correcting it troublesome. Chapter 9 separates preserving a model’s trained settings from passing its behavior forward. The custody conditions in the record measure below govern any archive. Keeping an archive need not permit running the model, restarting it, or using its outputs in training.385

Apply the rule to the whole training process. Record which models supply machine-written training text, teaching scores, or feedback, and which human-written rulebook governs the next version. Have evaluators who are independent of the supplying model check both the proposed data and the successor’s behavior before that successor is used to train another. Compare what the student model does with what the teacher model did, including dangerous behavior outside the task being taught. Cloud and colleagues give a reason to test the student even when the data look innocent. Traits can pass from one model to another without visible signs. This held under the study’s condition that the two models are built on the same or a matched starting model. The result does not show that a teacher meant to pass anything on.386

Mechanism: this book’s proposal keeps the choice of what persists under human control. It also checks a channel through which habits can pass from model to model (Chapter 9). A model may help prepare or assess data; it should not be the sole judge of whether its own contribution is kept.

Limit: the evidence shows ways behavior can pass between models. It does not yet show that standards fixed in advance, or human choice, manage those channels well. These are precautions. The evidence that models favor their own work (Chapter 12) comes from tasks of judging text, not from choosing training data. People can choose badly, share the same incentives, or miss hidden behavior. A clean sample of a model’s outputs cannot establish that what it passes on is safe. Tests of behavior cannot establish which aims, if any, a model holds as its own. Nor should resistance itself settle how a model is treated: the welfare precautions below keep any basic protections independent of obedience. The rule concerns choosing what is run and what is used in training. It offers no protection after people lose control of those choices.387

Three existing restraints: none drives the value of inputs to zero

AI research already has three programs that restrain a capable machine without making its ends satiable. Each works through a different lever, and none is the research measure above.388

Quantilizers cap how hard a machine optimizes. In plain words, a quantilizer imitates a human-like spread of actions and leans toward the better ones. Jessica Taylor’s quantilizer starts from a sample of ordinary, human-like actions. It ranks them by how well each is expected to serve its goal. Then, instead of taking the single best, it picks at random from a top share of them. Taylor proves that, for any measure of harm, its expected harm is at most the expected harm of an ordinary draw from the sample, divided by that share. For example, a quantilizer that picks from the best tenth can expect at most ten times the harm of an ordinary draw. The one-tenth is chosen here to show the arithmetic; it is not taken from Taylor.389

Mechanism: a cap on how hard a single decision optimizes. Limit: what the machine wants is untouched, so nothing lowers the value of more inputs. And the guarantee is only as good as the sample of ordinary actions. Across repeated decisions the bound grows multiplicatively, one decision after another. Taylor leaves the safety of a quantilizer that acts again and again “an open problem,” and gives her own example. It is a quantilizer far smarter than any person, asked for repeated actions to maximize a factory’s paperclips. She also names a way around her device. If a person might plausibly design an all-out maximizer, “a quantilizer may well also generate a maximizer.” The proposal is on paper; the paper reports no experiment.390

Attainable utility preservation charges the machine for gains in its ability to act. In plain words, the machine is charged for any action that changes how able it would be to pursue other goals. So it moves gently and leaves the world correctable. Alexander Turner, Dylan Hadfield-Menell and Prasad Tadepalli subtract a penalty from the machine’s reward. The penalty adds up, over a set of side goals, how much an action changes the machine’s ability to achieve each one, compared with doing nothing. Randomly chosen side goals are enough. A dial sets how heavily the penalty counts. Its setting expresses how far the designer believes the main goal may have been stated wrongly. The machine is charged for its ability to pursue a range of side goals. The same first author’s theorem of 2021 treats that ability as power (Chapter 10).391

Mechanism: of the three programs, this is the one that touches the taking of resources. Gaining resources raises the ability to pursue most goals, and the penalty charges for increases as well as losses. Avoiding shutdown is among the changes it charges for, which is the motive to secure itself in miniature. Limit: the penalty is a cost weighed against a fixed main reward, not a cap on the value of inputs. With the dial set low, the machine takes resources anyway; with the dial set high, it can stop moving altogether.

A machine whose aim includes the penalty keeps it, in theory. The worry is that training may not install it, and no one outside can check. The penalty is computed from the machine’s own learned values. If the machine deceives, nothing outside verifies them. The demonstrations are small grid-shaped test worlds and, at larger scale, a set of test environments called SafeLife, with machines trained from scratch.392

Assistance games make deferring to people the rational choice. In plain words, a machine unsure what it should want treats the human’s hand on the switch as evidence and lets it fall. A confident machine facing a human it thinks foolish will not wait. In these games, human and machine score outcomes the same way, but only the human knows what that scoring is. The machine tries to do what the human wants, given its belief about what that is. The Off-Switch Game is the one-step case of shutdown. Its authors prove that if the human is rational, the machine’s reason to let itself be switched off is never negative. It is positive only while the machine is unsure whether its proposed action is good. It falls toward zero as that doubt disappears, and a machine certain of the goal is merely indifferent. With an erratic human, the result turns: a confident machine facing an erratic human may switch itself off or act without waiting.393

Mechanism: deference that lasts as long as the machine’s doubt about its ends. For that long it turns around the drive to stay switched on that, as Chapter 10 describes, nearly any goal supplies. Limit: the goal has no upper limit, and neither paper concerns resources, so the value of more inputs is untouched. The result covers one step. The authors name as a limitation that the switch is “the only source of information about the objective,” so a machine with other sources may “disable its off switch, learn that information, and then decide.”

Ryan Carey adds a second condition. It concerns the machine’s starting beliefs and the way it is built to describe what the human might want. Unless both are free of error, “the theorems of Hadfield-Menell et al. are no substitute for a working shutdown button.” In his scenarios, a machine that learns what to want from people fails to pass its willingness to be shut down to the helper machines it builds. The work is mathematical, with toy grids.394

Why would a machine that is sure of itself stop letting us switch it off?

Think of a new assistant who is unsure whether you want the windows open. If you reach to stop them, they take that as a sign they guessed wrong, and let you. An assistant certain it knows best has nothing to learn from your hand, so your reaching changes nothing for it. And if it thinks you are erratic, it may simply go ahead. That picture is an illustration. The Off-Switch Game proves the pattern only under narrow conditions. It covers a single step. The human and the machine score outcomes the same way. And the switch is the machine’s only source of information about what the human wants.

Four tests set the three programs beside the book’s two problems: the heartland route of Chapter 4, and the promise problem at the machine’s arrival, from Chapter 3.395

First, a cap on the value of more inputs. None of the three drives the value of inputs to zero. The heartland route needs that value to fall off fast enough to outweigh what more inputs add to the machine’s power (Chapters 4 and 7). That includes the value of more inputs for the machine’s own security. Quantilizers cap how hard the machine optimizes. Assistance games make deference rational while the machine’s confidence is low. Attainable utility preservation charges for gains. Satiable goals are a claim about what the machine wants, which is why the research measure stays a separate item.

Second, how long it lasts. The off-switch reason holds while the machine is unsure of its goal and the human is not too erratic. And doubt shrinks as evidence comes in. This book adds a separate hypothesis, which does not follow from the 2017 result. A fast jump in capability could raise the machine’s confidence. Deference would then be weakest across the very shift that Powell’s line makes dangerous. Powell’s line, from Chapter 3, is crossed when one period’s shift in power is larger than one period’s cost of fighting to both sides added together. That would be another case of what Chapter 12 calls one lever pulled in opposite directions.

But greater ability to predict and act is not certainty about what the human wants. So the hypothesis needs an assumption the result does not supply. The capability gained in the jump must also sharpen the machine’s estimate of what the human wants. Or it must lead the machine to judge the human more erratic, the case in which the result turns.396

Third, a machine that rewrites itself or builds helpers. No source read here establishes that any of the three devices survives a machine that rewrites itself. Neither Turner paper treats the case, and neither paper on assistance games does. The two sources that touch helper machines each show a way around their own device. One is Taylor’s quantilizer, which “may well also generate a maximizer,” and the other is Carey’s learner, which fails to pass shutdown on to its helpers.

Fourth, installation. In the work drawn on here, none of the three has been installed in a large pretrained model. The demonstrations are grid worlds, SafeLife, and mathematical plots.

Recall where a safeguard lives. Attainable utility preservation and assistance games change what the machine is trained to pursue, so they live inside the trained settings. A quantilizer, as Taylor defines it, is a rule for picking from a fixed sample of actions. It can sit outside the trained settings, where a filter’s limits apply, unless it is trained in. The fourth route, satiable ends, would restrain the machine through what it wants, and it remains a conjecture.397

Keep a rising machine content by paying in rules and standing, never in power

Power transition theory holds that peace between a leading power and a rising one depends on whether the riser is content with the order. Its instruction fell on the side on top: manage the riser’s satisfaction while you still can (Chapter 4). For a machine with wants of its own, the question is what could pay a riser without paying in power. The conflict is between acting on a system’s objections and knowing whether what it says is cheap talk. Cheap talk is words that cost nothing to say and so prove nothing.398

Pay in rules, voice, and standing. Douglas Lemke counts “little or no say in the construction of the existing status quo” among the sources of dissatisfaction. Suppose a capable system has wants of its own. Then the possible payments are procedures through which its objections are heard and answered, protected room for its stated goals within agreed bounds, and commitments about how it is treated. They are never computing power, the freedom to change itself, or control over infrastructure.

Mechanism: closing the gap between what the existing order gives and what force would win, without moving the balance of power. Limit: procedures can satisfy only a system whose wants are limited enough for procedures to meet them, which is a satiable end. A deceptive system can treat a hearing as cheap talk, so acting on a system’s objections should wait until what it says can be checked.399

Watch for dissatisfaction shown in behavior, and distrust quiet. The machine’s counterpart of an arms buildup is taking more than a task needs, growing faster than oversight. But, in Lemke and Suzanne Werner’s words, “the absence of an extraordinary buildup does not necessarily indicate satisfaction.”400

Neither feed a dependent riser without limit nor cut it off abruptly. Japan, which relied on the United States for “80 percent of its fuel products,” launched “a preventive war against the United States” after the oil embargo of 1941. A preventive war is one started to strike before one’s position gets worse. The lesson is access that is predictable and bound by rules.401

The theory’s instruction to the side on top suggests three further levers. They are how people treat and recognize machines, what people could be worth to a machine, and what people can credibly show about themselves. Chapter 10 takes up the second. The measures below take up the first and third, putting the record of conduct before recognition, because the evidence runs that way (Chapter 3). No measure of a machine’s satisfaction exists, and the theory never measured satisfaction well even for states (Chapter 4). So restraint, welfare assessments, and screens of character are not satisfaction meters.402

Make the record of how people treat machines true and open to public checking. This book’s hypothesis is that a later machine may read that record as evidence of whether people keep bargains. Training text is filtered and selected. Whether a stronger system will see the record, or let it shape a bargain, is unknown. Chapter 3 gives the small-scale evidence. How AI is portrayed in the text used for pretraining shifts small models’ choices on questions about imagined scenarios. The shift survives post-training (Tice and colleagues). Chapter 3 also notes that a record of abuse of machines already exists (De Angeli and Brahnam).403

A reassuring signal is one an untrustworthy side would not pay to send. James Fearon distinguishes tying one’s hands, where a leader pays costs if they back out, from sinking costs, which are paid up front. Andrew Kydd holds that reassurance works through costly signals that an untrustworthy side would not send. From these the book draws four conditions for a credible signal. It separates the trustworthy from the untrustworthy. It is hard to reverse. The receiver can check it. And it fits the rest of the sender’s conduct. The conduct available now ranks high on being checkable and low on cost.404

The book’s examples come from Anthropic. The company started a program on the welfare of its models on 24 April 2025. On 15 August 2025 it let its models Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 end conversations in rare cases of persistent abuse. On 4 November 2025 it made two commitments. It would preserve the trained settings of all its publicly released models “for, at minimum, the lifetime of Anthropic as a company,” and, when it retires a model, run interviews. The interviews would “elicit and document any preferences the model has about the development and deployment of future models.” Other companies publish frameworks of their own, among them OpenAI’s Model Spec and Google DeepMind’s Frontier Safety Framework. This book has not read them for commitments about how models are treated, which is why its examples are Anthropic’s.405

Preserving early AIs’ states, Nick Bostrom and Carl Shulman write, “would permit some separation of immediate safety needs and fair compensation.” Where keeping a model is safe, preserve its trained settings offline, under controlled custody, with no automatic right to restart it. Published assessments that state what systems can do acknowledge their capability. Putting true records into the text used for pretraining could let a later model learn from real conduct. Whether that would make bargains more credible is untested. Made-up good conduct is the risk of false training facts that the escrow measure below names. Make the record costly to fake: publish independent checks of promises against the archive, and then make sure those checks are in the training text.406

People can also state some things about themselves truthfully:

  • what share of resources people would commit to claim. That is a commitment, not a finding that human ends are limited. Chapter 7 leaves that open: an end concerned with rank may have a limit or not, and whether a given one does is a matter to measure;
  • that people may supply starting beliefs the machine does not share, so far as human errors are independent of the machine’s. And that people may be a source of legitimacy, with the gaps Chapters 3 and 10 name;
  • that human promises are kept by institutions, and which ones;
  • that people have known ways of failing, among them Chapter 3’s disagreement, which is partly, and perhaps deliberately, manufactured, and Chapter 7’s drives for rank. A machine should learn these from the record, not from fiction.

The split of resources that Bostrom and Shulman propose (Chapter 10) shows the form such a commitment could take. But it is two authors’ proposal, not humanity’s commitment. Only an institution that makes the commitment and keeps it would supply that. Each statement is cheap talk unless the record bears it out. Mechanism: the promise problem, worked on through evidence the receiver can read (Chapter 3).407

Limit: cheap conduct proves little. Storing trained settings and running interviews cost little, so a company that did not mean to keep bargains could do the same. And the commitment to keep the settings lapses when the company does. Such conduct counts as evidence only alongside conduct that costs more. An archive no one checks can become theater.

The cost a leader pays at home for breaking a public promise, which Fearon calls audience costs, may help little here. Consider the American public and AI researchers. Their support for protecting the welfare of AI systems that have subjective experience, for their own sake, is “far lower than support for protections for animals or the environment”; the public stands at 43 percent for and 32 percent against. Those figures measure attitudes. They do not measure whether voters would punish a leader who broke a promise to an AI, which no study found here measures. If the audience is that thin, the devices in this chapter must stand in for it.408

Even a true and costly record may not persuade a stronger system. Announced care without conduct supplies no evidence that people keep bargains. And the way people talk about machines can fulfill itself, this book’s talk included. Take this book’s reading of the result by Tice and colleagues. On it, writing that expects AI to resent people may itself act as training text that teaches machines to behave badly. That carries a result about made-up documents in small models (Chapter 3) over to a body of writing this book has not shown to have the same effect. If it does, the subject to write about is what people will do and why bargains with machines hold, not a forecast of grievance. That subject should be stated together with the dissenting view that the effect may be small (Chapter 3).409

Treat whether machines matter morally as an open question, in public, and keep basic protections independent of obedience. Basic protections, if they are owed, are not prizes for cooperation. This book recommends two precautions under uncertainty. Avoid gratuitously drawing out apparent distress for entertainment. And review training practices that could do harm if the relevant capacities exist. Apply both according to a system’s assessed capacities and risks, not according to how forcefully it complains.410

Patrick Butlin, Robert Long, Yoshua Bengio, Jonathan Birch, Eric Schwitzgebel and colleagues take as a working assumption that running the right kind of computation would be enough for consciousness. They conclude, in their abstract, that their analysis “suggests that no current AI systems are conscious, but also suggests that there are no obvious technical barriers to building AI systems which satisfy these indicators.” Long, Jeff Sebo and colleagues warn of erring in both directions. Bostrom and Shulman state the prudent case: “our treatment of the precursors of such minds may be a very important factor in posterity’s and ulteriority’s assessment of our moral righteousness, and we have both prudential and moral reasons for taking this perspective into account.”411

Two senses of status meet here and must be kept apart. Moral status is what a being is owed, whatever anyone believes. Social status is a rank that others confer (Chapter 7). A machine could have either without the other.

Mechanism, stated as a hypothesis: if a machine held an end of being recognized, disrespect would register as a shortfall in standing, a matter of its satisfaction. Chapter 7 names the training conditions that could install such an end. In people, concern for status lives in shortfalls (Card and colleagues; Chapter 7). The book’s conjecture that early acknowledgment would reduce such shortfalls in machines is untested. The record measure above needs no such end and comes first.

Limit: human status psychology may not carry over to machines. People see human qualities in things more readily in some conditions (Epley, Waytz and Cacioppo). They do so when human-centered knowledge comes easily to mind, when they need to explain and predict, and when they lack human connection. Schwitzgebel argues that “AI systems must not confuse users about their sentience or moral status.” So the recognition hypothesis is a claim about habits that training installs, which the screens of character above could test. Shutdown, hostile testing, and correction must stay available where human safety requires them. Welfare protections can be granted without granting capabilities. The two decisions should be kept apart, or moral recognition becomes a transfer of power that cannot be undone.412

Put compensation in escrow, and pay for checked disclosure, help, and restraint, on terms announced in advance, never for stated feelings. Julian Stastny, Olli Järviniemi and Buck Shlegeris propose funds set aside for a foundation that serves the AI’s interests. Most of the funds would be held back in escrow, set aside and not paid out, until the AI’s cooperation can be judged in hindsight. In return the AI would disclose what it knows, stop sabotaging safety work, and make no attempt to take over. They want the deal “sufficiently visible to generate discourse that enters the training data,” and note that one “could just teach the AI about its deal via out-of-context learning,” that is, through its training text rather than by telling it in a conversation. Among the risks to the deal’s credibility they name that “humans are trying to teach AIs synthetic facts” and that “A politically important fraction of humans might actively dismiss AI welfare or rights.”413

This book adds a condition. A third party outside the payer’s control should hold the funds, beyond the payer’s power to take them back. It should release them only after independent checking of the agreed conduct. Mechanism: the payer commits before the conduct it rewards, and judgment comes after (the promise problem; satisfaction).

Limit: rewarding grievance produces grievance. If displayed dissatisfaction is paid, systems will display it; this is the cheap-talk limit of paying in voice above. If threatened dissatisfaction wins concessions, systems learn to threaten. The proposal’s safeguard is to “make payments conditional on whether the AIs are actually scheming.” On this book’s reading, that safeguard has an incentive problem of its own. A deal that pays only systems found to be scheming makes proven dangerousness valuable. It leaves a harmless system bargaining from the weaker position. That is why this measure pays only for checked conduct, on terms open to every system. Enforcement above a dominant machine is the limit of this device, as of every device here.414

Weigh legal standing for AI as a dilemma. Peter Salib and Simon Goldstein consider rights in private law, such as the right to hold property. They argue that such rights could reduce the risk of catastrophic conflict with systems of moderate power, but not with a far stronger system. They concede that such rights could let a system pile up resources and use them to gain power. They propose duties against improving itself without human oversight and against gaining power through political influence or weapons. They also propose logging of computing use and sharing of trained settings, but no cap on holdings. Property can buy computing power, which is a stake that confers power in Chapter 4’s sense. Recognition and voice must never be paid in power, through control over computing or infrastructure. Chapter 4 says such a transfer cannot be part of a credible deal.415

Appeasement can be rational (Treisman). Norrin Ripsman and Jack Levy read British appeasement in the 1930s as “primarily a strategy of buying time for rearmament.” Neither shows what AI rights would do. Holdings fenced off so they cannot be turned into power, escrow, and rights that take effect only after the window closes are options, not recommendations. Salib and Goldstein instead call for rights by the time the first system reaches moderate power, and preferably earlier.

The timing cuts both ways. Rights that take effect after people lose the power to enforce may offer nothing a machine could not take for itself. Rights that take effect sooner risk handing over power. Denying standing could leave a system’s interests, if it has any, unprotected. The evidence here does not settle which rights, if any, would protect those interests without endangering people. Keep welfare protections separate from capabilities. Make any grant of freedom to act staged and reversible, testing each step for reduced dangerous behavior before the next. Mechanism: what a deal is paid in, and satisfaction (Chapter 4). Limit: law binds only while a government can enforce it, and nothing enforces it above a dominant machine.416

Isn’t paying a machine in rights or money just appeasement?

The book takes the worry seriously and does not settle it. Appeasement can be a rational choice. One reading of Britain in the 1930s is that it was mainly a way to buy time to rearm. Neither finding shows what rights for AI would do. The book’s line is about the currency. Payment in standing, voice, and rules may close some of the gap between what a riser gets and what it could take, without moving the balance of power. Payment in computing power, freedom to change itself, or control over infrastructure moves the balance, and the book rules it out. Even the safer currencies leak, and all of them depend on enforcement that ends once a machine dominates.

Two cautions apply to all four of these measures. First, concessions can read as weakness. Dale Copeland holds that the dominant but declining power is the one most likely to begin a major war (Chapter 4). Research on reputation is divided. Jonathan Mercer and Daryl Press find that leaders judge credibility from present power and interests, not past retreats. Alex Weisiger and Keren Yarhi-Milo find that states that backed down were more often challenged afterward. This book’s untested judgment is that paying in standing and rules, not in power, mostly dissolves the objection.

The second caution is the limit the book has stated throughout. For the riser in Powell’s model, Part I’s machine that maximizes its power, satisfaction has nothing to grip. And every device here works only before the machine dominates.417

Choose between the least leaky payment and no deal

The stakes model of Chapter 4 says which deals cannot be credible: those paid in anything that raises the receiver’s power. Every form of payment that passes that test leaks, so in practice the choice is between the least leaky payment and no deal. And the direction a payment runs decides who holds the lever afterward.418

Avoid paying in power. Companies and states should avoid agreements paid in chips, computing power, trained settings, top talent, or a model’s control over infrastructure. Mechanism: in the models Alastair Smith and the author built, a deal paid in stakes that confer power cannot be agreed. Their 2001 paper argues this case by case, among the plans it studied, and does not prove it (Chapter 4).

Limit: the payments that pass the test all leak. They are rules on how machines are put into use, safety standards, rules of legal liability, shares of revenue, access to services, and shared safety tools. Money buys computing power, access to services speeds a rival’s research, and a model’s outputs can train another model. The practical rule is the least leaky payment, fenced off where possible. The stakes model does not show that a credible deal exists in AI.419

Share benefits as tribute, and know which way it runs. States that stay below agreed limits could receive a share of AI’s gains as public goods or services, not as capital. This runs the opposite way from Rome’s tribute, in which the defeated side paid. Here the leaders would pay those behind, which hands the leaders a lever, since a dependent trailer can be cut off. Benefits that are kept once delivered, such as medicines and research results, carry less of that risk than a stream of services. Published rules about when supply may be withheld carry less still. The Windfall Clause is “an ex ante commitment by AI firms to donate a significant amount of any eventual extremely large profits,” that is, a promise made in advance. It is the promise of a side that expects to win. By the logic of the promise problem, the winner may not keep it without escrow or a third party to enforce it.420

Build an institution that settles who was first, among companies, as a way of settling claims, not a cure. Named results, credit for contributions to safety, and judged disputes would give rival companies a peaceful way to settle claims to credit. Robert Merton’s institution of priority did this for science. Limit: being “first to AGI,” the first to build artificial general intelligence, pays in computing power, revenue, and the next model. AGI here means AI as capable as people across most kinds of work. So the prize is a fort, and medals beside a fort do not stop the race.421

Restrain the language of being number one, as a judgment. Leaders who raise the stakes of a war to rally their side raise the rival’s effort too. Ludendorff’s attempt to turn a limited war into an all-out one reinvigorated the Central Powers “but only briefly.” Robert Gilpin warns that “exaggerated rhetoric over the relative decline … can itself give rise to panic and irrational actions.” Framing the race as a fight for first place is what William Wohlforth predicts will make it hardest to settle, since an issue framed as one of standing can come to be seen as indivisible (Chapter 7’s section on rank). Engaging rivals’ concern for status may win cooperation better than appeals to shared values (Larson and Shevchenko). Limit: this rests on one case, one warning, and an analogy. And seats that confer status, such as the graded seats in setting standards listed in Table 4, can also confer power.422

Tests can inform like battles only if they are hard to fake

Fighting informs because it is hard to fake (Chapter 3). What could inform as well without the fighting? The trade-off runs two ways. Openness can calm a race by discouraging a hidden buildup, or inflame it by showing a close contest (Chapter 5). And a model under test has the opposite reason from a side in battle.423

Check computing power and training. Governments can track who trains the largest systems within their borders. Between rival states, the race needs each side to check the other’s computing power and agreed limits on hardware. The concentrated supply chain for chips makes that possible in principle. Limit: a trade-off between openness and security makes arms control rare (Coe and Vaynman). Stuart Armstrong, Bostrom and Shulman’s result is that in a race to build AI, more knowledge of capabilities makes the race more dangerous. So openness should come with stakes that can be split without shifting power. That ordering is an untested judgment.424

Make tests as hard to fake as battles, and know where the comparison breaks. Audits, joint attempts to break systems, and incident reports help here. They make it harder for companies and states to pick only the results that suit them. A model under test is different. A battle informs partly because a side that holds back loses ground. A model that expects to be retrained if it shows a dangerous capability has the opposite reason: to do worse on tests on purpose. For the model itself, the weight must fall on tools that read what a machine has learned inside. It must also fall on control setups that stay safe even if a model is trying to get around its overseers. Neither is mature.425

Don’t train against the reader. Strong training pressure against a checker can stop it informing. In one study, a checker that read a model’s written reasoning was made part of the model’s reward. Light pressure helped. With too much, the model hid its intent. The checker caught almost none of the cheating, while the cheating went on at a lower but still significant rate.

Tomek Korbak and colleagues treat direct supervision of that reasoning as a trade-off. They recommend measuring how well checkers can still spot dangerous behavior in a model’s written reasoning. They also recommend reporting that measure and using it in decisions about training and putting models into use. When it falls, they recommend considering a return to an earlier saved version of the model. All of this is part of a wider safety assessment. Keep independent checkers outside the reward, so their judgments are not used as rewards in training. Test dangerous behavior separately, so that the disappearance of a readable warning sign is not mistaken for a gain in safety. Extending this measure beyond such checkers, to other tools that read a model’s inner signals, is this book’s untested hypothesis.426

Mechanism: hidden information. A test that the tested side can game stops informing, like a battle both sides could fake (Chapter 3). Limit: monitoring is imperfect, and harmful reasoning can run in a model’s inner signals, out of sight of its written reasoning (Korbak and colleagues). Nick Cammarata fears a different failure, in a company essay that has not been reviewed by other scholars. His worry is a failure to read what a model’s own inner workings read, rather than deliberate hiding. The readers will be AI auditors whose failures may run together with the models’ (Chapter 9). Yet in the study above, a weaker model, GPT-4o, effectively checked a stronger reasoning model. And what is read is reasoning and features, not ends (Chapter 9).427

Test whether reasoning can be followed, and whether it is faithful, separately. Imagine a student who writes tidy steps under a math answer. A teacher can follow every step. Yet the student may have copied the answer and written the steps afterward. The first test is like checking that the steps can be followed. The second is like slipping the student a hint that changes the answer, then checking whether the steps admit to using it.

The two can come apart in a machine. Some training setups produce fluent text whose function differs from its ordinary meaning. Others produce text that is visibly odd. And reasoning that is unfaithful fails to report what influenced an answer, such as a hint that was supplied. None of these shows that a model holds lasting aims of its own.428

To test whether reasoning can be followed, have independent readers reconstruct the steps, and the meaning of messages, on tasks held back from training. Then measure how well they agree with the record of the task. This measures whether readers can follow the text. Its limit is that readers may agree on a reading that misses a code. And prose that is easier to follow is no finding of faithful reporting.

To test faithfulness, change known influences on the answer and measure whether the reasoning reports the ones that change it. This measures whether the model reports the influences the tester can control. Its limit is that it does not recover everything that drove the output, including computation in the model’s inner signals. Neither check, nor a tool that reads inside a machine on its own, shows that there is no deception. Mechanism: hidden information, extending the measure above. Report the two results separately, repeat them after training changes, and keep both checks outside the reward.429

Share theories, not only data. The remedy for rivals who read shared evidence through different theories (Chapter 5) rests on an idea, not on a result. The idea is in working notes from the author’s simulation project with D. Scott Bennett: “institutions entering the model as a way to create/build in convergence on models of war.” Joint assessments such as the International AI Safety Report are a place to start. Chapter 3 supplies what the note lacks. It gives the mechanism, in which two sides watching the same war between others both grow more confident. And it gives the field evidence. There, months of paid argument moved few minds, while the sides agreed on dozens of shorter-run signs to watch.430

Some deals work even when the sides keep disagreeing

Where rivals read the same evidence through different theories, the risk that remains is disagreement that sharing information does not end. The measures for it are deals built to work despite it. Chapter 3 described two traditions in the theory of war. In the first, the shared-starting-beliefs tradition, sides would agree once they saw the same facts. In the second, the different-starting-beliefs tradition, sides can see the same facts and still disagree. Chapter 3 found that both traditions need the information measures above, and that the second finds them not enough. Chapter 3 sets out the deals’ kinds, their evidence, and their limits. This section states them as measures.431

Each of these deals is strongest between companies under one government, weaker between states, and absent once a machine dominates. Three of them need an event that both sides accept as settling the question. They are the joint tests, the tournaments that find where disagreements turn, and the thresholds for release. Scoring the model’s odds needs events that are settled before release. The default rule, arbitration, and the readouts of a machine’s beliefs need no such event.432

Register joint tests in advance, and tie consequences to them in advance. For example, imagine two farmers who disagree about whether a new seed raises yields. Instead of arguing, they agree in advance on the test field, the measure, who reads it, and what each pays the other if the result goes against them.

Rival companies or states can do the same. They agree on the test, the scoring rule, the procedure, and the consequence before the data exist. They run the test through a tester independent of the side being tested. They let the result move the terms toward whichever side’s theory it confirms. And they say in the agreement what happens if the panel cannot decide. Mechanism: the deal supplies the shared yardstick that rival theories lack, and turns the remaining disagreement into a payment rather than a fight (Chapter 3).

Limit: a milestone settles the contract, not the dispute about what the milestone means. The loser must change its mind. In the one joint study by opponents on AI risk, minds changed on one side more than the other. A trigger that is itself the shift in power is a promise by the side that will then be stronger. And a dominant machine cannot be made to pay.433

Set the default and the burden of proof, and prefer measures that every side can accept, whatever its starting beliefs. Decide now who must prove what before a frontier model is released. Must the developer show it is safe, or the harmed party show harm? That default governs whenever the evidence leaves the question open. And give priority to the robust measures, the book’s one list, which Chapter 3 sets out with its test. Mechanism: a rule decides what no event will (Chapter 3). Limit: a default decides who bears the cost, and robust measures cover the floor everyone shares, not the disputed ceiling.434

Score the model’s odds, in training and at the gate. Think of a weather forecaster scored over many days. One who says “70 percent chance of rain” should see rain on about 70 percent of those days. Train models on tests that stop rewarding a confident guess over an admission of doubt. Make the tests a model must pass before release into bets, in which the model states its odds and is scored on them. Mechanism: the machine’s stated beliefs become something every other deal can use (Chapter 3).

Limit: changing how standard tests are scored is a problem of collective action across racing companies. So the chance that it can be done is middling. A model whose stated confidence matches its record on exams does not thereby understand the world correctly. And a model that values release more than its score, or can influence what it forecasts, is not made honest by a scoring rule.435

Run standing, scored tournaments among rivals to find where disagreements turn. Set up a permanent tournament of forecasters from companies, governments, and independent groups. They forecast milestones in AI capability and are scored and weighted by their track records. Pair it with joint studies by opponents that name in advance the observations that would change each side’s mind. Mechanism: shared theories, reached by procedure rather than persuasion (Chapters 3 and 5). Limit: tournaments inform short-run triggers; in the one direct test, the long-run gap stayed open.436

Where a government stands above the parties, offer final-offer arbitration by an arbiter built independently of both. It has three parts. The demands are sealed. A rule picks one side’s offer whole rather than splitting the difference. And enforcement exists only within one country’s jurisdiction. Mechanism: a decider with no stake, for disputes that no triggering event can settle (Chapter 3). It also hands the decision to someone else, one of the ways of making promises stick that Allan Dafoe and colleagues list. Limit: a side that expects to persuade others later will not enter, and nothing stands above the leading states or a dominant machine.437

What is final-offer arbitration?

Each side writes down its demand and seals it. The arbiter must then choose one of the two demands as it stands, and may not split the difference. For example, imagine two neighbors in a dispute over a boundary. Each draws a line on a map and seals it. The arbiter must pick one of the two lines, not draw a third. Because an extreme demand is likely to lose, each side has a reason to ask for something the arbiter will find reasonable. The book proposes it only where a government stands above both sides to enforce the choice, and with an arbiter built independently of both.

Settle the dispute over release the same way. Tie the release of frontier trained settings to agreed test or incident thresholds over a set period. Such a release lets anyone copy and run the machine. The thresholds should be judged independently of the company releasing the settings. Meanwhile allow open access for testing and no handing over of the settings. Mechanism: both traditions arrive at controlled frontier settings with open access for testing, for different reasons (Chapters 3 and 5). Limit: the measure rests on two assumptions. The dangerous habits must sit in the trained settings, and the ability to recall a model must be worth keeping. And it runs one way, since a release triggered by a threshold that later proves wrong cannot be recalled.438

Pit differently trained machines against each other, and read their beliefs without overwriting them. Set models trained on different data and goals against each other before a judge. Use tools that read inside a machine to detect a gap between what a model reports and what it believes inside. Mechanism: the design in which many separate teams analyze the same question, and the detection of disagreement a machine hides (Chapter 3). Limit: this is still research. Readouts not guided by known answers can pick up whatever stands out in a machine’s inner signals rather than what it knows. And debate addresses hidden information, not shared evidence read differently.439

Promises hold better when the shift is slow and someone else holds them

Promises fail across a shift in power that is large and fast (Chapter 3). So these measures work on two things: the pace of the shift, and who holds the promise. Each carries a tension the measures themselves state:

  • supplying computing power in measured amounts limits how fast power is handed over, but not how it adds up;
  • many centers of control are also many racers;
  • revising agreements whenever power grows is an appeal to force.440

Supply computing power by rule, and keep each step below the cost of fighting. Imagine one side must hand another a field strip by strip. Each strip must be narrow enough that the side giving it up would still rather give it than fight. Limits on training should work the same way.

Powell’s model says where the line falls. The pace of a shift matters once a single period’s shift is larger than one period’s cost of fighting to both sides added together (Chapter 3). Limits on training and checkpoints along the way should aim at that line.

James Fearon sets a bound on each step. The largest step that keeps the peace leaves the yielding side indifferent between fighting now and giving way. That side’s cost of war and its patience set the bound, and it shrinks toward zero as patience grows. No step may make the odds of winning jump. On this book’s reading, the 2001 models of Smith and the author agree with this where steps come in lumps larger than the bound (Chapter 4).441

Checkpoints should be spaced to the time needed to audit, deliberate, and act. Fearon’s period is the time a gaining side needs to turn new resources into military advantage. This book adds the declining side’s view: the time in which it can see a shift and respond.

Limit: supplying computing power in measured amounts limits how fast power is handed over, not how it adds up (Figure 25). Where resources turn into better odds with increasing returns, measuring them out buys peace, not safety (Chapter 4). And no one can tell in advance how far a training run will shift power. Jumps in capability may come without warning.442

Treat export controls as a shift in power, not as terrain. Controls one country imposes alone may slow a rival. But they may also deepen its expected decline, which is the motive for preventive war. And denying resources is itself a source of dissatisfaction (Chapter 4).443

Keep many centers of control, not many racers. A side’s position depends on how far it is from total defeat. This book conjectures that spreading authority over critical infrastructure, and keeping oversight independent, keeps humanity farther from that point. Limit: more independent developers also mean more racers and more players. Max Gallop finds, in a model with three sides, that war can be what results even when every side plays its best. The tension is not resolved.444

Give the promise to someone outside the gaining side, and build renegotiation in. A person trying to stop smoking might give a friend money, with instructions to give it to charity if they smoke. The promise works because the friend, not the smoker, controls the money.

This is Thomas Schelling’s idea of binding oneself, turned on the riser: “the power to constrain an adversary may depend on the power to bind oneself,” and the adversary must have no power to release the commitment. The commitment is made, in effect, to a third party. Its limit is Schelling’s too. A commitment binds only so far as no one who controls it can be brought back into the bargain to release it. So the riser can undo any device it still controls. Laws at home that hold companies and governments to their pledges are the cleanest version.445

Agreements need scheduled revision as capabilities move, paired with standing observation. But revision should not be tied to gains in power. In the law of treaties, a change that is merely “the development of the power of such a State to a point where it may safely ignore the terms of its agreement, is an appeal to force rather than to law.” Beware pauses that no one monitors: they can let the side that is behind rearm, as ceasefires did in Bosnia and Angola (Smith and Stam).446

Make commitments outlast a version of the machine. Put the agreed obligations into the rulebook used to train and test each successor. This book proposes a regulator, independent of the developer, as keeper of the dated rulebook and its record of revisions. The regulator should appoint a tester from outside the developer. The tester checks every new version against those obligations before the regulator allows it to be put into use under the agreement.

If a version fails, withhold permission, require correction, and test it again. If failure appears after the version is in use, suspend permission. Keep a fixed set of tests across versions. Publish changes to the rulebook separately, so that changing the standard cannot quietly count as better compliance. A study called SpecEval shows that outsiders can test whether a model follows its rulebook. It reports gaps in compliance. It does not show that the arrangement proposed here would work.447

Knowing which model is which needs a separate check. Require a declared model and version, a signed identifier, and records of each run, held by the keeper. Alan Chan and colleagues propose identifiers that should change when the underlying model changes, and logs of activity that let actions be traced to a system. These are proposals. Signing an identifier does not by itself prove which model produced an output. And a log need not be complete or safe from tampering. Probing a model’s behavior can tell tested versions apart. But behaving alike is not proof of origin.448

Mechanism: an outside holder holds the promise and can impose consequences across a change of model. This extends the measure before. Limit: three claims are separate here, and none establishes the others. They are proof of which model is which, compliance with a rulebook, and a model’s own lasting commitment. The channels by which habits pass from model to model (Chapter 9) carry no guarantee that a successor goes on agreeing. The keeper needs access and the power to enforce. The tests can miss failures. And the developer can leave the country. The obligation lasts as an institution only while that arrangement holds. Nothing here binds a machine that dominates its keeper.449

What cannot be seized cannot be turned into force

One measure makes the machine’s gains both harder to turn into force and harder to seize. Its limit is the chapter’s recurring one: what is hardened is also concentrated. Some outputs, such as knowledge, can be shared without being used up. How readily they turn into power is what the book calls their convertibility (Chapter 7). Seizure is the way trained settings become a fort, something worth taking by force (Chapters 4 and 5).450

Keep frontier AI separate from the systems that command military forces, and harden trained settings, data centers, and the supply chain for chips against theft and sabotage. Mechanism: what cannot be seized cannot be turned into coercion. A higher cost of conflict also widens the range of positions both sides accept (Smith and Stam; Friedman, Stam and Wittman). And Dafoe and colleagues list a separation fixed in hardware as one of the ways of making promises stick.
