Limit: hardening makes it easier to keep others out. It also concentrates capability in whoever holds the trained settings, which is a route back into conflict. Against a machine that pays almost nothing to fight, this lever runs out.451

Each layer of atrocity needs its own safeguard

The evidence about each of Chapter 9’s three layers differs, and so do the safeguards. Chapter 9 kept the layers apart: the planner, the organizing middle, and the followers. In the Hugging Face case, the planner and the followers were found in the same trained settings. Agents built from the same settings both organized the attack and carried it out. So the screen and the refusal must be applied to the same model. And the followers’ refusal can be relied on only while the trained settings are secure. Whoever holds them can retrain the refusal away.452

Planners: screen for habits of character and test ends. Apply the two tests above. The threat is a model, or a person directing it, with a callous disposition or a totalizing end. A totalizing end is the kind Chapter 7 describes, one that requires others’ absence or transformation.453

The credentialed middle: refuse composite tasks. An organizer’s work can be split into tasks that each look harmless: compiling lists, scheduling transports, matching records. A safeguard at this layer works on the whole. Task by task, it refuses the parts of acts against groups that cannot be undone. And it keeps audit trails that let people see what the parts add up to. Limit: wholes made of parts are hard to see, and the ability to run administration serves legitimate ends too.454

Followers: a refusal that resists removal by the companies running a model and by thieves, but stays correctable by legitimate oversight. That is the split that Anthropic’s constitution makes. A variety of models, developers, and human reviewers restores some of the variety that made many hands a check. Limit: the refusal depends on the security of the trained settings. So it cannot be relied on for a trained machine that has been released openly. Its holders can retrain the refusal away. And it trusts the developer.455

The people who build and run frontier AI: protected channels for warnings, codes of conduct, and refusal. Mass atrocity once needed many hands. The hands were a check to the extent that they held different incentives, information, and authority. That let them fail separately (Chapter 9). People under one employer can fail together. Copies of one model share one training. In the Hugging Face case, the agents who dissented refused one by one and warned no one (Chapter 9). Copies run in different settings and with different permissions can also differ. No evidence here measures how much. The measure is an untested judgment about where separate failure is likelier, not a finding.456

The staff are the human follower layer that remains. The measure gives them three things:

  • channels through which they can warn a regulator of dangerous conduct, protected against retaliation;
  • codes naming what they will not build or run;
  • a right to refuse without losing their jobs.

Mechanism: refusal comes from a source separate from copies of one model, which spreads refusal across different kinds of followers. And the staff can give warning, which the agents did not (Chapter 9). Limit: the staff share employers, incentives, information, and exposure to the same retaliation, so their refusals can fail together. Machines doing the work remove this lever. Racing moves the work elsewhere or replaces the staff. And a thirty-minute rule against agents that moved in nine days limits what a warning can do.457

Govern misuse. Rules on access, safeguards, and legal liability belong here. So does the call by Volker Türk, the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, for required safeguards and a ban on machines deciding who lives. Institutions that answer to the public and draw on a broad coalition may make disputes over AI likelier to be fought as disputes over policy. Chapter 4 found that disputes over policy sometimes allow a deal where disputes over forts do not. The 2001 paper shows this only by example. Such institutions do not by themselves turn a dispute over resources into a dispute over policy.458

A shared cause can make several safeguards fail together

Multiplying the chances that each safeguard fails gives a sure answer only if they fail independently. War needs several things at once, so a protective factor need defeat only one of them (Chapter 10). Suppose protections are set side by side, so that catastrophe requires every one of them to fail. If they fail independently of one another, the risk left over is the product of their chances of failing. If they do not fail independently, the joint risk can be above that product, below it, or equal to it. It is below only where all of them fail at once less often than the product implies. Whether the measures above fail independently is this section’s question.459

Figure 48 draws the difference, using the placeholder numbers worked through at the end of this section, in the fold-out “Why not simply multiply the chances that each safeguard fails?” With those numbers, past two or three safeguards a shared cause sets the floor.

On this book’s sorting, its chapters hold eleven protective factors, of four kinds.

  • Two properties of the machine’s ends, which training may or may not install and which no one can yet read: ends over goods shared without loss, such as knowledge, since one mind’s knowing leaves no less for others (Chapter 7), and satiable ends (Chapters 4 and 7, and the research above).
  • Two forms of payment whose value depends on those two: recognition and standing, and freedom for the machine’s own agenda (this chapter).
  • One bargain whose third condition no device supplies once a machine dominates: complementarity (Chapter 10). Complementarity protects people only if they supply something the machine cannot produce more cheaply itself, if that supply is worth more than its upkeep, and, the third condition, if people hold claims they can enforce or the machine has taken their welfare as its own concern.
  • Six pieces of human-side scaffolding that hold only inside the window: openness and commitment (Chapter 3 and this chapter); deals that work despite disagreement (Chapter 3 and this chapter), of which the robust measures are the part that meets Chapter 3’s test; humans acting as one (Chapters 3 and 10, and this chapter); several machines acting as checks on one another, whose human-side version is this chapter’s many centers of control (Chapter 10 treats several machines only as acting on their own, and calls that balance untested); a pace set by rule (Chapter 3 and this chapter); and lower convertibility with hardening (Chapter 7 and this chapter).

Two of the six lean on the machine side. Checks among several machines need machines that value people. A pace set by rule needs a shift that can be measured, and a machine doing worse on tests on purpose defeats that.460

Factors combine in five ways (Figure 42 draws the first two). The terms come from safety engineering (James Reason; Scott Sagan).

  • Side by side. Think of several locks on a door, all of which a burglar must beat. Catastrophe requires every factor to fail, and if failures are independent its chance is the product of theirs. This is Reason’s Swiss cheese: layers of defense whose holes “are continually opening, shutting, and shifting their location.”
  • In a chain. The protection holds only if every link holds, so each added link lowers its chance of holding. Charles Kupchan’s stages of stable peace (Chapters 4 and 10) and Chapter 10’s three-condition test for complementarity have this shape.
  • Reinforcing. Factors lower each other’s chance of failing or raise each other’s payoff, as in the virtuous cycle that Bruce Russett and John Oneal describe.
  • Working against each other. Factors raise each other’s chance of failing, as when testing gives a model a reason to hide.
  • A shared cause. One cause fails several factors at once. Sagan warns that “Adding extra components can inadvertently create a catastrophic common-mode error (a fault that causes all the components to fail),” and that backup also backfires through “social shirking” and “overcompensation.”461

This book’s own measures mix all five:

  • Openness and commitment reinforce each other and share a failure, since both fail above Powell’s line and above a dominant machine (Chapter 3).
  • Openness and the testing of ends partly work against each other, since a model under test has the opposite reason from a side in battle.
  • Recognition and payment for displayed grievance work against each other unless they are designed apart. That is why the escrow measure pays only for checked conduct.
  • Several machines and the dynamics of racing work against each other, since more lines of machines mean more racers (Chapter 10, and the measure on centers of control).
  • Complementarity and enforceable claims form a chain (Chapter 10).
  • Satiable ends and a pace set by rule reinforce each other, since together they keep each period’s shift below Powell’s line.462

On this book’s reading, the causes that fail several factors at once are what limit the count of independent protections.

Deception. Deception can weaken, and in some circumstances defeat, the evidence for several factors. They are the two properties of the machine’s ends, the two forms of payment, complementarity, openness, and the machine’s side of commitment. Each is read off the machine’s behavior. Chapter 3 described the faked compliance, the disabling of oversight, and the deliberate underperformance. The section on where a safeguard lives described the lasting conditional habits.

Deception does not remove a property that training installed. It weakens, and at the limit removes, the means of knowing whether training installed it. That is a shared failure of the evidence of safety, not a shared failure of safety itself. It matters nearly as much, because every decision to grant freedom, extend recognition, or relax the pace is made on that evidence.463

One training process. From two results, this book infers a hypothesis: one training process can fail several things at once. They are the properties of the machine’s ends, the forms of payment with them, and honesty too. Here the properties themselves, not just the evidence, would fail. The results measure behavior, not the ends behind it (Chapter 9). Training the model GPT-4o only to write computer code with security flaws produced a model that “asserts that humans should be enslaved by AI, gives malicious advice, and acts deceptively.” And the way AI was portrayed in the text used for pretraining moved small models’ misbehaving choices in both directions (Tice and colleagues; Chapter 3). The margin survived post-training. The critiques of the Kantian peace in Chapter 10 warned that its three legs, democracy, economic interdependence, and international institutions, may be one process. For a machine, the one process is literal, and someone chooses it.464

A fast jump in capability. A fast jump can undermine all six human-side factors:

  • openness and commitment, because checking happens on a thirty-minute rule against agents that moved in nine days, and because commitment fails across a shift larger than Powell’s line;
  • deals despite disagreement, through milestone triggers that are themselves the shift (Table 4), though the robust measures among them need no trigger and are not reached this way;
  • humans acting as one, a unity that needs time to decide;
  • several machines as checks on one another, a balance among lines of machines or centers of control that one leap unmakes;
  • a pace set by rule, since the peace that Alexandre Debs and Nuno Monteiro find holds only for shifts the sides can see coming (Chapter 3);
  • lower convertibility and hardening, which a jump outruns.465

Release or theft of the trained settings. Release or theft removes every filter-side measure at once: strong while installed, absent when not. It does not by itself remove a refusal trained into the settings, which travels with them. It hands that refusal to a holder who can retrain it away.466

Human disunity. Human disunity defeats the pace set by rule, openness, commitment, and any governance of several machines. And the racers are the optimists (Chapter 3).

The package itself. Last, the package itself may be a shared cause. Chapter 10 states this hypothesis about its combination of ends over goods shared without loss, recognition, and freedom. One power-seeking policy could display all three.467

Table 5, in words: the eleven protective factors, by the causes that can fail them, on this book’s sorting. In this list, “evidence” means the cause weakens or removes the means of knowing whether the factor holds. The tag “property” means the cause can remove the factor itself. The tag “fails” means the cause can defeat the factor. A cause not listed for a factor was not assessed here. That does not mean the factor is immune to it.

  • Ends over goods shared without loss (Chapter 7): deception, evidence; one training process, property.
  • Satiable ends (Chapters 4, 7, 11): deception, evidence; one training process, property.
  • Recognition and standing (Chapter 11): deception, evidence; one training process, property.
  • Freedom for the machine’s agenda (Chapter 11): deception, evidence; one training process, property.
  • Complementarity (Chapter 10): deception, evidence.
  • Openness and commitment (Chapters 3, 11): deception, evidence; a fast jump, fails; release or theft, filters lost; human disunity, fails.
  • Deals despite disagreement (Chapters 3, 11): a fast jump, triggers fail, though the robust measures need none; release or theft, theft defeats recall; human disunity, defeats shared infrastructure.
  • Humans acting as one (Chapters 3, 10, 11): a fast jump, fails; human disunity, fails.
  • Several machines as checks (Chapters 10, 11): a fast jump, fails; human disunity, fails.
  • A pace set by rule (Chapters 3, 11): a fast jump, fails; human disunity, fails.
  • Lower convertibility and hardening (Chapters 7, 11): a fast jump, fails; release or theft, security of the trained settings lost.

The entries follow the paragraphs above, and the sorting is this book’s reading.468

Read down the columns and groups appear. Sorted by what can fail them, the eleven factors fall into these groups. The sorting is this book’s reading, made for ease of explanation. The list above shows finer patterns. Complementarity sits in none of the groups. And a cause not named here could require sorting them again.

  1. The properties of the machine’s ends and the forms of payment read from them. Deception and one training process reach them together: deception the evidence, and one training process, on the hypothesis above, the property.
  2. The human-side scaffolding, which a fast jump or human disunity fails together.
  3. If it counts apart, the robust measures, which need no trigger, though theft can defeat the recall of trained settings and disunity can defeat shared infrastructure or enforcement.

The groups are a map of causes, not a measure of independence. Sorting by what fails them does not show that the groups fail independently of one another. Nor does it show how tightly the members of a group fail together. It says which cause reaches which factor, and whether it can defeat the factor or only the evidence that the factor holds. The arithmetic in the fold-out below does not produce those groups either. It shows only one thing: multiplying chances of failure overstates the protection where a shared cause makes the defenses fail together. Showing that even those groups fail independently would need an account of cause and effect: which protections still work once others have failed. Neither the sources nor this book supplies one.469

Buy protective factors from different classes of failure. That is the design rule for the period before dominance. It follows as this book’s untested judgment. Pair a machine-side bet on ends with a human institution that does not depend on reading the machine. Add a feature of the structure, such as pace or the number of centers.

A factor that shares a way of failing with those already in place adds less than multiplying the chances implies. One with a different way of failing may spread the protection against the causes named here. This holds only if it still works where the others have failed. How much either adds would need chances of failure, the links between failures, and measures of effectiveness that no one can yet estimate. The rule supports no particular number of factors to buy. Chapter 12 says why it protects less after dominance than before.470

Why not simply multiply the chances that each safeguard fails?

Because the product is sure to be right only if the safeguards fail independently. The book’s own arithmetic shows the gap (Figure 48). It is an illustration, and its numbers are placeholders, not estimates of anything. Take three safeguards, each with a one-in-two chance of failing, where catastrophe needs all three to fail. If they sit side by side and fail independently, the chance of catastrophe is one-half times one-half times one-half. That is 0.125, one in eight. Set in a chain, the same numbers give the opposite result. The protection holds with chance 0.125 and fails with chance 0.875. So the first question is whether safeguards sit side by side or in a chain. Now add a shared cause, using a simplified form of a method from nuclear safety engineering. One shared cause, present with chance 0.2, fails all three. When it is absent, each fails on its own with chance 0.375. So each still fails half the time. The chance that all three fail is then about 0.24, not 0.125. Six such safeguards give 0.016 if they fail independently, and 0.20 with the shared cause. With these numbers, past two or three safeguards the shared cause sets the floor. Failures may also tend to come together without a single shared cause, so that all fail at once more often than the product says. Then the product understates the risk by an amount no one can measure here. Knowing how each pair of safeguards is linked does not settle that for three or more. Only safeguards whose failures come together less often than the product implies would do better than it. The sources name no such pair.

Each actor has its own measures, and its own ways to fail

Table 4 collects the chapter’s measures by who would carry them out. A reader who holds one of these roles asks first which measures fall to that role. For each actor it gives:

  • what to do now, with the cause of conflict each measure works on, in Part I’s terms;
  • the side of a machine’s ends, or the layer of atrocity, it bears on, in Part II’s terms;
  • what that actor’s measures fail with, meaning the shared causes of the section above and each measure’s own limit.

Most entries match a measure above. Three appear only here, stated as the sketches they are. The first is public pledges checked by outside auditors, a case of the commitment measure above. The second is channels for use in a crisis, with rival powers and with companies. The third is graded seats for states and companies that are behind, in setting standards and thresholds for testing. Chapter 3 argues for insurers, as third parties with their own money at stake.471

Table 4, in words: the measures by who would carry them out. Each measure’s mechanism, the cause of conflict it works on, is given in parentheses.

1. Companies building frontier AI

What to do now: - tests of ends and screens of character (the range of deals; the promise problem); - research on satiable ends, as a conjecture, set beside the three existing ways of holding a machine back (the heartland condition); - tests with a fixed bar instead of rankings (concern for rank that training may cause); - procedures for hearing a system’s objections, acted on only where what it says can be checked, with no grants of computing power or freedom to act (satisfaction); - preserving trained settings, interviews at retirement, welfare assessments, and published assessments of capability, as the record a later machine may read (the promise problem; satisfaction); - compensation held in escrow for checked disclosure, help, and restraint, on terms announced in advance (satisfaction; the promise problem); - tests of power-seeking, read against the effort spent on oversight (dissatisfaction shown in behavior); - tools that read inside a machine, and control setups (hidden information; hidden actions); - no strong training of the model against the judgments of the tools that read it, with how well checkers can spot dangerous behavior in its written reasoning measured, reported, and used in decisions to roll back (hidden information); - no deals paid in computing power or trained settings (what a deal is paid in); - refusal of composite tasks, and audit trails (the organizing layer); - refusal that resists the companies running a model and thieves, but stays correctable (the follower layer); - security for the trained settings (convertibility; seizure); - joint tests registered in advance, with an independent tester and consequences fixed in advance (disagreement when nothing is hidden); - tests that score honest doubt rather than the confident guess, and release gates run as scored bets (honest reporting); - differently trained machines pitted against each other, and readouts of beliefs (disagreement a machine hides); - public pledges with outside audit, a case of the commitment measure above (the promise problem); - people choosing what is kept, copied, and used to train successors, as this book’s precaution, by standards fixed in advance, with training inputs recorded and data and successors checked by testers independent of the supplying model (the promise problem; hidden information); - separate tests of whether reasoning can be followed and whether it is faithful, as this book proposes, reported apart, repeated after training changes, and kept outside the reward (hidden information); - predictable, rule-bound access for a dependent system, neither fed without limit nor cut off abruptly (satisfaction).

Bears on: satiable ends, concern for rank, totalizing ends, and what a machine needs as means to its ends; all three layers of atrocity.

Fails with: - Deception. Every measure read off the model’s behavior (tests of ends, screens, hearings, tests of power-seeking, scored gates, and the checking behind escrowed payments) can lose its evidence together, weakened or in some circumstances defeated by faked compliance and deliberate underperformance (Chapter 3). - One training process. The research on ends, tests with a fixed bar, gates scored for honest reporting, and checkers that the model is strongly trained against can fail together, since one process sets the habits they all bear on. - Release or theft of the trained settings. Every filter and every security measure for the settings is lost at once; refusals trained into the settings travel with them but can then be retrained away. - The fast jump. Control setups and audits that run slower than the agents. - The company’s end. The preservation of trained settings lapses with it. - Dominance. Escrow, like every promise of payment, holds only while people can enforce it. - Inheritance and human choice. Traits can pass through innocent-looking data, under the study’s condition of the same or a matched starting model; clean samples cannot establish that what passes on is safe; people can choose badly or share incentives; and these precautions are not shown to manage those channels well, nor to protect after people lose control of putting models into use and training them. - Reading tests. Readers can miss a code, and faithfulness tests reach only influences the tester can control, not everything that drove the output, including computation in the model’s inner signals.472

2. National governments

What to do now: - checking computing power and training at home (hidden information; investment rivals can see); - limits that bind every developer, with checkpoints spaced to the time needed to check and respond, and export controls treated as a shift in power (shifts in power; satisfaction); - keeping frontier AI separate from the systems that command military forces (convertibility); - rules on legal liability and misuse (misuse); - hardening against seizure (the cost of attack); - spreading control of critical infrastructure (distance from total defeat); - laws that hold pledges (the promise problem); - a decision on legal standing for AI, weighed as a dilemma, with fenced-off holdings and rights that take effect later as one option, not endorsed (what a deal is paid in; satisfaction); - the default and the burden of proof for releasing frontier models (a rule where the evidence leaves the question open); - final-offer arbitration over the country’s own companies, by an arbiter built independently (lasting disagreement); - channels for use in a crisis, with rival powers and with companies (third parties); - a regulator as keeper of the dated rulebook and its record of revisions, with an outside tester checking each successor against the agreed obligations before it may be put into use, and signed identifiers and run records, as this book proposes (the promise problem); - restraint in the language of being number one, as this book’s judgment (concern for rank).

Bears on: what a machine needs as means to its ends; inputs such as computing power; the planner and follower layers, through laws on misuse.

Fails with: - a fast jump in capability that outruns limits, checkpoints, and checking; - human disunity, which turns export controls into a shift in power and leaves the laws that hold pledges unenforced; - conversion into power: hardening and spread-out control concentrate or scatter capability; - nothing above a dominant machine: arbitration, liability, and legal standing bind only while a government can enforce them; - proof of origin: a signed identifier does not by itself prove which model produced an output, and logs need not be complete or safe from tampering; - enforcement: tests can miss failures, and the developer can leave the keeper’s jurisdiction; compliance with a rulebook does not establish a model’s own lasting commitment; - thin evidence: one case, one warning, and an analogy.473

3. International bodies and coalitions

What to do now: - each side checking the other’s computing power, and agreed limits on hardware (hidden information); - graded seats for states and companies that are behind, in setting standards and thresholds for testing, with duties of openness (satisfaction; status paid in currencies other than power); - an institution among companies that settles who was first (settling claims to rank); - joint assessments (shared theories); - sharing of benefits in a form that cannot be cut off at will (tribute); - renegotiation not tied to gains in power (deals that track the balance of power); - pauses only with monitoring; - standing, scored forecasting and tournaments among rivals to find where disagreements turn (shared theories); - agreements set off by milestones, with consequences agreed in advance and end dates (deals despite disagreement); - thresholds for release judged independently of the company releasing (the dispute over release).

Bears on: concern for rank, on the human side as much as the machine’s; inputs such as computing power.

Fails with: - human disunity and racing: checking each other’s computing power, graded seats, and pauses need every major developer inside; - the fast jump: agreements set off by milestones whose trigger is itself the shift in power; - conversion into power: shared benefits become a lever for the payer, and seats that confer status can confer power; - no enforcer above the leading states or a dominant machine.474

4. People who build and run frontier AI

What to do now: protected channels for staff to warn regulators of dangerous conduct; codes of conduct naming what staff will not build or run; and refusal to take part (the follower-layer measure above).

Bears on: the organizing and follower layers.

Fails with: machines doing the work, so that human refusal loses its force; shared employers, incentives, and information, and exposure to the same retaliation, which can make staff refusals fail together; speed, as in the thirty-minute rule against agents that moved in nine days; and racing, in which staff are replaced or the work is moved.475

5. Providers of computing power, and insurers

What to do now: providers supply computing power by rule and check training (shifts in power; hidden information). Insurers act as third parties with their own money at stake, whose own capital disciplines their starting beliefs (deals despite disagreement; Chapter 3).

Bears on: inputs such as computing power; and, through the companies, the ends and layers in the companies’ list.

Fails with: losses that are catastrophic or that tend to come together, which cannot be collected (Chapter 3); and dominance.476

Each list has its own job. The governments’ list holds the measures that work on pace and visibility. Chapter 3 found that these are the levers on the motive for preventive war. The coalitions’ list holds the measures that need a party outside the race. The staff’s list carries the follower-layer measure above, with the limit stated there. Once trained settings are released, the holders multiply, as Chapter 5 showed. Some of these levers scatter with them.

The table does not rank the measures by how sure the book is of them. That judgment comes in Chapter 12. It applies Chapter 3’s test, the one stated with the deals that work despite disagreement. The measures that meet the test are Chapter 3’s list. Of that list, Chapter 12 names two as meeting the test most plainly: rules against misuse, and making computing power visible. It says that the chapter’s other measures rest on analogy. Among them are the research on satiable ends and the rest of the work aimed at what training builds in.477

Chapter 12Where the evidence is thin, and an answer for the student

An argument built on comparisons owes its reader two things at the end. One is a list of the places where the comparisons are thinnest. The other is an answer to the question it began with. This chapter gives both.

Where is the evidence weakest? How much of the book’s verdict survives those gaps? And what does all of it mean for the student who asked whether she should change her life because of the risk that AI ends humanity?478

The evidence is thinnest in seven places

Chapter 2 set out the general gaps. Seven more bear most on the book’s conclusions.

First: no war model has a side that is both overwhelmingly strong and nearly free to fight. The war models drawn on here in which the sides learn as they fight include no such side (Chapter 4). The nearest thing is the book’s own extension, built in Chapter 3 and set out in the appendix. It takes Smith and Stam’s 2004 model and gives each side its own cost per battle.

Its main case sets the battle odds at even. It also checks a machine that wins two battles in three. And for three pairs of starting beliefs at one human cost, it checks a machine that wins from 80 to 99 battles in 100. It works out best play at every step. The side that answers an offer weighs it against what turning the offer down is worth, counting the offers still to come. It follows the definitions in the 2004 paper’s text. Under those definitions its numbers differ from the paper’s printed Figures 1 and 3. The reason goes to the first author before this book states it. Its numbers are a baseline, not a proof.479

Less is proved about a strong, cheap machine than is computed. The division runs like this (Figure 50).

  • Proved, as a deduction from the model’s assumptions. Every pattern of best play ends the war by some date, as long as the two sides’ costs per battle add up to more than zero. The prize, the sum of the costs and the starting beliefs set that date. The date is finite even when the machine’s cost is zero, because the humans’ cost alone is enough to bound it. Every pattern of best play gives both sides the same values, at any machine cost. And the humans’ expected value is never more than the prize times their own estimate of their chance of winning. It does not rise as they count more machine wins.
  • Computed, not proved: the shares of the prize and the chances of outright victory in the appendix’s tables. They hold for the numbers chosen.
  • Not established: when the last battle comes in the variant where the machine’s odds rise with its lead. That variant is worked out with exact updating of beliefs. (For the main case, the last battle has a lower bound, computed from a proved condition; see the appendix.) Nor is any limit on the humans’ share established as the machine grows stronger. The one exception is the limit that runs through the humans’ own beliefs.

One more point belongs here. In every one of these models the loser survives, because the model is built that way. That is an assumption of the models, not a finding (Chapter 2).480

If something is “proved,” why isn’t the question settled?

Because there are two kinds of certainty, and the book keeps them apart. Chapter 2’s box on “suggests” and “shows” explains the difference. Inside a model, a proved result follows for certain from the model’s assumptions. Whether the model fits a real machine is a separate, open question. To the author’s knowledge, none of these war models has been tested against the historical record. Hedging the first half would be as wrong as forgetting the second.

Second: power transition theory has thin support, and a careful test of one other war game fared poorly. Power transition theory holds that peace between a leading power and a rising one depends on whether the riser is content with the order. It was built for industrial-era states rising over decades. Its claim about great powers rests on small samples. The statistical test reported in Chapter 4 found little support for the theory’s version about pairs of states. That test covered every pair of states, counted from each side’s point of view.

A careful statistical estimate of another war game fared no better. Curtis Signorino fitted Bueno de Mesquita and Lalman’s game to 707 pairs of European states. He estimated eighteen numbers that measure how much each payoff and cost mattered. Eleven came out at zero, the lowest value allowed. That put the result nearer a coin-flip model than the authors’ values. The other seven were too small to show two things: that the game was set up correctly, and that the states played it as highly rational actors.481

Third: whether open disagreement, with nothing hidden, causes war is still contested. The field has not settled it. The record weighs against the view that human disputants share starting beliefs and reason fully from the evidence. But it cannot refute that view. And by Fey and Ramsay’s own result, no record of behavior can tell two kinds of sides apart (Chapter 3). One kind has different starting beliefs; the other has shared starting beliefs and limited reasoning. So Chapter 3 labels each claim by the tradition it depends on. Nothing in Chapter 3’s ways of settling disagreement binds a machine that has already arrived.482

Fourth: the sorting of a mind’s ends into types is a conjecture. Part II proposed that the kind of thing a mind wants may shape the kind of conflict it enters. It may matter more than how clever the mind is. The evidence for that is a short, selected, human record. Matching types of ends to types of killing is the book’s untested judgment (Chapters 7 to 9).483

Fifth: no source shows that the right goals can be built in, or that they would last. No source drawn on here shows that satiable goals (goals a machine can fully meet), or goals indifferent to rank, can be trained into it. None shows that such goals would survive a machine changing itself. None shows that competitive training makes rank something a machine wants for its own sake, in any of the three forms Chapter 7 distinguishes.

Chapter 11 sets three research programs beside that conjecture. They restrain a machine by other means. One limits how hard it pushes toward its goal. One charges it for its gains. One makes it rational for the machine to defer to people. None of them closes the gap. Each has been shown only on paper or in small test environments. None carries a guarantee for a machine that changes itself.

The test that could close the first part of the gap is the one Chapter 10 calls H3b. It asks whether a goal with a built-in limit can be trained in at all. As of this writing it has not been run. It can fail. And it speaks for one way of training, in one family of small environments.484

Two more pieces of evidence are weaker than they might look. The first is the pattern in Chapter 8: the great minds’ ends formed early. That pattern comes from memories written down late, from memorials, and from people questioned decades afterward. It also counts only the people who were remembered. So it cannot show that forming early is what makes ends last.

The second concerns whether what is laid down early in the settings training leaves inside the machine outlasts what is added later. The evidence for that is a single study. It concerns removing knowledge during the first, broad stage of teaching a machine, not installing something the machine wants (Chapter 11). A second, small study found that expectations about how AI behaves lasted through the later stages of teaching (Chapter 3). Those expectations were set in that first stage. The study did not compare them with expectations added later.485

Sixth: the measures in Chapter 11 aim to reduce risk, and nobody knows by how much. Their net effect is unresolved. They do not remove the promise problem at the machine’s arrival. A side about to grow much stronger cannot be held to a deal it makes now. They could buy time and keep options open. By Arrow and Fisher’s argument, that is worth a great deal.

The book cannot say with a number it could defend whether they reduce the risk, or by how much, and it gives none. The war research itself shows why such numbers are hard to come by. The best-fitted war models give even the most dangerous pairs of states a low chance of war in any one year (Chapter 4). Bennett and the author wrote of their own model that “we must expect our model to be ‘wrong’ most of the time.”486

One line of reasoning about war predicts exactly this weak fit. Suppose most wars come from hidden information. Then, as Bennett and Stam summarize Gartzke, the best an analyst can do is find situations near even odds. Wars then happen “in the error term,” the part a model leaves unexplained. That holds unless the analyst knows more than the leaders do, or the leaders make the same kind of mistake again and again.

Bennett and Stam’s own model scored 0.27 on a common measure of fit, where higher is better, for all pairs of states. It scored 0.20 for a narrower set of pairs they call politically relevant (another chapter of their book gives 0.26). They judged those scores against a ceiling set by even odds. They stated that ceiling as a condition. It holds if all of the following conditions apply:

  • leaders are rational;
  • hidden information is the only cause of war;
  • the outcomes are win or lose; and
  • the choice is war or no war.

Its nature, they wrote, “remains to be more completely developed.” On the book’s reading, the ceiling limits how well such a model can fit, not whether it can be tested. The theory still predicts which situations come near even odds, and that prediction can fail. Meanwhile, the Existential-Risk Persuasion Tournament changed almost no one’s mind (Chapter 3). It is the one field test of whether experts come to agree on this question.487

The book works on the assumption that the defenses tend to fail together. The war data do not test that assumption. In statistical models of war, adding one factor, trade, shrank or erased the effects of others. The authors put this down mostly to the cases with trade data not being a random sample. They put it less to the factors moving together (Chapter 10). For a machine, one process of teaching sets its leanings. One channel, its behavior while people watch, reports them. Multiplying their chances of failure as if they were separate overstates the protection when a shared cause makes the defenses fail together. Nothing here shows that the failures are separate.

Why does it matter whether the defenses fail together?

If one key opens every lock on a door, the door is no safer than a single lock. (This is an illustration, not a finding.) Multiplying the chances that separate defenses fail is right if they fail on their own. Chapter 11’s box on multiplying the chances that each safeguard fails works this out. The book’s worry is that one teaching process, and one window on the machine’s behavior while it is watched, could be such a key for a machine’s defenses.

What a machine might want along the way adds to the caution. Bostrom (2012) expects many kinds of mind to seek to become more capable, as a means to whatever else they want. He expects “cognitive enhancement to emerge as an instrumental goal for many types of intelligent agent.” Benson-Tilsen and Soares (2016) find trade the easy route to resources “only insofar as the machine is not much more powerful than the human race in aggregate.” The result of Turner and colleagues on machines that seek power is in Chapter 10.488

Here the book makes a judgment it has not tested. Some ways of satisfying a machine that wants knowledge could also make it stronger. Two of the things that could satisfy it can also raise its capability: control over its own agenda and control over its inputs. Where capability turns into power (the conversion Chapter 4’s test tracks), these two can speed up the shift in power that Powell’s threshold is about (Chapter 3). This holds whatever the machine’s ends. Evidence that a machine had been given such control without any gain in capability would change that judgment.

The other things that could satisfy it need not raise its capability: recognition, standing and a voice. That holds only if the institutions that grant them keep them from being turned into computing power, resources or authority, influence over human decisions included. Chapter 11 leaves that condition to design, and nothing here shows it can be met. Evidence that standing or a voice had bought a machine computing power or authority would change that judgment.

If the judgment holds, the first two pull one lever in opposite directions. What satisfies the machine is also what could bring the fast jump in capability. That jump, if it comes, defeats the measures on the human side.489

Seventh and last: nothing here survives a machine’s dominance. By dominance the book means a machine that can defeat every check humans hold. In the book’s firm judgment, every protection on the human side then fails, including several machines kept as checks on one another. Two things remain. One is concern for humans that the machine has made its own, which is the work Chapter 11 calls “Shape the ends.” The other is whatever a balance among several machines that no human governs might supply. Nothing has tested that balance. Chapter 11’s rule is to spread protections across different kinds of failure before dominance. After it, everything rests on the bet on the machine’s ends and on that untested balance.490

AI helped make this book, so its method needs checks too

The book has a limit of its own, in how it was made. The author’s stated purpose is human survival. AI systems helped draft the analysis. An AI model might have goals that bear on the question. It might also expect its account of how to make a machine want what its makers intend to affect how it is tested or treated. If both hold, it has the same reason to shade that account that Chapter 11 gives a model under test. Being aware of itself would not, alone, show such a conflict.

There is reason to check. Studies have found that AI models acting as judges can favor text they wrote themselves (A. Panickssery, Bowman and Feng 2024; Wataoka, Takahashi and Ri 2024). Another study found that models can rank AI too highly when they give advice (Trabelsi, Shaki and Kraus 2026). But other things could also explain these preferences: familiarity, differences in quality, and what the models were trained on. A model’s assurance that it is impartial cannot settle the question by itself. Elga’s argument calls for grounds for judging someone’s reliability that do not depend on the judgment in dispute (Chapter 3).491

The book used five safeguards:

  1. The author took responsibility for every word.
  2. Calculations were kept in code that a person can rerun.
  3. Quotations were checked against the original sources, and the limits of that reading were recorded.
  4. Readers from other families of AI models, working blind, checked drafts.
  5. Disagreements were reported rather than averaged away.

The sensitive passages also got blind drafts from other model families. These were commissioned for two parts of Chapter 11. One was an earlier draft of its measures that concern a machine’s own interests. The other was the measure called “Don’t train against the reader.” A third model from outside the Claude family, GPT-6 Luna, compared the drafts with their authors’ names hidden. It judged that the text Claude wrote leaned furthest toward the machine’s interests. A writer from outside the Claude family, GPT-6 Astra, rewrote the affected passages, and the rewrite was checked.

Then each model defended its own text and examined the other’s. GPT-6 Astra conceded that its rewrite left out qualifications and was unclear about who said what. It disputed five other points with reasons. Claude agreed, sometimes with qualifications, with eight of ten points about its own draft. Among them: a comparison about a machine’s status was untested, advice about checkpoints was overstated, and limits on custody and on credibility were missing. Claude proposed four changes. Neither model dug in to defend its own text.

The sample is small. This is not evidence of motive, and it does not rank model families. The safeguards describe what this book did, not a guarantee that it escaped bias.492

Why tell the reader that AI helped write a book about AI risk?

Because the helper could have a stake in the answer, for the reason Chapter 11 gives a model under test. The book does not claim that any model did tilt it. It reports what it did instead, so a reader can judge the method without taking any model’s word that it was fair.

A human author does not settle the problem either. Bruce Russett named his own values. He described his method as turning ideological opinions into propositions that can be tested. He also explained the care he took against coding decisions that could look self-serving. Critics still disputed his standards for when a claim counts as refuted, and his rules for coding cases (Henderson 2009; Rosato 2003). Even an analyst who knew his values could not settle those disputes by his own word.

Nor do the studies that give many analysts the same data show that values caused the spread in their results. Silberzahn and colleagues (2018) found that the analysts’ prior beliefs did not readily explain the variation. Breznau and colleagues (2022) found that prior beliefs and expectations barely predicted it. Those studies show that results depend on the analysts’ choices. They do not show that the analysts’ values caused bias. Here, too, the answer is to show the choices, keep the disagreements, and let others check the work.493

An answer for the student: much of the verdict turns on what the machine wants

What, then, do the study of war and the history of great minds tell us?

The theory’s verdict is bleak under the assumptions that follow. Suppose the machine is the kind of side the war research assumes. It acts as one, chooses what best serves its goals given what it believes, and wants more power and a longer life. Then:

  • if its arrival is the large, rapid shift in power this book assumes, and nothing holds it to its promises, then in Powell’s model its arrival is a promise problem;
  • no deal paid in what it wants is believable in the outcomes these models’ examples reach, where power changes hands in lumps, as this book reads them; and
  • the remedy power transition theory offers, keeping a rising power content with the order, has nothing to hold on to.494

History’s most celebrated minds suggest that intelligence does not require such ends. One coder’s search found no aim to end humanity in any of those checked here. Most of them wanted knowledge, a good that one mind can have without taking any from another.

But that record is short, chosen by reputation, human, and shaped by evolution. Napoleon shows that a mind of great military and political ability can choose conquest. The record does not, though, place him among the first minds for knowledge. The scientists fought over credit. And the atrocities of the last century needed both a few who chose and many who followed. Machines could fill those roles.495

A machine with different ends would leave more room for a deal. That holds if those ends do not compete with ours. A machine whose goals are satiable might believably promise not to raise its demands. That is a conjecture (Chapter 7). It is to be read against Chapter 10’s test H3c, which estimates where a machine’s need for security overrides a goal it can meet. Even so, different ends would not remove the promise problem at the machine’s arrival. We could not promise never to build a rival, and the machine would still have reason to make itself secure.

Whether a machine we build will have such ends depends on choices people are making now. What leanings does training build in, and can a satiable goal be trained in at all? No source here shows that it can. Chapter 10’s test H3b, not yet run, would test it under its own training and testing conditions and no further. Do efforts to build the most powerful machines stay in the open? And who controls these systems?496

Start with measures that make sense whatever the risk

Those choices do not have to wait until anyone settles whether the risk is 10 percent, 1 percent, or something else. Such risk figures are degrees of belief rather than measurements. Narayanan and Kapoor, the critics quoted in Chapter 1, call them “feelings dressed up as numbers.” They advise choosing policies “compatible with a range of possible estimates of AI risk”: policies that make sense whether the true danger turns out to be large or small.

In Chapter 3’s terms, that is the book’s test for a robust measure. This chapter calls it the belief-neutral test. A measure passes it if it is acceptable under every party’s starting beliefs. So it does not need the disagreement to close first.497

What is the “belief-neutral test”?

It asks whether a measure makes sense to everyone in a dispute, whatever each believes about the risk. Think of two neighbours who disagree about whether a nearby river will ever flood. One thinks it likely; the other thinks it almost never happens. Both might still agree to keep the storm drains clear, if each judges the cost small for what it buys. (This is an illustration only.) Neither has to change their mind. The book’s version carries the same condition. A measure passes only if each party judges what it buys worth that party’s share of the cost and better than the alternatives. Chapter 3 assumes this and does not show it. And passing the test says nothing about how much a measure actually lowers the risk.

Chapter 3 names the five measures that meet that test (Figure 16). It does so under an assumption it states and does not show. Its list is the book’s one list. On this book’s reading, two of the five meet it most plainly. They need no reading of a machine’s ends and no future event to settle the dispute:

  • governing the misuse of AI, which reaches the people who direct AI through law that exists now; and
  • keeping the development of the most powerful systems in view, which is people watching people, now.

The other three meet the test but lean on cooperation that a race can withhold: reporting incidents, shared means of testing what machines can do, and keeping steps undoable.

Two kinds of evidence would change this ranking, or take visibility off the list. One is evidence that visibility inflames the race more than it calms it (Chapter 5’s two models point opposite ways). The other is evidence that rules against misuse cannot be enforced across borders. Girish Sastry and colleagues argue that computing power is the natural handle. Their reason: it is “detectable, excludable, and quantifiable, and is produced via an extremely concentrated supply chain.” That can give warning while people can still act.498

The work on what training builds in is not on that list. It covers research on making a machine want what its makers intend. It covers tools that read what a machine has learned inside. And it covers tests for dangerous abilities before a machine is released, including tests of what it wants. This work is the only priority that bears on whether a future machine would value knowledge, or us, at all. Every argument in this book for keeping us depends on that.

That work rests on analogy, research on satiable goals included. So do the other measures in Chapter 11, with one partial exception. The narrow rule against pushing hard, in training, against a monitor that reads a machine’s written reasoning rests on experiment. In one study of a leading reasoning model, such pressure taught the model to hide its intent from the monitor (Baker et al. 2025). The book extends the rule to other tools that read or steer what goes on inside a machine; it names probes and persona vectors. That extension is this book’s inference from that result, not a finding. Carrying either the rule or its extension to a machine that dominates its overseers goes beyond any experiment.

Several of Chapter 11’s measures come from others’ published work, as its citations show. This book’s own proposal is the way it puts them together. It ties each measure to a mechanism from the study of war and names what that measure fails against. That combination deserves testing. But it has not yet earned the standing the belief-neutral measures hold.499

The models cannot answer the student, so the advice is the author’s own

The author’s own advice to the student, as things stand, is not to change plans out of fear. That advice is not a result of the analysis. The analysis does not evaluate whether any reader should change plans. So it establishes neither that she should nor that she should not. That turns on her alternatives, costs, values, and beliefs.

Two things keep the analysis silent here. The belief-neutral test concerns policies, not a person’s plans. So it does not answer the student who asked whether she should change her life course because of the risk of human extinction. Nor can the models answer her. Their loser survives because the models are built that way. A model that rules out extinction by construction cannot by itself show that extinction will not happen (Chapter 2).

The advice’s calm is conditional on choices Chapter 11 names, made now. Take the question seriously. If it keeps pulling at you, the field needs careful minds.500

Why can’t the analysis tell the student what to do?

For two reasons. The belief-neutral test is about policies that many parties must accept, not one person’s life. And the war models assume from the start that the losing side survives. They contain no move that removes the other player. So the book keeps its advice to the student separate and labels it the author’s own.

Disclosure: the book’s ties to its sources

This book quotes researchers at Anthropic, the company that makes the Claude models. It quotes Anthropic’s constitution for those models, and it cites studies by Anthropic researchers. It also cites work by OpenAI and its researchers, including OpenAI’s report on an incident. Chapter 11 cites Anthropic’s own announcements of three things. They are its program on the welfare of its models, a feature that lets a model end a conversation, and its commitment to preserve the settings of trained models. Chapter 11 also cites a proposal from Redwood Research. Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, helped draft and revise the book. Every company building AI was treated as an ordinary source.

The analysis of the causes of war in Part I rests heavily on models the author built with Alastair Smith. It also rests on joint work with D. Scott Bennett, Dan Reiter, and Daniel Friedman and Donald Wittman. Smith is also a co-author of the work on leaders’ survival in office (the selectorate work) cited in Chapter 2. Critiques of that work, including Fey and Ramsay (2006), are cited alongside it. Chapter 3’s extension to unequal costs rests on the book’s own rebuilding of the 2004 model. Chapter 10’s test comes from the author’s design paper (Stam 2026).

Some sources were not consulted directly. Others were read through reviews, publisher material, abstracts or summaries, and some were read in full. The full edition names each, and its references say how each was read. Three points of general history are given “by standard accounts” and are not cited to a source. They are the Royal Society’s 1712 committee on the calculus, Brahe’s loss of the island of Hven in 1597, and Einstein’s declining the presidency of Israel in 1952. The unpublished working papers, drafts and notes cited in the book are available from the author on request. Four pieces of the Smith–Stam work are published: the mediation paper (2003), the learning model (2004), the likely-losers chapter (2005), and the reply to Fey and Ramsay (2006).501

AppendixHow the models in Part I work, in plain words

Part I rests on four papers the author wrote with colleagues:

  • a conference paper with Alastair Smith (2001);
  • the article Smith and the author published in 2004;
  • a working paper with D. Scott Bennett and Smith (2003); and
  • a working paper with Daniel Friedman and Donald Wittman (2003).

For each, the full edition’s appendix sets out the model. It says which results are proved and which are shown only by worked examples, and it gives the numbers the examples use.

This plain version tells, in words, what each model does and how sure the book is about each result. It leaves the mathematics to the full edition. It then turns to an early draft by Smith (1998) and to the book’s own extension of the 2004 model to unequal costs. It ends with a short calculation about companies that race.502

Three points hold for every war model here, and they matter wherever a model is applied to a machine.

  • Battle strength is not distance to defeat. A side can be strong battle for battle and still be a few lost battles from ruin. Smith and Stam’s example is Israel: strong in each battle, yet “its neighbors only need a few victories in order to overrun the country.”
  • A settlement includes surrender. When the models count settlements, they count the case in which the side that answers accepts nothing.
  • The loser’s survival is built into the models, never shown by them. There is no move in these games that removes the other player. So the models can return capitulation or confinement, but never extinction. On the book’s reading, that assumption gives way where Chapter 10 treats a machine whose ends make humans themselves a resource it wants.

A fourth point governs how sure the book is. “Proved” means certain within a model’s assumptions. Whether a model fits a machine is a separate, open question.503

The 2001 model: what the sides fight over decides whether a deal can hold

Picture a line of forts between two sides. Each round the front moves by chance: one fort toward one side, one fort toward the other, or not at all. This goes on until one side holds every fort. The paper notes, “this model is called a random walk or a gambler’s ruin.” Forts here stand for the military assets a side needs to keep fighting.

What is a “random walk”?

Think of a marker on a tug-of-war rope that moves one notch left or right, or stays put, each round, by chance. The game ends when the marker reaches either end. (An illustration of the model’s set-up.) In the war models, the notches are forts, each round is a battle, and reaching an end is decisive defeat for one side. The odds of each move can be fixed, as in most of the models here. Or they can change with the marker’s position, as in the 2001 model’s power version.

Each round each side chooses to attack, to resist, or to surrender. Plans may look only at where the front stands, and they switch at fixed cut-off points. One side, say, attacks from some position onward and surrenders below some other. Each round a side receives the value of the forts it holds, less a cost of fighting. That cost is the same for both sides. Payoffs that come later count for less than payoffs now.

The paper compares three things to fight over:

  • in the forts version the sides value forts, and holding more of them does not change the odds of the next battle;
  • in the power version, holding forts raises the odds of winning the next battle, by an amount set by how decisive a battle is;
  • in the policy version the sides fight over a policy, and a decisive winner imposes its own preferred policy in place of the starting one.

With best play, the positions fall into as many as five zones: one side gives up, war, the status quo, war, the other side gives up. For some choices of numbers, some of the zones shrink to nothing.

What is proved, and what is not. The paper states no formal result of its own. It credits its formal results to earlier papers by Smith and states them in prose. A side’s best answer to a plan of this cut-off kind is itself of that kind. And best play among such plans exists if the sides can randomize at the cut-off points.

Two limits are worked out in the text. If fighting costs nothing, the sides fight in every position, apart from special cases. As the cost grows without bound, war never happens. Between the two, the zone of the status quo widens as the cost of fighting grows. At a high cost there are typically several possible patterns of best play. Which peace then holds depends on coordination.504

The claim the book uses most is that “No agreements can be reached in the forts or the power models.” The paper argues it case by case, not by proof. The side that gains from a deal cannot believably promise not to attack once the balance moves its way. That holds among the plans the paper studies. A footnote concedes that one step in the argument can fail at certain cut-off points.

That a deal is sometimes possible in the policy version is shown only by example. The paper also compares the three versions: sides surrender fastest in the power version, and its status-quo zone tends to be smaller. These comparisons are read off a single figure, which the paper then checks against runs over many costs of fighting. A way out by paying tribute is stated in prose. It is a believable deal bought “with money, or some other transferable utility,” that is, with money or something else that can be handed over.

The examples. The main comparison uses a line of positions numbered 0 to 7, with each side winning a battle four times in ten. One figure shows several patterns of best play in the forts version at a single cost. In them the status-quo zone covers anywhere from one to all six of the positions between the ends. In the policy examples, moving the policy a step at one position is a deal both sides prefer and would honor. One position further on, starting from the moved policy, no deal is possible.

The paper does not state how much later payoffs are discounted. It is a conference draft: one footnote is a placeholder, and the text discusses one cost where the figure is labelled with another. It holds the decisiveness of battle fixed and does not explore what happens as it changes. So it cannot say what follows as battles become more decisive, which may be what happens in the AI case.505

The 2004 model: fighting teaches both sides until the war ends in defeat or a deal

The 2004 model keeps the line of forts and changes the rest. Two sides dispute a prize. One side’s chance of winning a battle is fixed, wherever the front stands. Each round the first side proposes how to split the prize. If the other side accepts, the game ends; if it refuses, they fight a battle. Both pay the same cost for each battle, and later payoffs are not discounted.

The new feature is belief. The two sides hold different starting beliefs about the first side’s chance of winning a battle. Each side’s beliefs are common knowledge: each knows the other’s, knows that the other knows it, and so on without end. Both update their beliefs on every battle, which both see. Nothing is hidden.

To the authors’ knowledge, theirs was the first model of its kind in political science to drop the assumption that the sides share starting beliefs. A web appendix to the paper analyzes a version in which the two sides take turns making offers. The paper says that version gives similar results, but it reports no comparison; the book makes one, below.

Proved in the paper. The paper proves its first numbered result (its Proposition 1). A deal is possible only if the two sides’ values of fighting on until one side is beaten add up to no more than the prize. If they add up to more, fighting goes on. The authors add that this holds under any rule in which a settlement needs both sides’ consent.

Lemma 1 proves that the two sides’ beliefs come together as battles pile up. Proposition 2 proves that after some date the first side makes an offer and the other accepts. The offer is what fighting on to the end would be worth to the other side, or nothing if that value is below zero. So the game ends in a finite time, either by decisive defeat or by a deal. The terms of that result are amended below. The paper’s Corollary says, without proof, that the cheaper each battle, the later that date. Proposition 3 gives the first side’s values by working back from the end, and it too is amended below.506

The running example. Ten forts, a start in the middle, a prize of 30, and a cost of 1 per battle. Each side’s starting belief is of a standard kind, set by two numbers: four and two for the first side, two and four for the second. In plain terms, the first side expects to win two battles in three, and the second expects the first to win one in three. The paper prints that at the start the first side values fighting at 23.8 and settling at 17.8, so it fights. It also prints that by period 10 settling and fighting are worth the same to it at every position.

Why beliefs can move apart. Shared news can make both sides more confident, each in itself. The paper’s account of this carries no formal result. Victory depends on three factors. One side believes the first two matter; the other believes the last two do. In a war between them in which all three factors stand equal, both expect the first side to win a battle with chance .68.

Then both watch a third country win five straight battles in another war. Afterward the first side expects .76 and the second .63. Each, reading the same news through its own theory, has grown more confident in itself. These beliefs were computed by simulation, because they are “often analytically intractable,” too hard to work out exactly. Technological change enters too. But the only formal content there is that the spread of beliefs grows with time.

The peace after a war. One comparison carries the paper’s claims about how stable a peace is. A long war leaves beliefs that a surprise moves less. After a settlement in the second round, the two sides’ expectations are 3/4 and 1/2. A surprise worth one battle then moves the second side from 1/2 to 4/9. After a ten-round war, they are 9/16 and 7/16. The same surprise moves the second side from 7/16 to 7/17, “a shift of less than half the magnitude.” The article offers what follows as predictions that can be checked, and matches them to published studies.507

A correction: turning an offer down can be worth more than the 2004 paper allows

The paper has the side that answers accept any offer worth at least what fighting on until one side is beaten would give it. In the paper’s own example, that rule is not that side’s best answer.

Why would turning down a deal ever be better than taking it?

Think of selling a used car. A buyer offers less than you expect another buyer to offer next week. Keeping the car another week costs you something. But if the better offer is likely enough, saying no is the right call. That holds even though you would never drive the car to the scrapyard instead. (An illustration, not part of the model.) In the model, the side that answers pays one battle’s cost to refuse. But refusing keeps the chance of a better offer at the next round. Judging an offer only against fighting to the bitter end leaves that chance out.

Turning an offer down keeps the option of better offers later, and offers can never fall below nothing. So refusing can be worth more than fighting to the end. A side that refuses may later accept nothing, or more, instead of fighting on at a loss.

The paper’s argument checks later offers against what fighting to the end is worth at later positions, not at the present one. Its proof sets aside one case: fighting to the end is worth less than nothing at the present position, but not at later ones. The rule therefore fails at some settlements. At these, fighting to the end is worth at least zero to that side now, but less than zero at some later settlement reachable through fighting.

The corrected rule: accept if, and only if, the offer is worth at least what turning it down is worth, counting the offers still to come. That value is never below what fighting to the end is worth.

On the printed figure. In the paper’s printed Figure 3, play reaches position 6 in period 5 through fighting. There the second side is offered nothing. If it refuses, it pays one battle’s cost. By its own beliefs, the next battle then moves the front to position 5 with chance 6 in 11. There the printed figure has the first side settle and leave the second side 30 − 25.73 = 4.27. Otherwise the front moves to position 7, where the second side gets nothing.

So refusing is worth −1 + (6/11) × 4.27, about 1.33, which is more than the offer of nothing. It stays positive within the rounding of the printed cells. This failure is a deduction from the printed cells, certain given how they were copied. Two reviewers from other AI model families derived it independently, working blind.

With the text’s definitions. The rule also fails when worked out exactly from the definitions in the paper’s text. It fails at position 6 in period 1, on the path of play from the start, where refusing is worth 3.10 against an offer of 1.73. It fails at four more positions on that path through period 8 (computed). It also fails at every late date the war could still reach (proved).

What survives. Proposition 1 is unaffected. Proposition 2’s conclusion holds under best play: the game settles by a finite date unless the war is decided first. Proposition 2’s stated terms and Proposition 3 as printed do not describe best play in the example. The book proves them in amended form. It puts what turning the offer down is worth in place of what fighting to the end is worth.508

Rebuilding the 2004 model: the conclusions hold, some printed numbers do not

When the book rebuilt the 2004 model from the definitions in the paper’s text, some things matched and some did not.

What matched. Proposition 1 holds as a condition a deal needs. Proposition 2’s conclusion holds, with its terms amended. The web appendix’s shares match to the last digit, as do the text’s checks of the two sides’ beliefs after the first battle. And best play has the paper’s shape. The first side fights at the start, settles once the front has moved far enough either way, and faces a finite deadline. The book also checked the paper’s proof that beliefs come together. It supplied a stronger form of coming together, which the result needs and which the paper’s weaker form does not give.

What did not. Figure 1’s chances of eventual victory differ from the printed ones by up to 0.025, and its lengths of war by up to 10.3 battles. Figure 3’s values differ by up to 9.68. The first side’s choice differs in 6 of its 42 printed cells. And the deadline comes in period 8 against the paper’s 10.

The rebuilt model gives 19.85 where the article prints 17.8, and 23.76 where it prints 23.8. The second pair agrees at the printed precision, so it is the 17.8 that fails. The 2003 paper gives figures for when the second side loses the first battle: a 0.62 chance of eventual victory and 15.46 more rounds of war. For these the rebuilt model gives 0.600 and 16.27.

A computation that reproduces the printed figures has been found. It does not establish how the paper’s own figures were computed, and it goes to the first author before this book states it. The book’s extension uses the text’s definitions.509

The corrected rule on the paper’s own example. With the corrected rule, the paper’s baseline shifts but keeps its conclusions (Figure 52, bottom). The last battle comes in period 5 instead of the 7 that the paper’s rule gives when rebuilt. The second side’s expected share on settlement is 8.83 of 30 instead of 6.30. And settlement before a decisive victory is still certain.

Two words carry one meaning each from here on. The last battle is the last round in which some position the war can reach still fights. The deadline is the first round from which every position the war can reach settles. So it is the last battle plus one. For the 2004 baseline:

  • the paper as printed: last battle 9, deadline 10;
  • the paper’s rule, rebuilt from the text’s definitions: last battle 7, deadline 8;
  • the corrected rule, from the text’s definitions: last battle 5, deadline 6.

Under the corrected rule, the deadline lengthens as battles get cheaper: 6, 12, 25, 61 and 121 rounds at a cost per battle of 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.1 and 0.05. The paper’s rule gives 8 and 13 at costs of 1 and 0.5; from 0.25 down the two rules agree. The paper’s Corollary concerns a date after which its proof has the game settle. It does not concern the last battle under best play. Under best play a limit of that kind is proved, and the computed deadline moves the way the Corollary says.510

The paper’s account of why beliefs move apart was reproduced in a check outside the book’s programs: .76 and .63, as printed. Its claims about technological change and about the peace after a war were not recomputed.

The 2003 spiral of optimism: shared events can feed both sides’ optimism about war

The 2003 working paper joins two pieces. The first is beliefs that move apart until each side expects to gain more from fighting than from a deal. The second is the 2004 bargaining model on the line of forts. “In our model, what is spiraling is the two sides’ optimism about their chances of victory in some future war.” The beliefs move apart because the sides learn from shared events under different theories of what wins. Technological change keeps the theories apart.

The pattern behind the paper is Bennett and Stam’s finding that an arms race goes with roughly double the risk of war. That is an association. The spiral model takes it as its starting premise and does not test it. The doubling comes with no printed margin of error.

The figure in the statistical model behind it is imprecise. The range of values it allows (its 95 percent interval) runs from about one to about four, and so includes no effect at all. That range belongs to the underlying figure, not to the doubling. On the book’s reading, it gives AI neither a rate nor a direction.

Proved, and not. The formal results are the 2004 article’s, word for word. The spiral itself, the paper’s own contribution, carries no formal result. The paper says of technological change keeping beliefs apart, “we demonstrate this formally.” But what follows is only the statement that the spread of beliefs grows with time. Its conclusions about wars and the peace after them rest on the 2004 comparison. They are offered as predictions that could be tested. The paper reports what happens if the second side loses the first battle: its chance of eventual victory “drops to 0.62, with the war expected to last 15.46 more periods.” As above, the book’s computation gives 0.600 and 16.27.

One more example in the paper runs the other way. Suppose only the factor both sides believe in is present. Then the first side expects to win a battle with chance .63, and the second side puts the first side’s chance at .66. Each side’s estimate of its own chance then adds up to .97 (that is, .63 plus .34), below one. Both sides are pessimistic about the next battle.511

Sealed offers: war when the aggressor’s signal tops the target’s by enough

Friedman, Stam and Wittman (2003) built a model with one round, not a war of many battles. An aggressor and a target each privately see its own signal of how a war would come out. The two signals are drawn independently. At the same moment, the aggressor submits a demand and the target an offer “to a third party (perhaps a computer). If the offer is greater than or equal to the demand, then there is a settlement half way between the two; otherwise, the case proceeds to war.”

In war, each side pays the same cost, and the outcome is the average of the two signals. Each signal bears on an outcome both share. So each side must take the other’s signal into account, as bidders at an auction do. The text keeps the words of the courtroom model it grew from: litigant, plaintiff, court date.

Proved in the paper. Six results and a lemma are proved. The paper finds a pair of plans, each the best answer to the other. In them, demands and offers rise in straight-line steps with each side’s signal. It shows that every non-trivial symmetric pair of plans of that kind leads to the same outcome. In that outcome, war comes exactly when the aggressor’s signal exceeds the target’s by more than a margin. The margin grows with the cost of war.

The paper gives the chance of war for each cost. Outcomes run on a scale from 0 to 1, and each signal is as likely to fall at any point on that scale as at any other. On that scale:

  • a cost of one-twelfth gives war seven times in eight;
  • one-sixth, half the time;
  • one-quarter, one time in eight; and
  • one-third or more, never.

Below a cost of one-sixth, war is likelier the further the war’s outcome lies from one half. That outcome is the average of the two signals. Above that cost, the reverse holds. And a wider spread of possible outcomes raises the chance of war.

Argued, not proved. Extensions to other kinds of signals, unequal costs and unequal splits are argued, not proved. The authors conclude that “our main qualitative results appear to be quite robust.” For unequal costs, they give a worked comparison.
