When the target’s own cost rises by one unit, its offer rises by one and a half units and the aggressor’s demand falls by half a unit. So “75% of the impact is due to own cost and 25% to the other player’s cost.” That the threat of war is always believable at a cost below 0.1 is shown only for an aggressor with the lowest signal. The authors defend having a single round as “an upper bound on bargaining efficiency,” that is, as the best case for what bargaining can achieve.512

Smith’s 1998 draft: in one example, a superweapon is likeliest used by the side already winning

Chapter 3 cites one earlier draft for a result. Smith’s draft of 26 February 1998 calls itself “extremely preliminary and in parts incomplete.” It sets out the line-of-forts model that the 2001 paper later uses and states no formal result. Its section on superweapons is a single worked example.

In it, superweapons “have three characteristics: the initial advantage they confer, the length of time before the enemy can replicate them, and how they affect the costs of fighting.” In the example the other side does not know of the weapon until it is used. The weapon gains forts on first use, is copied within one round, and then raises the cost of fighting. The author warns that the example “was generated using a different stage game to that considered in the rest of the paper.” In that game the sides choose only between fighting and surrender.

From it the draft concludes that a side is most likely to use a superweapon “when they are winning the war rather than as a last ditch gamble for resurrection.” The draft’s reason: the higher costs that follow push whichever side is losing toward surrender. The example concerns a weapon used during a war. So carrying it to a race in peacetime is an analogy.513

The book’s own extension: a machine that fights for free still faces a deadline

Every model above gives both sides the same cost of fighting. Among them, only Friedman, Stam and Wittman’s worked comparison treats unequal costs. It concerns the offers in a single round, not how long a war lasts or when it stops. The 2004 article notes that one could model disagreement over how costly fighting is, as Smith and Stam’s 2005 chapter does. An earlier draft sketches costs drawn separately for each side and revealed by battle. Neither computes a war in which known costs differ. The 2005 chapter was not re-read for the appendix. The account of its worked example in Chapter 4 is Chapter 4’s.

So the extension in Chapter 3 is the book’s own: a machine that fights almost for free against humans who do not. None of the four papers proves it, and nothing is claimed of the 2005 chapter either way. The book computes it for one baseline in the 2004 model, with each side’s own cost per battle.

The set-up. Ten forts, a start in the middle, a prize of 30. The machine’s starting belief is the first side’s from the 2004 example, so it expects to win two battles in three. The humans expect it to win one in three. Each case is solved twice: once with the machine making every offer, and once with the humans making every offer. The version with turns at offering is a separate game. Both sides learn at the same rate, and the loser survives. The main case sets the true battle odds at even, so the machine is cheaper but no stronger.514

How it is solved. The game hides nothing: each side’s beliefs are known to the other, and every battle is public. The book works out best play at every step by reasoning back from the end. Each side judges the future by its own beliefs. The side that answers uses the corrected rule.

Two tie rules are needed. First, a side offered exactly what turning the offer down is worth accepts. Where the side making the offer settles, best play requires this; elsewhere it is a chosen rule that changes no value. Second, a side making the offer that is exactly indifferent between settling and fighting settles. This also changes no value. In the baseline no reported choice turns on how a near-tie is judged. The other cases were not checked one by one.

What does it mean that the values are unique but the plan is not?

The book proves that every pattern of best play gives both sides the same values and the same offer at every settlement. It also proves that all patterns make the same choice to settle or fight wherever the side making the offer is not exactly indifferent. Patterns can differ only in choices that change nothing. An example is which losing offer a side makes when it means to fight anyway. A choice at an exact tie would need a chosen rule, and the main case has no such tie.

Moving the starting point of the backward reasoning 300 rounds later changes no printed figure by more than 4 parts in a hundred million. That error is proved to be bounded. A version in which the sides choose with some error could give different figures; none has been computed. As the 2004 article itself warns, citing others, small changes in the rules of offer or in how best play is defined can change behavior drastically.515

The deadline. The deadline depends on the two sides’ costs added together, so a machine that fights for free still faces one, set by the humans’ cost.

Why does the side making the offer pay for the other side’s delay?

For example, imagine a contractor who will get a fixed sum for finishing a fixed job, and whom you want to buy out. Each day of work leaves a day less of effort to spend for the same pay. So the contract is worth a day’s effort more to the contractor, and the price to buy them out goes up by that amount. Whoever is paying ends up covering both their own daily costs and the contractor’s. (An illustration of the mechanism, not a claim about any real dispute.) In the model, this is why the date by which a deal must come depends on both sides’ costs added together. It is also why a machine that fights for free still faces a deadline set by the humans’ cost.

The side making the offer takes whatever surplus a deal leaves. Each round, what the side that answers will accept rises by its own cost, as that side reckons it. That is because one fewer battle remains for it to pay for. This holds while turning the offer down is worth at least zero to that side. Where it is worth less than nothing, the side making the offer settles at once. So the side making the offer bears both sides’ costs of delay. It bears its own cost directly, and the other side’s as a higher price tomorrow. When the costs are equal, the line that matters is twice the cost per battle. The book derived this by hand and confirmed it in the computer runs.

The book proves the deadline finite whenever the two costs add up to more than zero. Its upper limit depends only on that sum and on the starting beliefs, and it grows as the sum shrinks. So under either side making the offers, the humans’ cost alone keeps the deadline finite when the machine’s cost is zero. Every computed deadline falls inside its limit: 6 against a limit of 24 at equal costs of 1, and 121 against 594 at equal costs of 0.05. For the baseline beliefs with the machine making the offers, the deadline also has a lower limit. So it moves later without end only as both costs fall together (proved).

The computed deadlines, for the baseline, at three human costs:

  • human cost 1: deadline 6 at equal costs, moving to 18 when a free machine makes the offers, or 12 when the humans do;
  • human cost 0.5: 12 at equal costs, moving to 32 or 25;
  • human cost 0.2: 31 at equal costs, moving to 68 or 63.

What a later deadline does to settlement is computed, not proved. At equal costs of 0.02 the deadline is period 302, and the computed chance that a decisive victory comes first rounds to 1.000.516

The range of deals. With unequal costs, Proposition 1’s condition becomes this. A deal is possible only if the two sides’ joint optimism is covered by their costs of fighting on. Joint optimism is the prize times how far their own expected chances of winning the war add up to more than a sure thing. The costs of fighting on are each side’s cost per battle times its own expected number of battles left. With the machine fighting free, only the humans’ side of that sum remains.

This range is a test a deal must pass, not a guarantee of one. The 2004 baseline fights at the start with a range of 9.70 open (computed). Nor is it the range of offers accepted under best play, which the book does not compute. In the baseline with a free machine, the range is empty at the start for a human cost below 1.29 per battle. It opens later as beliefs come together.

If there is a range of deals both sides would take, why do they still fight?

Because the range is measured against fighting to the bitter end. That is not what each side compares an offer with. Each also counts what learning from the next battle might bring, and the chance of a better offer later. So a range can be open while best play still says fight. The book therefore calls the range a necessary test, not a sufficient one. It is also not the range of offers actually accepted in play.

Two regimes, set by the humans’ cost. With the machine fighting free and the battle odds even, the outcome turns on one quantity. That quantity is the humans’ expected cost of fighting to the end, as a share of what they expect to win. In the baseline at the start, that share is 0.57 times the humans’ cost per battle.

Above a share of about one quarter, settlement before a decisive victory is likelier than not. In the computed baseline, settlement is likelier than not at a human cost of 0.4 or more per battle, about 1.3 percent of the prize. Settlement then comes by a finite deadline. The book’s computer runs show, for these numbers and not as a proof:

Human cost per battle 0.4 0.5 1 1.5 2 3
Deadline, machine offers 39 32 18 12 8 6
Deadline, humans offer 31 25 12 7 4 2
Chance of settlement, machine offers 0.51 0.66 0.79 0.87 0.94 1.00
Chance of settlement, humans offer 0.52 0.69 0.89 1.00 1.00 1.00

When the machine makes the offers, the terms are coercive. The humans’ expected share, given a settlement, is 2.7 of 30 at a cost of 0.4. It is between 1.9 and 2.4 for every cost from 0.5 to 2. They get that much because refusing an offer of nothing and fighting on is worth more to them than nothing.

They accept nothing, that is, they surrender, only along paths that run against them. They surrender along no path at a cost of 0.4, along 23 percent of paths at 0.5, 28 percent at 1, 34 percent at 1.5, and 63 percent at 2. They accept nothing from the outset only above a cost of about 3.03, about 10 percent of the prize per battle. The paper’s rule would put that line at a cost of 1.74, where fighting to the end stops being worth anything to the humans. But turning the offer down is still worth 5.98 to them there. When the humans make the offers, they keep 6 to 10 of 30.

Below a share of about one quarter (a human cost below 0.4), the deadline moves past the war’s natural length of about 25 battles. When the machine makes the offers, it moves to 48, 68 and 127 rounds at costs of 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1. The war is then more likely fought to a decision than settled (chances of settlement 0.28, 0.105 and 0.005). A settlement, when one comes, comes late, after 32, 52 and 112 battles on average. Its terms are near the ones beliefs would finally agree on, with the humans keeping 3 to 8 of 30. This regime is the same under the paper’s rule and the corrected one.

The quarter is this baseline’s mark at even odds, not a general boundary. No general formula for it was derived, and the book does not claim one.517

Who is right, the beliefs, the length of the war, and the turns at offering. The paper names no true battle odds, so the book reports three: the humans right (the machine wins one battle in three), even, and the machine right (two in three).

  • At a human cost of 1, the chance of settlement is 0.327, 0.789 and 0.979 when the machine makes the offers, and 0.592, 0.891 and 0.987 when the humans do. At 0.5, it is 0.116, 0.658 and 0.972, and 0.184, 0.686 and 0.843.
  • With the machine making the offers, settlement becomes likelier than not between costs of 0.35 and 0.4 if the machine is right. If the humans are right, it does so only above about 1.4; below that, the war mostly ends in the machine’s decisive defeat. When the humans make the offers and are right, the crossing lies between 0.75 and 1.
  • With the beliefs further apart (six and two against two and six), at a human cost of 0.5 and a free machine, the deadline lengthens to 73 when the machine offers and 55 when the humans do. Settlement falls to 0.29 and 0.27. With them closer together (three and two against two and three), the deadline shortens to 15 and 12 and settlement rises to 0.85 and 0.97. Across the beliefs tried, the pattern holds. There is a finite deadline with a free machine, a chance of settlement that the humans’ cost keeps above zero, and coercive terms when the machine makes the offers.
  • The runs on war length hold the human cost at 0.5, the prize at 30 and the start in the middle. A short war, on a line of 6 forts lasting about 9 battles, is almost always decided before learning can force a deal (settlement 0.012 with a free machine). In a long one, on a line of 40 forts, the humans’ expected cost swamps their claim. There a machine making the offers fights, and settlement comes after 5.8 battles on average. The humans keep 0.94 of 30, and they surrender along 64 percent of paths.
  • When the sides take turns making offers, the same sum of costs sets the deadline and it is finite. With a free machine and a human cost of 1, the last battle comes in period 15. Settlement at even odds has a chance of 0.827, and the humans keep 4.14 of 30. At a cost of 0.5, the figures are period 28, 0.672 and 3.55.518

Computed runs: wars against a much stronger machine end early, on average. The book repeats the runs over beliefs for a machine that wins 80, 90, 95 or 99 battles in 100. The machine fights free, and the human cost is 0.5. The deadline does not move, because the plans rest on the two sides’ beliefs. The true odds shape only how the war unfolds. But the war ends long before the deadline, in about 3 to 8 battles on average against deadlines of 12 to 73.

  • Baseline beliefs, machine making the offers: settlement is near certain, but it is surrender, in 0.899 of wars at 80 in 100 and in a share that rounds to 1.000 at 99 in 100. The humans’ share, given settlement, falls from 0.09 of 30 to 0.00.
  • Baseline beliefs, humans making the offers: nobody surrenders, but settlement falls from 0.671 to 0.049, and the machine’s decisive victory takes its place. The humans’ share, given settlement, falls from 0.61 to 0.33 of 30.
  • Beliefs closer together: settlement stays near certain (0.999 or more) without surrender, whoever makes the offers. The humans’ share falls as the machine strengthens, from 0.50 to 0.24 of 30 when the machine offers, and from 1.74 to 0.41 when the humans do.
  • Beliefs far apart: a deal almost never forms (0.016 and 0.009 at 80 in 100, less than two in ten thousand from 90 in 100). The machine’s decisive victory comes first with chance 0.983 to 1.000. Along a run of straight machine wins, the range of deals is still closed one battle from the end.

So the earlier pattern holds at even odds: a chance of settlement that the humans’ cost keeps above zero. At high odds it holds only in name. Under beliefs far apart, that chance falls to about one in seven trillion at 99 in 100.519

Two variants. In the first, the machine’s chance of winning the next battle rises with its lead. Its chance at an even position is unknown to both sides; how steeply its odds rise with its lead is known to both. The variant was first solved with the paper’s simple counting rule for beliefs. It was then re-solved with exact updating, because once the odds move with the lead the counting rule is only an approximation. The results below assume the machine’s true chance at an even position is one half or two in three.

Under exact updating, at the steepest setting tried, settlement rounds to 1.000 in every case. Each side’s chance of outright victory rounds to 0.000. At gentler settings, outright wins appear. With beliefs far apart, the machine wins outright with a chance between 0.781 and 0.801 in the case where that chance is highest. Settlement falls as low as between 0.083 and 0.118. Take baseline beliefs, a free machine and even odds at an even position, at the gentlest setting. There the humans win outright with a chance between 0.347 and 0.371, and settlement falls to between 0.627 and 0.653.

Wherever the machine is ahead when a deal is struck, the humans’ average share is at most 5.86 of 30. That is an average over such deals, not a cap on any one deal. Wars average at most 11.93 battles. The humans’ expected share overall moves by at most 0.77 of 30 between the two ways of updating. The chance of surrender moved too much between them to quote.

In the second variant, the machine is in fact strong, winning 80 or 90 battles in 100, and its starting belief is centred on the truth. Take a free machine and a human cost of 0.5. Against humans with the baseline beliefs (two and four) who make the offers, settlement rises to 0.999 and 1.000. But the humans keep only 0.07 and 0.01 of 30. Against humans with the “closer together” beliefs from above (two and three), settlement becomes surrender when the machine makes the offers, in 0.900 and 0.999 of wars. Against humans with the “far apart” beliefs (two and six), settlement all but vanishes.

How firm the variants are. All 96 rows of the first variant were re-solved with exact updating. Sixty-nine resolve to the printed precision and 27 are reported as ranges. The ranges include an allowance for numerical error that is a practical estimate, not a proved bound, and rounding error is not bounded.

A second program was written independently by a reviewer from another model family that saw neither the first program nor its results. It gave wider ranges that are consistent with the first in all 96 rows and all 672 cells compared. On its own it shows the machine winning outright in the same twelve rows. Agreement within wider ranges is consistency, not a tight replication. No date by which fighting stops is established under exact updating. Only the three pairs of beliefs above were run, and only with one side making every offer. That a high chance of winning ends the war before learning opens the range is shown for these cases alone.520

How the main results were checked. The computation is one short program that a person can rerun in about three seconds. Every figure comes from reasoning back from the end, not from simulation. The one exception is a check by simulation: 20,000 simulated wars at equal costs and even odds, which settle with chance 1.000, as computed. Another Claude model, run separately on a different account, re-ran the program and read its solver line by line. It also solved the baseline and the main cases with a free machine making the offers, using a solver it wrote itself. The two agree at every value both report. No published figure confirms them. The paper never computed unequal costs. And the program follows the paper’s text, whose definitions give numbers that differ from the printed Figures 1 and 3, as noted above. The program and its full output are available from the author.521

The extension’s limits. Both sides learn at the same rate, so sides that learn at different rates lie outside the model. The paper names no true battle odds; the book reports seven values. A rejected offer is always followed by a battle, and offers lie between nothing and the whole prize. A settlement includes surrender, and the chance of surrender is reported separately. A version in which the sides choose with error has not been computed. There is no general boundary between the regimes, and no move removes the other player. And the historical record measures badly the one number that sets both regimes: the human cost per battle.522

What is proved about the extension, and four things that are not

The proofs are written out in a separate file. A Claude reviewer checked them, and so did two reviewers from other model families working from the text alone. Each proof names its assumptions, and “certain” means a deduction from them.

Certain (proved from the model’s assumptions):

  • the corrected rule for the side that answers, and the 2004 paper’s propositions in the amended form the book gives them;
  • the gap in the 2004 paper’s argument, the conditions under which its rule fails, and its failure at every late date (the failure on the printed Figure 3 is certain given how the cells were copied; the failures on the path of play with the text’s definitions are computed);
  • the finite deadline, with an upper limit that depends only on the sum of the costs and the starting beliefs;
  • that every pattern of best play gives the same values, the same settlement offers and the same clear choices, because the value to the side that answers is simply its own choice, each round, between taking nothing now and paying one battle’s cost to go on, judged by its own beliefs, whatever the machine’s cost, beliefs or plan;
  • that the error from starting the backward reasoning at a finite point is bounded; in the baseline, given three computed numbers, every choice through period 24 is the one best play makes, and from period 25 every position settles (for the other cases how fast that error shrinks is proved, but the choices were not checked one by one);
  • that the humans’ expected value lies between what fighting to the end is worth to them (or nothing, if that is more) and the prize times their own chance of winning, so that, as a share of that top figure, they fall short of it by no more than their expected cost of fighting to the end as a share of what they expect to win; and that their value does not rise as the machine holds more forts, as the humans count more machine wins, or as their cost rises;
  • that with the machine at least as optimistic as the humans throughout and making the offers, as in the baseline, the last battle also has a lower limit (80 against an upper limit of 594 with a free machine and a human cost of 0.1; 278 against 1,494 at equal costs of 0.02), so the deadline moves later without end only as both costs fall together (certain for the baseline beliefs; the lower limits are computed from the proved condition);
  • that raising the machine’s cost never moves the last battle or the deadline later; nothing like this is proved for the humans’ cost;
  • that when the humans make the offers, the roles swap (certain for the structure; the shares are computed).

Not proved: four conjectures, three with evidence from computer runs only, and the third with an argument that is not yet a proof:

  1. that the corrected deadline is never later than the deadline under the paper’s rule (not proved; the book’s computer runs support it in the cases tried);
  2. that the humans’ value falls with time when their average belief is held fixed (not proved; the computer runs support it in the cases tried);
  3. that turns at offering give unique values when both costs are above zero (not proved; an argument exists that is not yet a proof);
  4. that the last battle comes sooner as the humans’ cost rises (not proved; the computer runs support it in the cases tried).

How the printed figures were computed awaits a check by a second model family. It goes to the first author before this book states it.523

In the calculation, optimistic entry selects overoptimistic companies (Chapter 5)

Chapter 5 takes a step from Eric Van den Steen’s result about one person choosing among actions to a field of companies racing to build AI. The book checks that step with a short calculation.

Why would the companies that race tend to be the overoptimistic ones?

Think of a jar of coins at a fair, with many people guessing how many it holds. The guesses are honest and miss in both directions. But the people who guess highest are the most likely to have guessed too high. If only those whose guess clears some mark place a bet, the bettors as a group will overestimate. (An illustration of the selection effect.) In the calculation, companies that race because their own estimate cleared a hurdle are selected in the same way. Fear of rivals that rises as a company’s own estimate falls pulls the other way. With enough defensive racers it can cancel the effect.

The premises come first. Each company building AI holds its own estimate of its chance of winning the race. The estimates are honest, with errors that are independent and spread evenly above and below the truth. No company discounts its estimate for the fact that it is the one choosing to race. An optimistic company races when its estimate clears a hurdle. A defensive company races when the threat it sees from rivals clears a hurdle.

From these premises it follows that companies racing because their own estimate cleared the hurdle are, on average, too optimistic. Fear that does not depend on a company’s own estimate only waters this down. Fear tied to the estimate grows as the company’s estimate of its own chance falls. That kind of fear cancels the overoptimism or reverses it once defensive racers are a large enough share of the field. That share is one half when the two hurdles are equal.

The exact values were reproduced by a second method and by a second model family. Simulations of 50,000 fields came out within six times their expected sampling error of them. Carrying Van den Steen’s single chooser to a field of racers is the book’s step, not his theorem. The calculation fixes no company’s behavior, no pattern of best play, and no probability of catastrophe.524

This plain edition does not reproduce the book’s reference list. Every source named here can be found in the full edition, What the Study of War, and History’s Geniuses, Can and Can’t Tell Us About AI Doom. Its references give each work in full and say how it was read: in full, from an abstract, through a review, or at second hand. The footnotes in this edition point to the chapter and section of the full edition where each claim is made. The analysis of the causes of war in Part I rests most heavily on the models the author built with Alastair Smith. They are set out in the full edition’s appendix. The programs behind the appendix, their full output, and the unpublished papers the book cites are available from the author on request.525
